# Task 001: Classify every unclassified census clause

## Objective

Give all 408 census clauses a family or an explicit recorded disposition, so
acceptance gate 1 -- "all candidate clauses have a recorded disposition" -- can
be evaluated at all.

`effect_semantics.py` emits every segmented clause and marks the ones its
matchers do not recognise `pending_classification`. There are 82 of them, and
nothing downstream can be estimated, sequenced or deferred while they have no
family: they are not known to be work, and not known to be ignorable.

This card classifies them deterministically. It does not structure them. A
clause that gains the family `token_create` here is still unstructured
afterwards, and that is the correct outcome -- the point is to convert an
unknown into a scoped known.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] No census row is left with an empty `families` list and no recorded disposition; `clauses_pending_classification` in the census summary reaches zero
- [ ] Bare keyword clauses (47 of the 82: `Trample`, `Flying`, `Flash`, `Vigilance`, `Reach`, `deathtouch`, and comma-joined combinations) are recognised as static keyword grants and disposed of with a stated reason, not silently dropped
- [ ] Mode headers (9 of the 82, e.g. `Choose one -`) are recognised as structural markers rather than effects, and disposed of with a stated reason
- [ ] Named-mechanic clauses (10 of the 82, e.g. `Storied (...)`, `Kicker {2}{W}{W} (...)`) are attributed to the mechanic that owns them, and the disposition names the layer that represents them
- [ ] The 16 remaining clauses map to families that already exist in the vocabulary, with no new family invented: 6 land-ETB replacement, 2 `Ward {N}`, 2 `Enchant creature` attachment, 2 additional-trigger copy, 2 zone-change return/move, 1 granted-abilities, 1 characteristic-defining power
- [ ] Classification is deterministic and contains no card-name or UUID branches (repair-instructions acceptance gate 7); the same Oracle text classifies the same way on every run
- [ ] A test asserts zero rows carry an empty `families` list without a disposition, and fails if a future clause regresses to unclassified
- [ ] A test asserts each of the four disposition kinds the spec defines is reachable, so a disposition that no rule can produce is caught
- [ ] Two serial census generations are byte-identical
- [ ] Frozen artifacts are unchanged, and `effect_records.jsonl` is unchanged -- this card classifies, it does not structure

## Inputs

- src/hobkg/effect_semantics.py

## Modifies

- src/hobkg/effect_semantics.py
- tests/test_effect_census.py

## See Also

- docs/hob_effect_semantics_repair_instructions.md
- docs/hob_orchestration_scope.md

## Requirements

- The four dispositions are the ones the repair instructions define: structured and projected; structured but intentionally not pair-projected, with a reason; deliberately ignored, with a reason; unresolved or nonexecutable, with a reason and provenance. Do not invent a fifth
- A keyword ability is not an effect clause, but it is also not nothing. Dispose of it with a reason that names where keywords are represented, rather than deleting the row
- Do not add a family that no clause needs. The 16 residue all map to existing families; if one genuinely does not, report that rather than widening the vocabulary silently
- Do not touch `effect_records.jsonl` or any frozen artifact. A classification card that changes structured output has done something else as well
- Keyword detection works from a declared keyword set, not from a per-card list

## Output Validation

- python -m pytest tests/test_effect_census.py -q

## Notes

The 82 were measured on 2026-09-02 and bucket as follows:

    47  bare keyword abilities
    16  genuine effects the matchers miss
    10  named mechanic plus reminder parenthetical
     9  mode headers

The 16 in full, with the family each belongs to:

    replacement   This land enters tapped.                    (Lake-town, Goblin-town,
                                                               Iron Hills, Elvenking's
                                                               Halls, Mirkwood)
    replacement   This land enters tapped unless you control an Equipment.
                                                              (The Lonely Mountain)
    keyword       Ward {3} / Ward {2}                         (Gandalf, Lake-town Mariners)
    attachment    Enchant creature                            (Eagle's Rescue,
                                                               Enchanted River's Grotto)
    copy          ...that ability triggers an additional time. (Wizard's Staff, Bifur)
    return_move   Put a card exiled with this Saga into its owner's hand.
                                                              (Roads Go Ever, Ever On)
    return_move   Target creature's owner puts it on their choice of the top or
                  bottom of their library.                    (Uneasy Partings)
    grant_ability Thranduil has all activated abilities of all Elf cards in your
                  graveyard.                                  (Thranduil)
    modify_pt     Esgaroth Garrison's power is equal to the number of creatures
                  you control.                                (Esgaroth Garrison)

Note that `Ward {N}` failed keyword detection only because of its reminder
parenthetical, and `Enchant creature` is an attachment clause whose family is
already carried by the equip tier. Neither is a new capability; both are gaps in
the matcher's reach.

The census emitting zero-family rows at all is a review-driven decision from
Phase 2 pt2 -- the comment at `effect_semantics.py` line 155 records that an
undetected clause must still appear, precisely so it can be counted. This card
is the other half of that decision: counted, then disposed.

# Project Registry: HOB Mechanistic Knowledge Graph

## Description

A mechanistic knowledge graph for Magic: The Gathering -- The Hobbit (HOB): a typed
multigraph of cards, faces, abilities, operations, conditions and gates, plus the
derived card-pair projections over it.

This registry brings the project under `ratchet`, the adaptive epistemic
development orchestrator. The build itself long predates that: phases 0-6 of
`docs/hob-knowledge-graph-build-spec.md` are complete and frozen, and the
effect-semantics overlay of `docs/hob_effect_semantics_repair_instructions.md`
has reached Phase 4f. What changes is how the remaining work is governed  -- 
implement, verify, review, classify, route -- rather than what the work is.

Read `docs/hob_orchestration_scope.md` before working any card. The trailer
defect in section 2 is the first thing to fix and the reason this registry
exists at all.

## Repo Path

`C:/GitHub/magic_the_gathering_theorycrafting`

## Tech Stack

- Python 3.11+
- pydantic 2
- jsonschema 4
- pytest

## Dependencies

- control_plane
- adaptive_orchestrator

## Success Criteria

- Every commit carries a handshake trailer block that git's own parser can read
- The declared epoch onward rebuilds as a ratchet cycle ledger, byte-identically
- A committed phase contract exists, with each semantic invariant mapped to a named test
- The verification command set is declared in configuration, not run by hand
- The two defect classes that recurred in the Phase 6 arc are registered with live guard tests
- Frozen artifacts stay byte-identical, and two serial builds agree

## Default Checks

- python -m pytest -q

Introduction

This document is the ultimate authority for Magic: The Gathering┬« competitive game play. It consists of a series of numbered rules followed by a glossary. Many of the numbered rules are divided into subrules, and each separate rule and subrule of the game has its own number. 1. Game Concepts
┬á
100. General
┬á
100.1. These Magic rules apply to any Magic game with two or more players, including two-player games and multiplayer games.
┬á
100.1a A two-player game is a game that begins with only two players.
┬á
100.1b A multiplayer game is a game that begins with more than two players. See section 8, ΓÇ£Multiplayer Rules.ΓÇ¥
┬á
100.2. To play, each player needs their own deck of traditional Magic cards, small items to represent any tokens and counters, and some way to clearly track life totals.
┬á
100.2a In constructed play (a way of playing in which each player creates their own deck ahead of time), each deck has a minimum deck size of 60 cards. A constructed deck may contain any number of basic land cards and no more than four of any card with a particular English name other than basic land cards. For the purposes of deck construction, cards with interchangeable names have the same English name (see rule 201.3).
┬á
100.2b In limited play (a way of playing in which each player gets the same quantity of unopened Magic product such as booster packs and creates their own deck using only this product and basic land cards), each deck has a minimum deck size of 40 cards. A limited deck may contain as many duplicates of a card as are included with the product.
┬á
100.2c Commander decks are subject to additional deckbuilding restrictions and requirements. See rule 903, ΓÇ£Commander,ΓÇ¥ for details.
┬á
100.2d Some formats and casual play variants allow players to use a supplementary deck of nontraditional Magic cards (see rule 108.2a). These supplementary decks have their own deck construction rules. See rule 717, ΓÇ£Attraction Cards;ΓÇ¥ rule 901, ΓÇ£Planechase;ΓÇ¥ and rule 904, ΓÇ£Archenemy.ΓÇ¥
┬á
100.3. Some cards require coins or traditional dice. Some casual variants require additional items, such as specially designated cards, nontraditional Magic cards, and specialized dice.
┬á
100.4. Each player may also have a sideboard, which is a group of additional cards the player may use to modify their deck between games of a match. Sideboard rules and restrictions for some formats are modified by the Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules (found at WPN.Wizards.com/en/rules-documents).
┬á
100.4a In constructed play, a sideboard may contain no more than fifteen cards. The four-card limit (see rule 100.2a) applies to the combined deck and sideboard.
┬á
100.4b In limited play involving individual players, all cards in a playerΓÇÖs card pool not included in their deck are in that playerΓÇÖs sideboard.
┬á
100.4c In limited play involving the Two-Headed Giant multiplayer variant, all cards in a teamΓÇÖs card pool but not in either playerΓÇÖs deck are in that teamΓÇÖs sideboard.
┬á
100.4d In limited play involving other multiplayer team variants, each card in a teamΓÇÖs card pool but not in any playerΓÇÖs deck is assigned to the sideboard of one of those players. Each player has their own sideboard; cards may not be transferred between players.
┬á
100.5. If a deck must contain at least a certain number of cards, that number is referred to as a minimum deck size. There is no maximum deck size for non-Commander decks.
┬á
100.6. Most Magic tournaments (organized play activities where players compete against other players to win prizes) have additional rules covered in the Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules (found at WPN.Wizards.com/en/rules-documents). These rules may limit the use of some cards, including barring all cards from some older sets.
┬á
100.6a Tournaments usually consist of a series of matches. A two-player match usually involves playing until one player has won two games. A multiplayer match usually consists of only one game.
┬á
100.6b Players can use the Magic Store & Event Locator at Locator.Wizards.com to find tournaments in their area.
┬á
100.7. Certain cards are intended for casual play and may have features and text that arenΓÇÖt covered by these rules. These include Mystery Booster playtest cards, promotional cards and cards in ΓÇ£Un-setsΓÇ¥ that were printed with a silver border, and cards in the UnfinityΓäó expansion that have an acorn symbol at the bottom of the card.
┬á
101. The Magic Golden Rules
┬á
101.1. Whenever a cardΓÇÖs text directly contradicts these rules, the card takes precedence. The card overrides only the rule that applies to that specific situation. The only exception is that a player can concede the game at any time (see rule 104.3a).
┬á
101.2. When a rule or effect allows or directs something to happen, and another effect states that it canΓÇÖt happen, the ΓÇ£canΓÇÖtΓÇ¥ effect takes precedence.
Example: If one effect reads ΓÇ£You may play an additional land this turnΓÇ¥ and another reads ΓÇ£You canΓÇÖt play lands this turn,ΓÇ¥ the effect that precludes you from playing lands wins.
┬á
101.2a Adding abilities to objects and removing abilities from objects donΓÇÖt fall under this rule. (See rule 113.10.)
┬á
101.3. Any part of an instruction thatΓÇÖs impossible to perform is ignored. (In many cases the card will specify consequences for this; if it doesnΓÇÖt, thereΓÇÖs no effect.)
┬á
101.4. If multiple players would make choices and/or take actions at the same time, the active player (the player whose turn it is) makes any choices required, then the next player in turn order (usually the player seated to the active playerΓÇÖs left) makes any choices required, followed by the remaining nonactive players in turn order. Then the actions happen simultaneously. This rule is often referred to as the ΓÇ£Active Player, Nonactive Player (APNAP) orderΓÇ¥ rule.
Example: A card reads ΓÇ£Each player sacrifices a creature.ΓÇ¥ First, the active player chooses a creature they control. Then each of the nonactive players, in turn order, chooses a creature they control. Then all creatures chosen this way are sacrificed simultaneously.
┬á
101.4a If an effect has each player choose a card in a hidden zone, such as their hand or library, those cards may remain face down as theyΓÇÖre chosen. However, each player must clearly indicate which face-down card they are choosing.
┬á
101.4b A player knows the choices made by the previous players when making their choice, except as specified in 101.4a.
┬á
101.4c If a player would make more than one choice at the same time, the player makes the choices in the order specified. If no order is specified, the player chooses the order.
┬á
101.4d If a choice made by a nonactive player causes the active player, or a different nonactive player earlier in the turn order, to have to make a choice, APNAP order is restarted for all outstanding choices.
┬á
101.4e If multiple players would make choices or take actions while starting the game, the starting player is considered the active player and each other player is considered a nonactive player.
┬á
102. Players
┬á
102.1. A player is one of the people in the game. The active player is the player whose turn it is. The other players are nonactive players.
┬á
102.2. In a two-player game, a playerΓÇÖs opponent is the other player.
┬á
102.3. In a multiplayer game between teams, a playerΓÇÖs teammates are the other players on their team, and the playerΓÇÖs opponents are all players not on their team.
┬á
102.4. A spell or ability may use the term ΓÇ£your teamΓÇ¥ as shorthand for ΓÇ£you and/or your teammates.ΓÇ¥ In a game that isnΓÇÖt a multiplayer game between teams, ΓÇ£your teamΓÇ¥ means the same thing as ΓÇ£you.ΓÇ¥
┬á
103. Starting the Game
┬á
103.1. At the start of a game, the players determine which one of them will choose who takes the first turn. In the first game of a match (including a single-game match), the players may use any mutually agreeable method (flipping a coin, rolling dice, etc.) to do so. In a match of several games, the loser of the previous game chooses who takes the first turn. If the previous game was a draw, the player who made the choice in that game makes the choice in this game. The player chosen to take the first turn is the starting player. The gameΓÇÖs default turn order begins with the starting player and proceeds clockwise.
┬á
103.1a In a game using the shared team turns option, there is a starting team rather than a starting player.
┬á
103.1b In an Archenemy game, these methods arenΓÇÖt used to determine who takes the first turn. Rather, the archenemy takes the first turn.
┬á
103.1c One card (Power Play) states that its controller is the starting player. This effect applies after this determination has happened and supersedes these methods.
┬á
103.2. Some games require additional steps that are taken after the starting player has been determined. Perform the actions listed in 103.2aΓÇôe in order, as applicable.
┬á
103.2a If any players are using sideboards (see rule 100.4) or cards being represented by substitute cards (see rule 713), those cards are set aside. After this happens, each playerΓÇÖs deck is considered their starting deck.
┬á
103.2b If any players wish to reveal a card with a companion ability that they own from outside the game, they may do so. A player may reveal no more than one card this way, and they may do so only if their deck fulfills the condition of that cardΓÇÖs companion ability. The revealed card remains outside the game. (See rule 702.139, ΓÇ£Companion.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
103.2c In a Commander game, each player puts their commander from their deck face up into the command zone. See rule 903.6.
┬á
103.2d In a constructed game, each player playing with sticker sheets reveals all of their sticker sheets and chooses three of them at random. In a limited game, each player chooses up to three sticker sheets from among those in the sealed product they opened and reveals them. In either case, that player has access to only the stickers on the chosen sheets during the game, and those sticker sheets remain revealed. (See rule 123, ΓÇ£Stickers.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
103.2e In a Conspiracy Draft game, each player puts any number of conspiracy cards from their sideboard into the command zone. See rule 905.4.
┬á
103.3. After the starting player has been determined and any additional steps performed, each player shuffles their deck so that the cards are in a random order. Each player may then shuffle or cut their opponentsΓÇÖ decks. The playersΓÇÖ decks become their libraries.
┬á
103.3a In a game using one or more supplementary decks of nontraditional cards (see rule 100.2d), each supplementary deckΓÇÖs owner shuffles it so the cards are in a random order. Each player may then shuffle or cut their opponentsΓÇÖ supplementary decks.
┬á
103.4. Each player begins the game with a starting life total of 20. Some variant games have different starting life totals.
┬á
103.4a In a Two-Headed Giant game, each teamΓÇÖs starting life total is 30.
┬á
103.4b In a Vanguard game, each playerΓÇÖs starting life total is 20 plus or minus the life modifier of their vanguard card.
┬á
103.4c In a Commander game, each playerΓÇÖs starting life total is 40.
┬á
103.4d In a two-player Brawl game, each playerΓÇÖs starting life total is 25. In a multiplayer Brawl game, each playerΓÇÖs starting life total is 30.
┬á
103.4e In an Archenemy game, the archenemyΓÇÖs starting life total is 40.
┬á
103.5. Each player draws a number of cards equal to their starting hand size, which is normally seven. (Some effects can modify a playerΓÇÖs starting hand size.) A player who is dissatisfied with their initial hand may take a mulligan. First, the starting player declares whether they will take a mulligan. Then each other player in turn order does the same. Once each player has made a declaration, all players who decided to take mulligans do so at the same time. To take a mulligan, a player shuffles the cards in their hand back into their library, draws a new hand of cards equal to their starting hand size, then puts a number of those cards equal to the number of times that player has taken a mulligan on the bottom of their library in any order. Once a player chooses not to take a mulligan, the remaining cards become that playerΓÇÖs opening hand, and that player may not take any further mulligans. This process is then repeated until no player takes a mulligan. A player can take mulligans until their opening hand would be zero cards, after which they may not take further mulligans.
┬á
103.5a In a Vanguard game, each playerΓÇÖs starting hand size is seven plus or minus the hand modifier of their vanguard card.
┬á
103.5b If an effect allows a player to perform an action ΓÇ£any time [that player] could mulligan,ΓÇ¥ the player may perform that action at a time they would declare whether they will take a mulligan. This need not be in the first round of mulligans. Other players may have already made their mulligan declarations by the time the player has the option to perform this action. If the player performs the action, they then declare whether they will take a mulligan.
┬á
103.5c In a multiplayer game and in any Brawl game, the first mulligan a player takes doesnΓÇÖt count toward the number of cards that player will put on the bottom of their library or the number of mulligans that player may take. Subsequent mulligans are counted toward these numbers as normal.
┬á
103.5d In a multiplayer game using the shared team turns option, first each player on the starting team declares whether that player will take a mulligan, then the players on each other team in turn order do the same. Teammates may consult while making their decisions. Then all mulligans are taken at the same time. A player may take a mulligan even after a teammate has decided to keep their opening hand.
┬á
103.6. Some cards allow a player to take actions with them from their opening hand. Once the mulligan process (see rule 103.5) is complete, the starting player may take any such actions in any order. Then each other player in turn order may do the same.
┬á
103.6a If a card allows a player to begin the game with that card on the battlefield, the player taking this action puts that card onto the battlefield.
┬á
103.6b If a card allows a player to reveal it from their opening hand, the player taking this action does so. The card remains revealed until the first turn begins. Each card may be revealed this way only once.
┬á
103.6c In a multiplayer game using the shared team turns option, first each player on the starting team, in whatever order that team likes, may take such actions. Teammates may consult while making their decisions. Then each player on each other team in turn order does the same.
┬á
103.7. In a Planechase game, the starting player moves the top card of their planar deck off that planar deck and turns it face up. If itΓÇÖs a phenomenon card, the player puts that card on the bottom of their planar deck and repeats this process until a plane card is turned face up. The face-up plane card becomes the starting plane. (See rule 901, ΓÇ£Planechase.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
103.8. The starting player takes their first turn.
┬á
103.8a In a two-player game, the player who plays first skips the draw step (see rule 504, ΓÇ£Draw StepΓÇ¥) of their first turn.
┬á
103.8b In a Two-Headed Giant game, the team who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn.
┬á
103.8c In all other multiplayer games, no player skips the draw step of their first turn.
┬á
104. Ending the Game
┬á
104.1. A game ends immediately when a player wins, when the game is a draw, or when the game is restarted.
┬á
104.2. There are several ways to win the game.
┬á
104.2a A player still in the game wins the game if that playerΓÇÖs opponents have all left the game. This happens immediately and overrides all effects that would preclude that player from winning the game.
┬á
104.2b An effect may state that a player wins the game.
┬á
104.2c In a multiplayer game between teams, a team with at least one player still in the game wins the game if all other teams have left the game. Each player on the winning team wins the game, even if one or more of those players had previously lost that game.
┬á
104.2d In an Emperor game, a team wins the game if its emperor wins the game. (See rule 809.5.)
┬á
104.3. There are several ways to lose the game.
┬á
104.3a A player can concede the game at any time. A player who concedes leaves the game immediately. That player loses the game.
┬á
104.3b If a playerΓÇÖs life total is 0 or less, that player loses the game the next time a player would receive priority. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.)
┬á
104.3c If a player is required to draw more cards than are left in their library, they draw the remaining cards and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.)
┬á
104.3d If a player has ten or more poison counters, that player loses the game the next time a player would receive priority. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.)
┬á
104.3e An effect may state that a player loses the game.
┬á
104.3f If a player would both win and lose the game simultaneously, that player loses the game.
┬á
104.3g In a multiplayer game between teams, a team loses the game if all players on that team have lost the game.
┬á
104.3h In a multiplayer game using the limited range of influence option (see rule 801), an effect that states that a player wins the game instead causes all of that playerΓÇÖs opponents within the playerΓÇÖs range of influence to lose the game. This may not cause the game to end.
┬á
104.3i In an Emperor game, a team loses the game if its emperor loses the game. (See rule 809.5.)
┬á
104.3j In a Commander game, a player whoΓÇÖs been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704. See also rule 903.10.)
┬á
104.3k In a tournament, a player may lose the game as a result of a penalty given by a judge. See rule 100.6.
┬á
104.4. There are several ways for the game to be a draw.
┬á
104.4a If all the players remaining in a game lose simultaneously, the game is a draw.
┬á
104.4b If a game thatΓÇÖs not using the limited range of influence option (including a two-player game) somehow enters a ΓÇ£loopΓÇ¥ of mandatory actions, repeating a sequence of events with no way to stop, the game is a draw. Loops that contain an optional action donΓÇÖt result in a draw.
┬á
104.4c An effect may state that the game is a draw.
┬á
104.4d In a multiplayer game between teams, the game is a draw if all remaining teams lose simultaneously.
┬á
104.4e In a multiplayer game using the limited range of influence option, the effect of a spell or ability that states that the game is a draw causes the game to be a draw for that spell or abilityΓÇÖs controller and all players within their range of influence. Only those players leave the game; the game continues for all other players.
┬á
104.4f In a multiplayer game using the limited range of influence option, if the game somehow enters a ΓÇ£loopΓÇ¥ of mandatory actions, repeating a sequence of events with no way to stop, the game is a draw for each player who controls an object thatΓÇÖs involved in that loop, as well as for each player within the range of influence of any of those players. Only those players leave the game; the game continues for all other players.
┬á
104.4g In a multiplayer game between teams, the game is a draw for a team if the game is a draw for all remaining players on that team.
┬á
104.4h In the Emperor variant, the game is a draw for a team if the game is a draw for its emperor. (See rule 809.5.)
┬á
104.4i In a tournament, all players in the game may agree to an intentional draw. See rule 100.6.
┬á
104.5. If a player loses the game, that player leaves the game. If the game is a draw for a player, that player leaves the game. The multiplayer rules handle what happens when a player leaves the game; see rule 800.4.
┬á
104.6. One card (Karn Liberated) restarts the game. All players still in the game when it restarts then immediately begin a new game. See rule 727, ΓÇ£Restarting the Game.ΓÇ¥
┬á
105. Colors
┬á
105.1. There are five colors in the Magic game: white, blue, black, red, and green.
┬á
105.2. An object can be one or more of the five colors, or it can be no color at all. An object is the color or colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost, regardless of the color of its frame. An objectΓÇÖs color or colors may also be defined by a color indicator or a characteristic-defining ability. See rule 202.2.
┬á
105.2a A monocolored object is exactly one of the five colors.
┬á
105.2b A multicolored object is two or more of the five colors.
┬á
105.2c A colorless object has no color.
┬á
105.3. Effects may change an objectΓÇÖs color or give a color to a colorless object. If an effect gives an object a new color, the new color replaces all previous colors the object had (unless the effect said the object became that color ΓÇ£in additionΓÇ¥ to its other colors). Effects may also make a colored object become colorless.
┬á
105.4. If a player is asked to choose a color, they must choose one of the five colors. ΓÇ£MulticoloredΓÇ¥ is not a color. Neither is ΓÇ£colorless.ΓÇ¥
┬á
105.5. If an effect refers to a color pair, it means exactly two of the five colors. There are ten color pairs: white and blue, white and black, blue and black, blue and red, black and red, black and green, red and green, red and white, green and white, and green and blue.
┬á
106. Mana
┬á
106.1. Mana is the primary resource in the game. Players spend mana to pay costs, usually when casting spells and activating abilities.
┬á
106.1a There are five colors of mana: white, blue, black, red, and green.
┬á
106.1b There are six types of mana: white, blue, black, red, green, and colorless.
┬á
106.2. Mana is represented by mana symbols (see rule 107.4). Mana symbols also represent mana costs (see rule 202).
┬á
106.3. Mana is produced by the effects of mana abilities (see rule 605). It may also be produced by the effects of spells, as well as by the effects of abilities that arenΓÇÖt mana abilities. A spell or ability that produces mana instructs a player to add that mana. If mana is produced by a spell, the source of that mana is that spell. If mana is produced by an ability, the source of that mana is the source of that ability (see rule 113.7).
┬á
106.4. When an effect instructs a player to add mana, that mana goes into a playerΓÇÖs mana pool. From there, it can be used to pay costs immediately, or it can stay in the playerΓÇÖs mana pool as unspent mana. Each playerΓÇÖs mana pool empties at the end of each step and phase, and the player is said to lose this mana. Cards with abilities that produce mana or refer to unspent mana have received errata in the OracleΓäó card reference to no longer explicitly refer to the mana pool.
┬á
106.4a If any mana remains in a playerΓÇÖs mana pool after mana is spent to pay a cost, that player announces what mana is still there.
┬á
106.4b If a player passes priority (see rule 117) while there is mana in their mana pool, that player announces what mana is there.
┬á
106.5. If an ability would produce one or more mana of an undefined type, it produces no mana instead.
Example: Meteor Crater has the ability ΓÇ£{T}: Choose a color of a permanent you control. Add one mana of that color.ΓÇ¥ If you control no colored permanents, activating Meteor CraterΓÇÖs mana ability produces no mana.
┬á
106.6. Some spells or abilities that produce mana restrict how that mana can be spent, have an additional effect that affects the spell or ability that mana is spent on, or create a delayed triggered ability (see rule 603.7a) that triggers when that mana is spent. This doesnΓÇÖt affect the manaΓÇÖs type.
Example: A playerΓÇÖs mana pool contains {R}{G} which can be spent only to cast creature spells. That player activates Doubling CubeΓÇÖs ability, which reads ΓÇ£{3}, {T}: Double the amount of each type of unspent mana you have.ΓÇ¥ The playerΓÇÖs mana pool now has {R}{R}{G}{G} in it, {R}{G} of which can be spent on anything.
┬á
106.6a Some replacement effects increase the amount of mana produced by a spell or ability. In these cases, any restrictions or additional effects created by the spell or ability will apply to all mana produced. If the spell or ability creates a delayed triggered ability that triggers when the mana is spent, a separate delayed triggered ability is created for each mana produced. If the spell or ability creates a continuous effect or replacement effect if the mana is spent, a separate effect is created once for each mana produced.
┬á
106.7. Some abilities produce mana based on the type of mana another permanent or permanents ΓÇ£could produce.ΓÇ¥ The type of mana a permanent could produce at any time includes any type of mana that an ability of that permanent would produce if the ability were to resolve at that time, taking into account any applicable replacement effects in any possible order. Ignore whether any costs of the ability could or could not be paid. If that permanent wouldnΓÇÖt produce any mana under these conditions, or no type of mana can be defined this way, thereΓÇÖs no type of mana it could produce.
Example: Exotic Orchard has the ability ΓÇ£{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce.ΓÇ¥ If your opponent controls no lands, activating Exotic OrchardΓÇÖs mana ability will produce no mana. The same is true if you and your opponent each control no lands other than Exotic Orchards. However, if you control a Forest and an Exotic Orchard, and your opponent controls an Exotic Orchard, then each Exotic Orchard could produce {G}.
┬á
106.8. If an effect would add mana represented by a hybrid mana symbol to a playerΓÇÖs mana pool, that player chooses one half of that symbol. If a colored half is chosen, one mana of that color is added to that playerΓÇÖs mana pool. If a generic half is chosen, an amount of colorless mana represented by that halfΓÇÖs number is added to that playerΓÇÖs mana pool.
┬á
106.9. If an effect would add mana represented by a Phyrexian mana symbol to a playerΓÇÖs mana pool, one mana of the color of that symbol is added to that playerΓÇÖs mana pool.
┬á
106.10. If an effect would add mana represented by a generic mana symbol to a playerΓÇÖs mana pool, that much colorless mana is added to that playerΓÇÖs mana pool.
┬á
106.11. If an effect would add mana represented by one or more snow mana symbols to a playerΓÇÖs mana pool, that much colorless mana is added to that playerΓÇÖs mana pool.
┬á
106.12. To ΓÇ£tap [a permanent] for manaΓÇ¥ is to activate a mana ability of that permanent that includes the {T} symbol in its activation cost. See rule 605, ΓÇ£Mana Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
106.12a An ability that triggers whenever a permanent ΓÇ£is tapped for manaΓÇ¥ or is tapped for mana of a specified type triggers whenever such a mana ability resolves and produces mana or the specified type of mana.
┬á
106.12b A replacement effect that applies if a permanent ΓÇ£is tapped for manaΓÇ¥ or tapped for mana of a specific type and/or amount modifies the mana production event while such an ability is resolving and producing mana or the specified type and/or amount of mana.
┬á
106.13. One card (Drain Power) causes one player to lose unspent mana and another to add ΓÇ£the mana lost this way.ΓÇ¥ (Note that these may be the same player.) 107. Numbers and Symbols
┬á
107.1. The only numbers the Magic game uses are integers.
┬á
107.1a You canΓÇÖt choose a fractional number, deal fractional damage, gain fractional life, and so on. If a spell or ability could generate a fractional number, the spell or ability will tell you whether to round up or down.
┬á
107.1b Most of the time, the Magic game uses only positive numbers and zero. You canΓÇÖt choose a negative number, deal negative damage, gain negative life, and so on. However, itΓÇÖs possible for a game value, such as a creatureΓÇÖs power, to be less than zero. If a calculation or comparison needs to use a negative value, it does so. If a calculation that would determine the result of an effect yields a negative number, zero is used instead, unless that effect doubles, triples, or sets to a specific value a playerΓÇÖs life total or the power and/or toughness of a creature or creature card.
Example: If a 3/4 creature gets -5/-0, itΓÇÖs a -2/4 creature. It doesnΓÇÖt assign damage in combat. Its total power and toughness is 2. Giving it +3/+0 would raise its power to 1.
Example: Viridian Joiner is a 1/2 creature with the ability ΓÇ£{T}: Add an amount of {G} equal to this creatureΓÇÖs power.ΓÇ¥ An effect gives it -2/-0, then its ability is activated. The ability adds no mana to your mana pool.
Example: Chameleon Colossus is a 4/4 creature with the ability ΓÇ£{2}{G}{G}: This creature gets +X/+X until end of turn, where X is its power.ΓÇ¥ An effect gives it -6/-0, then its ability is activated. It remains a -2/4 creature. It doesnΓÇÖt become -4/2.
┬á
107.1c If a rule or ability instructs a player to choose ΓÇ£any number,ΓÇ¥ that player may choose any positive number or zero.
┬á
107.2. If anything needs to use a number that canΓÇÖt be determined, either as a result or in a calculation, it uses 0 instead.
┬á
107.3. Many objects use the letter X as a placeholder for a number that needs to be determined. Some objects have abilities that define the value of X; the rest let their controller choose the value of X.
┬á
107.3a If a spell or activated ability has a mana cost, alternative cost, additional cost, and/or activation cost with an {X}, [-X], or X in it, and the value of X isnΓÇÖt defined by the text of that spell or ability, the controller of that spell or ability chooses and announces the value of X as part of casting the spell or activating the ability. (See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥) While a spell is on the stack, any X in its mana cost or in any alternative cost or additional cost it has equals the announced value. While an activated ability is on the stack, any X in its activation cost equals the announced value.
┬á
107.3b If a player is casting a spell that has an {X} in its mana cost, the value of X isnΓÇÖt defined by the text of that spell, and an effect lets that player cast that spell while paying neither its mana cost nor an alternative cost that includes X, then the only legal choice for X is 0. This doesnΓÇÖt apply to effects that only reduce a cost, even if they reduce it to zero. See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥
┬á
107.3c If a spell or activated ability has an {X}, [-X], or X in its cost and/or its text, and the value of X is defined by the text of that spell or ability, then thatΓÇÖs the value of X while that spell or ability is on the stack. The controller of that spell or ability doesnΓÇÖt get to choose the value. Note that the value of X may change while that spell or ability is on the stack.
┬á
107.3d If a cost associated with a special action, such as a suspend cost or a morph cost, has an {X} or an X in it, the value of X is chosen by the player taking the special action immediately before they pay that cost.
┬á
107.3e If a spell or ability refers to the {X} or X in the mana cost, alternative cost, additional cost, or activation cost of another object, any X in that spell or abilityΓÇÖs text uses the value of X used by the other object.
┬á
107.3f Sometimes X appears in the text of a spell or ability but not in a mana cost, alternative cost, additional cost, or activation cost. If the value of X isnΓÇÖt defined, the controller of the spell or ability chooses the value of X at the appropriate time (either as itΓÇÖs put on the stack or as it resolves).
┬á
107.3g If a card in any zone other than the stack has an {X} in its mana cost, the value of {X} is treated as 0, even if the value of X is defined somewhere within its text.
┬á
107.3h If an effect instructs a player to pay an objectΓÇÖs mana cost that includes {X}, the value of X is treated as 0 unless the object is a spell on the stack. In that case, the value of X is the value chosen or determined for it as the spell was cast.
┬á
107.3i Normally, all instances of X on an object have the same value at any given time.
┬á
107.3j If an object gains an ability, the value of X within that ability is the value defined by that ability, or 0 if that ability doesnΓÇÖt define a value of X. This is an exception to rule 107.3i. This may occur with ability-adding effects, text-changing effects, or copy effects.
┬á
107.3k If an objectΓÇÖs activated ability has an {X}, [-X], or X in its activation cost, the value of X for that ability is independent of any other values of X chosen for that object or for other instances of abilities of that object. This is an exception to rule 107.3i.
┬á
107.3m If an objectΓÇÖs enters-the-battlefield triggered ability or replacement effect refers to X, and the spell that became that object as it resolved had a value of X chosen for any of its costs, the value of X for that ability is the same as the value of X for that spell, although the value of X for that permanent is 0. This is an exception to rule 107.3i.
┬á
107.3n If a delayed triggered ability created by a resolving spell or ability refers to X, X is not defined in the text of that triggered ability, and the spell or ability that created it had a value of X chosen for any of its costs, the value of X for the triggered ability is the same as the value of X for the spell of ability that created it.
┬á
107.3p Some objects use the letter Y in addition to the letter X. Y follows the same rules as X.
┬á
107.4. The mana symbols are {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, {G}, and {C}; the numerical symbols {0}, {1}, {2}, {3}, {4}, and so on; the variable symbol {X}; the hybrid symbols {W/U}, {W/B}, {U/B}, {U/R}, {B/R}, {B/G}, {R/G}, {R/W}, {G/W}, and {G/U}; the monocolored hybrid symbols {2/W}, {2/U}, {2/B}, {2/R}, {2/G}, {C/W}, {C/U}, {C/B}, {C/R}, and {C/G}; the Phyrexian mana symbols {W/P}, {U/P}, {B/P}, {R/P}, and {G/P}; the hybrid Phyrexian symbols {W/U/P}, {W/B/P}, {U/B/P}, {U/R/P}, {B/R/P}, {B/G/P}, {R/G/P}, {R/W/P}, {G/W/P}, and {G/U/P}; and the snow mana symbol {S}.

107.4a There are five primary colored mana symbols: {W} is white, {U} blue, {B} black, {R} red, and {G} green. These symbols are used to represent colored mana, and also to represent colored mana in costs. Colored mana in costs can be paid only with the appropriate color of mana. See rule 202, ΓÇ£Mana Cost and Color.ΓÇ¥

107.4b Numerical symbols (such as {1}) and variable symbols (such as {X}) represent generic mana in costs. Generic mana in costs can be paid with any type of mana. For more information about {X}, see rule 107.3.
┬á
107.4c The colorless mana symbol {C} is used to represent one colorless mana, and also to represent a cost that can be paid only with one colorless mana.
┬á

┬á
107.4e A hybrid mana symbol is also a colored mana symbol, even if one of its components is colorless. Each one represents a cost that can be paid in one of two ways, as represented by the two halves of the symbol. A hybrid symbol such as {W/U} can be paid with either white or blue mana, and a monocolored hybrid symbol such as {2/B} can be paid with either one black mana or two mana of any type. A hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors.
Example: {G/W}{G/W} can be paid by spending {G}{G}, {G}{W}, or {W}{W}.
┬á
107.4f Phyrexian mana symbols are colored mana symbols: {W/P} is white, {U/P} is blue, {B/P} is black, {R/P} is red, and {G/P} is green. A Phyrexian mana symbol represents a cost that can be paid either with one mana of its color or by paying 2 life. There are also ten hybrid Phyrexian mana symbols. A hybrid Phyrexian mana symbol represents a cost that can be paid with one mana of either of its component colors or by paying 2 life. A hybrid Phyrexian mana symbol is both of its component colors.
Example: {W/P}{W/P} can be paid by spending {W}{W}, by spending {W} and paying 2 life, or by paying 4 life.
┬á
107.4g In rules text, the Phyrexian symbol {H} with no colored background means any of the fifteen Phyrexian mana symbols.
┬á
107.4h When used in a cost, the snow mana symbol {S} represents a cost that can be paid with one mana of any type produced by a snow source (see rule 106.3). Effects that reduce the amount of generic mana you pay donΓÇÖt affect {S} costs. The {S} symbol can also be used to refer to mana of any type produced by a snow source spent to pay a cost. 107.5. The tap symbol is {T}. The tap symbol in an activation cost means ΓÇ£Tap this permanent.ΓÇ¥ A permanent thatΓÇÖs already tapped canΓÇÖt be tapped again to pay the cost. A creatureΓÇÖs activated ability with the tap symbol in its activation cost canΓÇÖt be activated unless the creature has been under its controllerΓÇÖs control continuously since their most recent turn began. 107.6. The untap symbol is {Q}. The untap symbol in an activation cost means ΓÇ£Untap this permanent.ΓÇ¥ A permanent thatΓÇÖs already untapped canΓÇÖt be untapped again to pay the cost. A creatureΓÇÖs activated ability with the untap symbol in its activation cost canΓÇÖt be activated unless the creature has been under its controllerΓÇÖs control continuously since their most recent turn began. 107.7. Each activated ability of a planeswalker has a loyalty symbol in its cost. Positive loyalty symbols point upward and feature a plus sign followed by a number. The same is true of the power/toughness box printed within that striation, indicated here as ΓÇ£[P/T].ΓÇ¥ See rule 711, ΓÇ£Leveler Cards.ΓÇ¥

107.8a ΓÇ£{LEVEL N1-N2} [Abilities] [P/T]ΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£As long as this creature has at least N1 level counters on it, but no more than N2 level counters on it, it has base power and toughness [P/T] and has [abilities].ΓÇ¥

107.8b ΓÇ£{LEVEL N3+} [Abilities] [P/T]ΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£As long as this creature has N3 or more level counters on it, it has base power and toughness [P/T] and has [abilities].ΓÇ¥

107.11. The Planeswalker symbol is {PW}. It appears on one face of the planar die used in the Planechase casual variant. It has five tines at the top and tapers to a point at the bottom. See rule 901, ΓÇ£Planechase.ΓÇ¥

107.12. The chaos symbol is {CHAOS}. It appears on one face of the planar die used in the Planechase casual variant, as well as in abilities that refer to the results of rolling the planar die. It looks like a swirling vortex. See rule 901, ΓÇ£Planechase.ΓÇ¥

107.13. A color indicator is a circular symbol that appears to the left of the type line on some cards. The color of the symbol defines the cardΓÇÖs color or colors. See rule 202, ΓÇ£Mana Cost and Color.ΓÇ¥

108. Cards
┬á
108.1. Use the Oracle card reference when determining a cardΓÇÖs wording. A cardΓÇÖs Oracle text can be found using the Gatherer card database at Gatherer.Wizards.com.
┬á
108.2. When a rule or text on a card refers to a ΓÇ£card,ΓÇ¥ it means only a Magic card or an object represented by a Magic card.
┬á
108.2a Most Magic games use only traditional Magic cards, which measure approximately 2.5 inches (6.3 cm) by 3.5 inches (8.8 cm). Traditional Magic cards are included in playersΓÇÖ decks. Certain formats also use nontraditional Magic cards. Nontraditional Magic cards are not included in playersΓÇÖ decks. They may be used in supplementary decks. 108.2b Tokens arenΓÇÖt considered cardsΓÇöeven a card-sized game supplement that represents a token isnΓÇÖt considered a card for rules purposes.

108.3. The owner of a card in the game is the player who started the game with it in their deck. If a card is brought into the game from outside the game rather than starting in a playerΓÇÖs deck, its owner is the player who brought it into the game. If a card starts the game in the command zone, its owner is the player who put it into the command zone to start the game. 108.3a In a Planechase game using the single planar deck option, the planar controller is considered to be the owner of all cards in the planar deck. See rule 901.6.
┬á
108.3b Some spells and abilities allow a player to take cards they own from outside the game and bring them into the game. (See rule 400.11b.) If a card outside that game is involved in a Magic game, its owner is determined as described in rule 108.3. If a card outside that game is in the sideboard of a Magic game (see rule 100.4), its owner is considered to be the player who started the game with it in their sideboard. In all other cases, the owner of a card outside the game is its legal owner.
┬á
108.4. A card doesnΓÇÖt have a controller unless that card represents a permanent or spell; in those cases, its controller is determined by the rules for permanents or spells. See rules 110.2 and 112.2.
┬á
108.4a If anything asks for the controller of a card that doesnΓÇÖt have one (because itΓÇÖs not a permanent or spell), use its owner instead.

If an effect would bring a nontraditional Magic card other than a dungeon card (see rule 309, ΓÇ£DungeonsΓÇ¥) into the game from outside the game, it doesnΓÇÖt; that card remains outside the game.

109. Objects
┬á
109.1. An object is an ability on the stack, a card, a copy of a card, a token, a spell, a permanent, or an emblem.
┬á
109.2. If a spell or ability uses a description of an object that includes a card type or subtype, but doesnΓÇÖt refer to a specific zone or include the word ΓÇ£card,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£spell,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£source,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£scheme,ΓÇ¥ it means a permanent of that card type or subtype on the battlefield.

109.2b If a spell or ability uses a description of an object that includes the word ΓÇ£spell,ΓÇ¥ it means a spell matching that description on the stack.

109.3. An objectΓÇÖs characteristics are name, mana cost, color, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, abilities, power, toughness, loyalty, defense, hand modifier, and life modifier. Objects can have some or all of these characteristics. Any other information about an object isnΓÇÖt a characteristic. For example, characteristics donΓÇÖt include whether a permanent is tapped, a spellΓÇÖs target, an objectΓÇÖs owner or controller, what an Aura enchants, and so on.

109.4. Only objects on the stack or on the battlefield have a controller. Objects that are neither on the stack nor on the battlefield arenΓÇÖt controlled by any player. See rule 108.4. There are six exceptions to this rule:
┬á
109.4a The controller of a mana ability is determined as though it were on the stack. See rule 605, ΓÇ£Mana Abilities.ΓÇ¥

109.4b A triggered ability that has triggered but is waiting to be placed on the stack is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered, unless itΓÇÖs a delayed triggered ability. To determine the controller of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7dΓÇôf. See also rule 603, ΓÇ£Handling Triggered Abilities.ΓÇ¥

109.4c An emblem is controlled by the player who puts it into the command zone. See rule 114, ΓÇ£Emblems.ΓÇ¥

The words ΓÇ£youΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£yourΓÇ¥ on an object refer to the objectΓÇÖs controller, its would-be controller (if a player is attempting to play, cast, or activate it), or its owner (if it has no controller). For a static ability, this is the current controller of the object itΓÇÖs on. For an activated ability, this is the player who activated the ability. For a triggered ability, this is the controller of the object when the ability triggered, unless itΓÇÖs a delayed triggered ability. To determine the controller of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7dΓÇôf.

110. Permanents
┬á
110.1. A permanent is a card or token on the battlefield. A permanent remains on the battlefield indefinitely. A card or token becomes a permanent as it enters the battlefield and it stops being a permanent as itΓÇÖs moved to another zone by an effect or rule.

110.2. A permanentΓÇÖs owner is the same as the owner of the card that represents it (unless itΓÇÖs a token; see rule 111.2). A permanentΓÇÖs controller is, by default, the player under whose control it entered the battlefield. Every permanent has a controller.

(This distinction is relevant in multiplayer games; see rule 800.4c.)

Some kindred cards can enter the battlefield and some canΓÇÖt, depending on their other card types. See section 3, ΓÇ£Card Types.ΓÇ¥

110.4b The term ΓÇ£permanent spellΓÇ¥ is used to refer to a spell that will enter the battlefield as a permanent as part of its resolution. Specifically, it means an artifact, battle, creature, enchantment, or planeswalker spell.

110.5. A permanentΓÇÖs status is its physical state. There are four status categories, each of which has two possible values: tapped/untapped, flipped/unflipped, face up/face down, and phased in/phased out. Each permanent always has one of these values for each of these categories.

Example: Dimir Doppelganger says ΓÇ£{1}{U}{B}: Exile target creature card from a graveyard. This creature becomes a copy of that card, except it has this ability.ΓÇ¥ It becomes a copy of Jushi Apprentice, a flip card. Through use of Jushi ApprenticeΓÇÖs ability, this creature flips, making it a copy of Tomoya the Revealer with the Dimir Doppelganger ability. 111. Tokens

111.1. Some effects put tokens onto the battlefield. A token is a marker used to represent any permanent that isnΓÇÖt represented by a card.

111.3. The spell or ability that creates a token may define the values of any number of characteristics for the token. 111.11. 112. Spells
┬á
112.1. A spell is a card on the stack. As the first step of being cast (see rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting SpellsΓÇ¥), the card becomes a spell and is moved to the top of the stack from the zone it was in, which is usually its ownerΓÇÖs hand. (See rule 405, ΓÇ£Stack.ΓÇ¥) A spell remains on the stack as a spell until it resolves (see rule 608, ΓÇ£Resolving Spells and AbilitiesΓÇ¥), is countered (see rule 701.6), or otherwise leaves the stack. For more information, see section 6, ΓÇ£Spells, Abilities, and Effects.ΓÇ¥

112.1a A copy of a spell is also a spell, even if it has no card associated with it. See rule 707.10.
┬á
112.1b Some effects allow a player to cast a copy of a card; if the player does, that copy is a spell as well. See rule 707.12.

112.2. A spellΓÇÖs owner is the same as the owner of the card that represents it, unless itΓÇÖs a copy. In that case, the owner of the spell is the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A spellΓÇÖs controller is, by default, the player who put it on the stack. Every spell has a controller.

112.2a Some effects instruct a player to create a copy of a card and say they may cast it. In that case, the owner of that copy is the player who is instructed to create it and given permission to cast it.

113. Abilities
┬á
113.1. An ability can be one of three things:
┬á
113.1a An ability can be a characteristic an object has that lets it affect the game. An objectΓÇÖs abilities are defined by its rules text or by the effect that created it. Abilities can also be granted to objects by rules or effects. (Effects that grant abilities usually use the words ΓÇ£has,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£have,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£gains,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£gain.ΓÇ¥) Abilities generate effects. (See rule 609, ΓÇ£Effects.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
113.1b An ability can be something that a player has that changes how the game affects the player. A player normally has no abilities unless granted to that player by effects.
┬á
113.1c An ability can be an activated or triggered ability on the stack. This kind of ability is an object. (See section 6, ΓÇ£Spells, Abilities, and Effects.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
113.2. Abilities can affect the objects theyΓÇÖre on. They can also affect other objects and/or players.
┬á
113.2a Abilities can be beneficial or detrimental.
Example: ΓÇ£This creature canΓÇÖt blockΓÇ¥ is an ability.
┬á
113.2b An additional cost or alternative cost to cast a card is an ability of the card.
┬á
113.2c An object may have multiple abilities. If the object is represented by a card, then aside from certain defined abilities that may be strung together on a single line (see rule 702, ΓÇ£Keyword AbilitiesΓÇ¥), each paragraph break in a cardΓÇÖs text marks a separate ability. If the object is not represented by a card, the effect that created it may have given it multiple abilities. An object may also be granted additional abilities by a spell or ability. If an object has multiple instances of the same ability, each instance functions independently. This may or may not produce more effects than a single instance; refer to the specific ability for more information.
┬á
113.2d Abilities can generate one-shot effects or continuous effects. Some continuous effects are replacement effects or prevention effects. See rule 609, ΓÇ£Effects.ΓÇ¥
┬á
113.3. There are four general categories of abilities:
┬á
113.3a Spell abilities are abilities that are followed as instructions while an instant or sorcery spell is resolving. Any text on an instant or sorcery spell is a spell ability unless itΓÇÖs an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability that fits the criteria described in rule 113.6.
┬á
113.3b Activated abilities have a cost and an effect. They are written as ΓÇ£[Cost]: [Effect.] [Activation instructions (if any).]ΓÇ¥ A player may activate such an ability whenever they have priority. Doing so puts it on the stack, where it remains until itΓÇÖs countered, it resolves, or it otherwise leaves the stack. See rule 602, ΓÇ£Activating Activated Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
113.3c Triggered abilities have a trigger condition and an effect. They are written as ΓÇ£[Trigger condition], [effect],ΓÇ¥ and include (and usually begin with) the word ΓÇ£when,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£whenever,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£at.ΓÇ¥ Whenever the trigger event occurs, the ability is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority and stays there until itΓÇÖs countered, it resolves, or it otherwise leaves the stack. See rule 603, ΓÇ£Handling Triggered Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
113.3d Static abilities are written as statements. TheyΓÇÖre simply true. Static abilities create continuous effects which are active while the permanent with the ability is on the battlefield and has the ability, or while the object with the ability is in the appropriate zone. See rule 604, ΓÇ£Handling Static Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
113.4. Some activated abilities and some triggered abilities are mana abilities. Mana abilities follow special rules: They donΓÇÖt use the stack, and, under certain circumstances, a player can activate mana abilities even if they donΓÇÖt have priority. See rule 605, ΓÇ£Mana Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
113.5. Some activated abilities are loyalty abilities. Loyalty abilities follow special rules: A player may activate a loyalty ability of a permanent they control any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn, but only if no player has previously activated a loyalty ability of that permanent that turn. See rule 606, ΓÇ£Loyalty Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
113.6. Abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that object is on the stack. Abilities of all other objects usually function only while that object is on the battlefield. The exceptions are as follows:
┬á
113.6a Characteristic-defining abilities function everywhere, even outside the game and before the game begins. (See rule 604.3.)
┬á
113.6b An ability that states which zones it functions in functions only from those zones.
┬á
113.6c An ability that states which zones it doesnΓÇÖt function in functions everywhere except for the specified zones, even outside the game and before the game begins.
┬á
113.6d An objectΓÇÖs ability that allows a player to pay an alternative cost rather than its mana cost or otherwise modifies what that particular object costs to cast functions on the stack.
┬á
113.6e An objectΓÇÖs ability that restricts or modifies how that particular object can be played or cast functions in any zone from which it could be played or cast and also on the stack. An objectΓÇÖs ability that grants it another ability that restricts or modifies how that particular object can be played or cast functions only on the stack.
┬á
113.6f An objectΓÇÖs ability that restricts or modifies what zones that particular object can be played or cast from functions everywhere, even outside the game.
┬á
113.6g An objectΓÇÖs ability that states it canΓÇÖt be countered or canΓÇÖt be copied functions on the stack.
┬á
113.6h An objectΓÇÖs ability that modifies how that particular object enters the battlefield functions as that object is entering the battlefield. See rule 614.12.
┬á
113.6i An objectΓÇÖs ability that states counters canΓÇÖt be put on that object functions as that object is entering the battlefield in addition to functioning while that object is on the battlefield.
┬á
113.6j An objectΓÇÖs activated ability that has a cost that canΓÇÖt be paid while the object is on the battlefield functions from any zone in which its cost can be paid.
┬á
113.6k A trigger condition that canΓÇÖt trigger from the battlefield functions in all zones it can trigger from. Other trigger conditions of the same triggered ability may function in different zones.
Example: Absolver Thrull has the ability ΓÇ£When this creature enters or the creature it haunts dies, destroy target enchantment.ΓÇ¥ The first trigger condition functions from the battlefield and the second trigger condition functions from the exile zone. (See rule 702.55, ΓÇ£Haunt.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
113.6m An ability whose cost or effect specifies that it moves the object itΓÇÖs on out of a particular zone functions only in that zone, unless its trigger condition or a previous part of its cost or effect specifies that the object is put into that zone or, if the object is an Aura, that the object it enchants leaves the battlefield. ┬á
113.6n An ability that modifies the rules for deck construction functions before the game begins. Such an ability modifies not just the Comprehensive Rules, but also the Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules and any other documents that set the deck construction rules for a specific format. However, such an ability canΓÇÖt affect the format legality of a card, including whether itΓÇÖs banned or restricted. The current Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules can be found at WPN.Wizards.com/en/rules-documents.

113.6p Abilities of emblems, plane cards, vanguard cards, scheme cards, and conspiracy cards function in the command zone. See rule 114, ΓÇ£EmblemsΓÇ¥; rule 901, ΓÇ£PlanechaseΓÇ¥; rule 902, ΓÇ£VanguardΓÇ¥; rule 904, ΓÇ£ArchenemyΓÇ¥; and rule 905, ΓÇ£Conspiracy Draft.ΓÇ¥
┬á
113.7. The source of an ability is the object that generated it. The source of an activated ability on the stack is the object whose ability was activated. The source of a triggered ability (other than a delayed triggered ability) on the stack, or one that has triggered and is waiting to be put on the stack, is the object whose ability triggered. To determine the source of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7dΓÇôf.
┬á
113.7a Once activated or triggered, an ability exists on the stack independently of its source. Destruction or removal of the source after that time wonΓÇÖt affect the ability. Note that some abilities cause a source to do something (for example, ΓÇ£This creature deals 1 damage to any targetΓÇ¥) rather than the ability doing anything directly. In these cases, any activated or triggered ability that references information about the source for use while announcing an activated ability or putting a triggered ability on the stack checks that information when the ability is put onto the stack. Otherwise, it will check that information when it resolves. In both instances, if the source is no longer in the zone itΓÇÖs expected to be in at that time, its last known information is used. The source can still perform the action even though it no longer exists.
┬á
113.8. The controller of an activated ability on the stack is the player who activated it. The controller of a triggered ability on the stack (other than a delayed triggered ability) is the player who controlled the abilityΓÇÖs source when it triggered, or, if it had no controller, the player who owned the abilityΓÇÖs source when it triggered. To determine the controller of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7dΓÇôf.
┬á
113.9. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack arenΓÇÖt spells, and therefore canΓÇÖt be countered by anything that counters only spells. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. Static abilities donΓÇÖt use the stack and thus canΓÇÖt be countered at all.
┬á
113.10. Effects can add or remove abilities of objects. An effect that adds an ability will state that the object ΓÇ£gainsΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£hasΓÇ¥ that ability, or similar. An effect that removes an ability will state that the object ΓÇ£losesΓÇ¥ that ability.

113.10a An effect that adds an activated ability may include activation instructions for that ability. These instructions become part of the ability thatΓÇÖs added to the object.

113.10b Effects that remove an ability remove all instances of it.
┬á
113.10c If two or more effects add and remove the same ability, in general the most recent one prevails. See rule 613 for more information about the interaction of continuous effects.
┬á
113.11. Effects can stop an object from having a specified ability. These effects say that the object ΓÇ£canΓÇÖt haveΓÇ¥ that ability. If the object has that ability, it loses it. ItΓÇÖs also impossible for an effect or keyword counter to add that ability to the object. 113.12. An effect that sets an objectΓÇÖs characteristic, or simply states a quality of that object, is different from an ability granted by an effect. When an object ΓÇ£gainsΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£hasΓÇ¥ an ability, that ability can be removed by another effect. 114. Emblems
┬á
114.1. Some effects put emblems into the command zone. An emblem is a marker used to represent an object that has one or more abilities, but usually no other characteristics.
┬á
114.2. An effect that creates an emblem is written ΓÇ£[Player] gets an emblem with [ability].ΓÇ¥ This means that [player] puts an emblem with [ability] into the command zone. The emblem is both owned and controlled by that player.

114.3. An emblem has no characteristics other than the abilities defined by the effect that created it. In particular, an emblem has no types, no mana cost, and no color. Most emblems also have no name.

114.4. Abilities of emblems function in the command zone.

114.5. An emblem is neither a card nor a permanent. Emblem isnΓÇÖt a card type.

115. Targets
┬á
115.1. Some spells and abilities require their controller to choose one or more targets for them. The targets are object(s) and/or player(s) the spell or ability will affect. These targets are declared as part of the process of putting the spell or ability on the stack. The targets canΓÇÖt be changed except by another spell or ability that explicitly says it can do so.

115.1a An instant or sorcery spell is targeted if its spell ability identifies something it will affect by using the phrase ΓÇ£target [something],ΓÇ¥ where the ΓÇ£somethingΓÇ¥ is a phrase that describes an object and/or player. The target(s) are chosen as the spell is cast; see rule 601.2c. (If an activated or triggered ability of an instant or sorcery uses the word target, that ability is targeted, but the spell is not.)
Example: A sorcery card has the ability ΓÇ£When you cycle this card, target creature gets -1/-1 until end of turn.ΓÇ¥ This triggered ability is targeted, but that doesnΓÇÖt make the card itΓÇÖs on targeted.

An Aura permanent doesnΓÇÖt target anything; only the spell is targeted. (An activated or triggered ability of an Aura permanent can also be targeted.)

115.1c An activated ability is targeted if it identifies something it will affect by using the phrase ΓÇ£target [something],ΓÇ¥ where the ΓÇ£somethingΓÇ¥ is a phrase that describes an object and/or player. The target(s) are chosen as the ability is activated; see rule 602.2b.

115.1d A triggered ability is targeted if it identifies something it will affect by using the phrase ΓÇ£target [something],ΓÇ¥ where the ΓÇ£somethingΓÇ¥ is a phrase that describes an object and/or player. The target(s) are chosen as the ability is put on the stack; see rule 603.3d.

115.1e Some keyword abilities, such as equip and modular, represent targeted activated or triggered abilities, and some keyword abilities, such as mutate, cause spells to have targets. In those cases, the phrase ΓÇ£target [something]ΓÇ¥ appears in the rule for that keyword ability rather than in the ability itself. (The keywordΓÇÖs reminder text will often contain the word ΓÇ£target.ΓÇ¥) See rule 702, ΓÇ£Keyword Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
115.2. Only permanents are legal targets for spells and abilities, unless a spell or ability (a) specifies that it can target an object in another zone or a player, or (b) targets an object that canΓÇÖt exist on the battlefield, such as a spell or ability. See also rule 115.4.

115.3. The same target canΓÇÖt be chosen multiple times for any one instance of the word ΓÇ£targetΓÇ¥ on a spell or ability. 115.4. Some spells and abilities that refer to damage require ΓÇ£any target,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£another target,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£two targets,ΓÇ¥ or similar rather than ΓÇ£target [something].ΓÇ¥ These targets may be creatures, players, planeswalkers, or battles. 115.5. A spell or ability on the stack is an illegal target for itself.
┬á
115.6. A spell or ability that requires targets may allow zero targets to be chosen. Such a spell or ability is still said to require targets, but that spell or ability is targeted only if one or more targets have been chosen for it.
┬á
115.7. Some effects allow a player to change the target(s) of a spell or ability, and other effects allow a player to choose new targets for a spell or ability.
┬á
115.7a If an effect allows a player to ΓÇ£change the target(s)ΓÇ¥ of a spell or ability, each target can be changed only to another legal target. If a target canΓÇÖt be changed to another legal target, the original target is unchanged, even if the original target is itself illegal by then. If all the targets arenΓÇÖt changed to other legal targets, none of them are changed.
┬á
115.7b If an effect allows a player to ΓÇ£change a targetΓÇ¥ of a spell or ability, the process described in rule 115.7a is followed, except that only one of those targets may be changed (rather than all of them or none of them).
┬á
115.7c If an effect allows a player to ΓÇ£change any targetsΓÇ¥ of a spell or ability, the process described in rule 115.7a is followed, except that any number of those targets may be changed (rather than all of them or none of them).
┬á
115.7d If an effect allows a player to ΓÇ£choose new targetsΓÇ¥ for a spell or ability, the player may leave any number of the targets unchanged, even if those targets would be illegal. If the player chooses to change some or all of the targets, the new targets must be legal and must not cause any unchanged targets to become illegal.
┬á
115.7e When changing targets or choosing new targets for a spell or ability, only the final set of targets is evaluated to determine whether the change is legal.
Example: Arc Trail is a sorcery that reads ΓÇ£Arc Trail deals 2 damage to any target and 1 damage to any other target.ΓÇ¥ The current targets of Arc Trail are Runeclaw Bear and Llanowar Elves, in that order. You cast Redirect, an instant that reads ΓÇ£You may choose new targets for target spell,ΓÇ¥ targeting Arc Trail. You can change the first target to Llanowar Elves and change the second target to Runeclaw Bear.
┬á
115.7f A spell or ability may ΓÇ£divideΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£distributeΓÇ¥ an effect (such as damage or counters) among one or more targets. When changing targets or choosing new targets for that spell or ability, the original division canΓÇÖt be changed.
┬á
115.8. Modal spells and abilities may have different targeting requirements for each mode. An effect that allows a player to change the target(s) of a modal spell or ability, or to choose new targets for a modal spell or ability, doesnΓÇÖt allow that player to change its mode. (See rule 700.2.)
┬á
115.9. Some objects check what another spell or ability is targeting. Depending on the wording, these may check the current state of the targets, the state of the targets at the time they were selected, or both.
┬á
115.9a An object that looks for a ΓÇ£[spell or ability] with [a number of] targetsΓÇ¥ checks the number of times any object or player was chosen as the target of that spell or ability when it was put on the stack, not the number of its targets that are currently legal. If the same object or player became a target more than once, each of those instances is counted separately.
┬á
115.9b An object that looks for a ΓÇ£[spell or ability] that targets [something]ΓÇ¥ checks the current state of that spell or abilityΓÇÖs targets. If an object it targets is still in the zone itΓÇÖs expected to be in or a player it targets is still in the game, that targetΓÇÖs current information is used, even if itΓÇÖs not currently legal for that spell or ability. If an object it targets is no longer in the zone itΓÇÖs expected to be in or a player it targets is no longer in the game, that target is ignored; its last known information is not used.
┬á
115.9c An object that looks for a ΓÇ£[spell or ability] that targets only [something]ΓÇ¥ checks the number of different objects or players that were chosen as targets of that spell or ability when it was put on the stack (as modified by effects that changed those targets), not the number of those objects or players that are currently legal targets. If that number is one (even if the spell or ability targets that object or player multiple times), the current state of that spell or abilityΓÇÖs target is checked as described in rule 115.9b.
┬á
115.10. Spells and abilities can affect objects and players they donΓÇÖt target. In general, those objects and players arenΓÇÖt chosen until the spell or ability resolves. See rule 608, ΓÇ£Resolving Spells and Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
115.10a Just because an object or player is being affected by a spell or ability doesnΓÇÖt make that object or player a target of that spell or ability. Unless that object or player is identified by the word ΓÇ£targetΓÇ¥ in the text of that spell or ability, or the rule for that keyword ability, itΓÇÖs not a target.
┬á
115.10b In particular, the word ΓÇ£youΓÇ¥ in an objectΓÇÖs text doesnΓÇÖt indicate a target.
┬á
116. Special Actions
┬á
116.1. Special actions are actions a player may take when they have priority that donΓÇÖt use the stack. These are not to be confused with turn-based actions and state-based actions, which the game generates automatically. (See rule 703, ΓÇ£Turn-Based Actions,ΓÇ¥ and rule 704, ΓÇ£State-Based Actions.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
116.2. There are twelve special actions:
┬á
116.2a Playing a land is a special action. To play a land, a player puts that land onto the battlefield from the zone it was in (usually that playerΓÇÖs hand). By default, a player can take this action only once during each of their turns. A player can take this action any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn. See rule 305, ΓÇ£Lands.ΓÇ¥
┬á
116.2b Turning a face-down creature face up is a special action. A player can take this action any time they have priority. See rule 708, ΓÇ£Face-Down Spells and Permanents.ΓÇ¥
┬á
116.2c Some effects allow a player to take an action at a later time, usually to end a continuous effect or to stop a delayed triggered ability from triggering. Doing so is a special action. A player can take such an action any time they have priority, unless that effect specifies another timing restriction, for as long as the effect allows it.
┬á
116.2d Some effects from static abilities allow a player to take an action to ignore the effect from that ability for a duration. Doing so is a special action. A player can take such an action any time they have priority.
┬á
116.2e One card (Circling Vultures) has the ability ΓÇ£You may discard Circling Vultures any time you could cast an instant.ΓÇ¥ Doing so is a special action. A player can take such an action any time they have priority.
┬á
116.2f A player who has a card with suspend in their hand may exile that card. This is a special action. A player can take this action any time they have priority, but only if they could begin to cast that card by putting it onto the stack. See rule 702.62, ΓÇ£Suspend.ΓÇ¥
┬á
116.2g A player who has chosen a companion may pay {3} to put that card from outside the game into their hand. This is a special action. A player can take this action any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn, but only if they havenΓÇÖt done so yet this game. (See rule 702.139, ΓÇ£Companion.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
116.2h A player who has a card with foretell in their hand may pay {2} and exile that card face down. This is a special action. A player may take this action any time they have priority during their turn. See rule 702.143, ΓÇ£Foretell.ΓÇ¥
┬á
116.2i In a Planechase game, rolling the planar die is a special action. A player can take this action any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn. Taking this action costs a player an amount of mana equal to the number of times they have previously taken this action on that turn. Note that this number wonΓÇÖt be equal to the number of times the player has rolled the planar die that turn if an effect has caused the player to roll the planar die that turn. See rule 901, ΓÇ£Planechase.ΓÇ¥
┬á
116.2j In a Conspiracy Draft game, turning a face-down conspiracy card in the command zone face up is a special action. A player can take this action any time they have priority. See rule 905.4a.
┬á
116.2k A player who has a card with plot in their hand may exile that card. This is a special action. A player can take this action any time they have priority during their own turn while the stack is empty. See rule 702.170, ΓÇ£Plot.ΓÇ¥
┬á
116.2m A player who controls a permanent that has one or more locked halves (see rule 709.5) may pay the mana cost of a locked half of that permanent to give that permanent the appropriate unlocked designation. This cost is referred to as an ΓÇ£unlock cost.ΓÇ¥ A player can take this action any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn.
┬á
116.3. If a player takes a special action, that player receives priority afterward.
┬á
117. Timing and Priority
┬á
117.1. Unless a spell or ability is instructing a player to take an action, which player can take actions at any given time is determined by a system of priority. The player with priority may cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions.
┬á
117.1a A player may cast an instant spell any time they have priority. A player may cast a noninstant spell during their main phase any time they have priority and the stack is empty.
┬á
117.1b A player may activate an activated ability any time they have priority.
┬á
117.1c A player may take some special actions any time they have priority. A player may take other special actions during their main phase any time they have priority and the stack is empty. See rule 116, ΓÇ£Special Actions.ΓÇ¥
┬á
117.1d A player may activate a mana ability whenever they have priority, whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment, or whenever a rule or effect asks for a mana payment (even in the middle of casting or resolving a spell or activating or resolving an ability).
┬á
117.2. Other kinds of abilities and actions are automatically generated or performed by the game rules, or are performed by players without receiving priority.
┬á
117.2a Triggered abilities can trigger at any time, including while a spell is being cast, an ability is being activated, or a spell or ability is resolving. (See rule 603, ΓÇ£Handling Triggered Abilities.ΓÇ¥) However, nothing actually happens at the time an ability triggers. Each time a player would receive priority, each ability that has triggered but hasnΓÇÖt yet been put on the stack is put on the stack. See rule 117.5.
┬á
