117.2b Static abilities continuously affect the game. Priority doesnΓÇÖt apply to them. (See rule 604, ΓÇ£Handling Static Abilities,ΓÇ¥ and rule 611, ΓÇ£Continuous Effects.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
117.2c Turn-based actions happen automatically when certain steps or phases begin. TheyΓÇÖre dealt with before a player would receive priority. See rule 117.3a. Turn-based actions also happen automatically when each step and phase ends; no player receives priority afterward. See rule 703, ΓÇ£Turn-Based Actions.ΓÇ¥
┬á
117.2d State-based actions happen automatically when certain conditions are met. See rule 704. TheyΓÇÖre dealt with before a player would receive priority. See rule 117.5.
┬á
117.2e Resolving spells and abilities may instruct players to make choices or take actions, or may allow players to activate mana abilities. Even if a player is doing so, no player has priority while a spell or ability is resolving. See rule 608, ΓÇ£Resolving Spells and Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
117.3. Which player has priority is determined by the following rules:
┬á
117.3a The active player receives priority at the beginning of most steps and phases, after any turn-based actions (such as drawing a card during the draw step; see rule 703) have been dealt with and abilities that trigger at the beginning of that phase or step have been put on the stack. No player receives priority during the untap step. Players usually donΓÇÖt get priority during the cleanup step (see rule 514.3).
┬á
117.3b The active player receives priority after a spell or ability (other than a mana ability) resolves.
┬á
117.3c If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward.
┬á
117.3d If a player has priority and chooses not to take any actions, that player passes. If any mana is in that playerΓÇÖs mana pool, they announce what mana is there. Then the next player in turn order receives priority.
┬á
117.4. If all players pass in succession (that is, if all players pass without taking any actions in between passing), the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves or, if the stack is empty, the phase or step ends.
┬á
117.5. Each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event (see rule 704, ΓÇ£State-Based ActionsΓÇ¥), then repeats this process until no state-based actions are performed. Then triggered abilities are put on the stack (see rule 603, ΓÇ£Handling Triggered AbilitiesΓÇ¥). These steps repeat in order until no further state-based actions are performed and no abilities trigger. Then the player who would have received priority does so.
┬á
117.6. In a multiplayer game using the shared team turns option, teams rather than individual players have priority. See rule 805, ΓÇ£Shared Team Turns Option.ΓÇ¥
┬á
117.7. If a player with priority casts a spell or activates an activated ability while another spell or ability is already on the stack, the new spell or ability has been cast or activated ΓÇ£in response toΓÇ¥ the earlier spell or ability. The new spell or ability will resolve first. See rule 608, ΓÇ£Resolving Spells and Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
118. Costs
┬á
118.1. A cost is an action or payment necessary to take another action or to stop another action from taking place. To pay a cost, a player carries out the instructions specified by the spell, ability, or effect that contains that cost.
┬á
118.2. If a cost includes a mana payment, the player paying the cost has a chance to activate mana abilities. Paying the cost to cast a spell or activate an activated ability follows the steps in rules 601.2fΓÇôh.
┬á
118.3. A player canΓÇÖt pay a cost without having the necessary resources to pay it fully. For example, a player with only 1 life canΓÇÖt pay a cost of 2 life, and a permanent thatΓÇÖs already tapped canΓÇÖt be tapped to pay a cost. See rule 202, ΓÇ£Mana Cost and Color,ΓÇ¥ and rule 602, ΓÇ£Activating Activated Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
118.3a Paying mana is done by removing the indicated mana from a playerΓÇÖs mana pool. (Players can always pay 0 mana.) If excess mana remains in that playerΓÇÖs mana pool after making that payment, the player announces what mana is still there.
┬á
118.3b Paying life is done by subtracting the indicated amount of life from a playerΓÇÖs life total. (Players can always pay 0 life.)
┬á
118.3c Activating mana abilities is not mandatory, even if paying a cost is.
┬á
118.4. Some costs include an {X} or an X. See rule 107.3.
┬á
118.5. Some costs are represented by {0}, or are reduced to {0}. The action necessary for a player to pay such a cost is the playerΓÇÖs acknowledgment that they are paying it. Even though such a cost requires no resources, itΓÇÖs not automatically paid.
┬á
118.5a A spell whose mana cost is {0} must still be cast the same way as one with a cost greater than zero; it wonΓÇÖt cast itself automatically. The same is true for an activated ability whose cost is {0}.
┬á
118.6. Some objects have no mana cost. This represents an unpayable cost. An ability can also have an unpayable cost if its cost is based on the mana cost of an object with no mana cost. Attempting to cast a spell or activate an ability that has an unpayable cost is a legal action. However, attempting to pay an unpayable cost is an illegal action.
┬á
118.6a If an unpayable cost is increased by an effect or an additional cost is imposed, the cost is still unpayable. If an alternative cost is applied to an unpayable cost, including an effect that allows a player to cast a spell without paying its mana cost, the alternative cost may be paid.
┬á
118.7. What a player actually needs to do to pay a cost may be changed or reduced by effects. If the mana component of a cost is reduced to nothing by cost reduction effects, itΓÇÖs considered to be {0}. Paying a cost changed or reduced by an effect counts as paying the original cost.
┬á
118.7a Effects that reduce a cost by an amount of generic mana affect only the generic mana component of that cost. They canΓÇÖt affect the colored or colorless mana components of that cost.
┬á
118.7b If a cost is reduced by an amount of colored or colorless mana, but the cost doesnΓÇÖt require mana of that type, the cost is reduced by that amount of generic mana.
┬á
118.7c If a cost is reduced by an amount of colored mana that exceeds its mana component of that color, the costΓÇÖs mana component of that color is reduced to nothing and the costΓÇÖs generic mana component is reduced by the difference.
┬á
118.7d If a cost is reduced by an amount of colorless mana that exceeds its colorless mana component, the costΓÇÖs colorless mana component is reduced to nothing and the costΓÇÖs generic mana component is reduced by the difference.
┬á
118.7e If a cost is reduced by an amount of mana represented by a hybrid mana symbol, the player paying that cost chooses one half of that symbol at the time the cost reduction is applied (see rule 601.2f). If a colored or colorless half is chosen, the cost is reduced by one mana of that type. If a generic half is chosen, the cost is reduced by an amount of generic mana equal to that halfΓÇÖs number.
┬á
118.7f If a cost is reduced by an amount of mana represented by a Phyrexian mana symbol, the cost is reduced by one mana of that symbolΓÇÖs color.
┬á
118.7g If a cost is reduced by an amount of mana represented by one or more snow mana symbols, the cost is reduced by that much generic mana.
┬á
118.8. Some spells and abilities have additional costs. An additional cost is a cost listed in a spellΓÇÖs rules text, or applied to a spell or ability from another effect, that its controller must pay at the same time they pay the spellΓÇÖs mana cost or the abilityΓÇÖs activation cost. Note that some additional costs are listed in keywords; see rule 702.
┬á
118.8a Any number of additional costs may be applied to a spell as itΓÇÖs being cast or to an ability as itΓÇÖs being activated. The controller of the spell or ability announces their intentions to pay any or all of those costs as described in rule 601.2b.
┬á
118.8b Some additional costs are optional.
┬á
118.8c If an effect instructs a player to cast a spell ΓÇ£if able,ΓÇ¥ and that spell has a mandatory additional cost that includes actions involving cards with a stated quality in a hidden zone, the player isnΓÇÖt required to cast that spell, even if those cards are present in that zone.
┬á
118.8d Additional costs donΓÇÖt change a spellΓÇÖs mana cost, only what its controller has to pay to cast it. Spells and abilities that ask for that spellΓÇÖs mana cost still see the original value.
┬á
118.9. Some spells have alternative costs. An alternative cost is a cost listed in a spellΓÇÖs text, or applied to it from another effect, that its controller may pay rather than paying the spellΓÇÖs mana cost. Alternative costs are usually phrased, ΓÇ£You may [action] rather than pay [this objectΓÇÖs] mana cost,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£You may cast [this object] without paying its mana cost.ΓÇ¥ Note that some alternative costs are listed in keywords; see rule 702.
┬á
118.9a Only one alternative cost can be applied to any one spell as itΓÇÖs being cast. The controller of the spell announces their intentions to pay that cost as described in rule 601.2b.
┬á
118.9b Alternative costs are generally optional. An effect that allows you to cast a spell may require a certain alternative cost to be paid.
┬á
118.9c An alternative cost doesnΓÇÖt change a spellΓÇÖs mana cost, only what its controller has to pay to cast it. Spells and abilities that ask for that spellΓÇÖs mana cost still see the original value.
┬á
118.9d If an alternative cost is being paid to cast a spell, any additional costs, cost increases, and cost reductions that affect that spell are applied to that alternative cost. (See rule 601.2f.)
┬á
118.10. Each payment of a cost applies to only one spell, ability, or effect. For example, a player canΓÇÖt sacrifice just one creature to activate the activated abilities of two permanents that each require sacrificing a creature as a cost. Also, the resolution of a spell or ability doesnΓÇÖt pay another spell or abilityΓÇÖs cost, even if part of its effect is doing the same thing the other cost asks for.
┬á
118.11. The actions performed when paying a cost may be modified by effects. Even if they are, meaning the actions that are performed donΓÇÖt match the actions that are called for, the cost has still been paid.
Example: A player controls Psychic Vortex, an enchantment with a cumulative upkeep cost of ΓÇ£Draw a card,ΓÇ¥ and Obstinate Familiar, a creature that says ΓÇ£If you would draw a card, you may skip that draw instead.ΓÇ¥ The player may decide to pay Psychic VortexΓÇÖs cumulative upkeep cost and then draw no cards instead of drawing the appropriate amount. The cumulative upkeep cost has still been paid.
┬á
118.12. Some spells, activated abilities, and triggered abilities read, ΓÇ£[Do something]. If [a player] [does, doesnΓÇÖt, or canΓÇÖt], [effect].ΓÇ¥ Or ΓÇ£[A player] may [do something]. If [that player] [does, doesnΓÇÖt, or canΓÇÖt], [effect].ΓÇ¥ The action [do something] is a cost, paid when the spell or ability resolves. The ΓÇ£If [a player] [does, doesnΓÇÖt, or canΓÇÖt]ΓÇ¥ clause checks whether the player chose to pay an optional cost or started to pay a mandatory cost, regardless of what events actually occurred.
Example: You control Standstill, an enchantment that says ΓÇ£When a player casts a spell, sacrifice this enchantment. If you do, each of that playerΓÇÖs opponents draws three cards.ΓÇ¥ A spell is cast, causing StandstillΓÇÖs ability to trigger. Then an ability is activated that exiles Standstill. When StandstillΓÇÖs ability resolves, youΓÇÖre unable to pay the ΓÇ£sacrifice StandstillΓÇ¥ cost. No player will draw cards.
Example: Your opponent has cast Gather Specimens, a spell that says ΓÇ£If a creature would enter the battlefield under an opponentΓÇÖs control this turn, it enters under your control instead.ΓÇ¥ You control a face-down Dermoplasm, a creature with morph that says ΓÇ£When this creature is turned face up, you may put a creature card with morph from your hand onto the battlefield face up. If you do, return this creature to its ownerΓÇÖs hand.ΓÇ¥ You turn Dermoplasm face up, and you choose to put a creature card with morph from your hand onto the battlefield. Due to Gather Specimens, it enters the battlefield under your opponentΓÇÖs control instead of yours. However, since you chose to pay the cost, Dermoplasm is still returned to its ownerΓÇÖs hand.
┬á
118.12a Some spells, activated abilities, and triggered abilities read, ΓÇ£[Do something] unless [a player does something else].ΓÇ¥ This means the same thing as ΓÇ£[A player may do something else]. If [that player doesnΓÇÖt], [do something].ΓÇ¥
┬á
118.12b Some effects offer a player a choice to search a zone and take additional actions with the cards found in that zone, followed by an ΓÇ£If [a player] doesΓÇ¥ clause. This clause checks whether the player chose to search, not whether the player took any of the additional actions.
┬á
118.13. Some costs contain mana symbols that can be paid in multiple ways. These include hybrid mana symbols and Phyrexian mana symbols.
┬á
118.13a If the mana cost of a spell or the activation cost of an activated ability contains a mana symbol that can be paid in multiple ways, the choice of how to pay for that symbol is made as its controller proposes that spell or ability (see rule 601.2b).
┬á
118.13b If a cost paid during the resolution of a spell or ability contains a mana symbol that can be paid in multiple ways, the player paying that cost chooses how to pay for that symbol immediately before they pay that cost.
┬á
118.13c If the cost associated with a special action contains a mana symbol that can be paid in multiple ways, the player taking the special action chooses how to pay for that symbol immediately before they pay that cost.
┬á
118.14. Some effects say that ΓÇ£mana of any type can be spentΓÇ¥ to pay a cost. This means that players may spend mana as though it were colorless mana or mana of any color to pay that cost. If that effect also gives a player permission to cast spells, this applies only to mana that player spends to cast spells that way. See rule 609.4b.
┬á
119. Life
┬á
119.1. Each player begins the game with a starting life total of 20. Some variant games have different starting life totals.
┬á
119.1a In a Two-Headed Giant game, each teamΓÇÖs starting life total is 30. See rule 810, ΓÇ£Two-Headed Giant Variant.ΓÇ¥
┬á
119.1b In a Vanguard game, each playerΓÇÖs starting life total is 20 plus or minus the life modifier of their vanguard card. See rule 902, ΓÇ£Vanguard.ΓÇ¥
┬á
119.1c In a Commander game, each playerΓÇÖs starting life total is 40. See rule 903, ΓÇ£Commander.ΓÇ¥
┬á
119.1d. In a two-player Brawl game, each playerΓÇÖs starting life total is 25. In a multiplayer Brawl game, each playerΓÇÖs starting life total is 30. See rule 903.12, ΓÇ£Brawl Option.ΓÇ¥
┬á
119.1e In an Archenemy game, the archenemyΓÇÖs starting life total is 40. See rule 904, ΓÇ£Archenemy.ΓÇ¥
┬á
119.2. Damage dealt to a player normally causes that player to lose that much life. See rule 120.3.
┬á
119.3. If an effect causes a player to gain life or lose life, that playerΓÇÖs life total is adjusted accordingly.
┬á
119.4. If a cost or effect allows a player to pay an amount of life greater than 0, the player may do so only if their life total is greater than or equal to the amount of the payment. If a player pays life, the payment is subtracted from their life total; in other words, the player loses that much life.
┬á
119.4a If a cost or effect allows a player to pay an amount of life greater than 0 in a Two-Headed Giant game, the player may do so only if their teamΓÇÖs life total is greater than or equal to the total amount of life both team members are paying for that cost or effect. If a player pays life, the payment is subtracted from their teamΓÇÖs life total.
┬á
119.4b Players can always pay 0 life, no matter what their (or their teamΓÇÖs) life total is, and even if an effect says players canΓÇÖt pay life.
┬á
119.5. If an effect sets a playerΓÇÖs life total to a specific number, the player gains or loses the necessary amount of life to end up with the new total.
┬á
119.6. If a player has 0 or less life, that player loses the game as a state-based action. See rule 704.
┬á
119.7. If an effect says that a player canΓÇÖt gain life, that player canΓÇÖt make an exchange such that the playerΓÇÖs life total would become higher; in that case, the exchange wonΓÇÖt happen. Similarly, if an effect redistributes life totals, a player canΓÇÖt receive a new life total such that the playerΓÇÖs life total would become higher. In addition, a cost that involves having that player gain life canΓÇÖt be paid, and a replacement effect that would replace a life gain event affecting that player wonΓÇÖt do anything.
┬á
119.8. If an effect says that a player canΓÇÖt lose life, that player canΓÇÖt make an exchange such that the playerΓÇÖs life total would become lower; in that case, the exchange wonΓÇÖt happen. Similarly, if an effect redistributes life totals, a player canΓÇÖt receive a new life total such that the playerΓÇÖs life total would become lower. In addition, a cost that involves having that player pay life canΓÇÖt be paid.
┬á
119.9. Some triggered abilities are written, ΓÇ£Whenever [a player] gains life, . . . .ΓÇ¥ Such abilities are treated as though they are written, ΓÇ£Whenever a source causes [a player] to gain life, . . . .ΓÇ¥ If a player gains 0 life, no life gain event has occurred, and these abilities wonΓÇÖt trigger.
┬á
119.10. Some replacement effects are written, ΓÇ£If [a player] would gain life, . . . .ΓÇ¥ Such abilities are treated as though they are written, ΓÇ£If a source would cause [a player] to gain life, . . . .ΓÇ¥ If a player gains 0 life, no life gain event would occur, and these effects wonΓÇÖt apply.
┬á
120. Damage
┬á
120.1. Objects can deal damage to battles, creatures, planeswalkers, and players. This is generally detrimental to the object or player that receives that damage. An object that deals damage is the source of that damage.
┬á
120.1a Damage canΓÇÖt be dealt to an object thatΓÇÖs not a battle, a creature, or a planeswalker.
┬á
120.2. Any object can deal damage.
┬á
120.2a Damage may be dealt as a result of combat. Each attacking and blocking creature deals combat damage equal to its power during the combat damage step.
┬á
120.2b Damage may be dealt as an effect of a spell or ability. The spell or ability will specify which object deals that damage.
┬á
120.3. Damage may have one or more of the following results, depending on whether the recipient of the damage is a player or permanent, the characteristics of the damageΓÇÖs source, and the characteristics of the damageΓÇÖs recipient (if itΓÇÖs a permanent).
┬á
120.3a Damage dealt to a player by a source without infect causes that player to lose that much life.
┬á
120.3b Damage dealt to a player by a source with infect causes that sourceΓÇÖs controller to give the player that many poison counters.
┬á
120.3c Damage dealt to a planeswalker causes that many loyalty counters to be removed from that planeswalker.
┬á
120.3d Damage dealt to a creature by a source with wither and/or infect causes that sourceΓÇÖs controller to put that many -1/-1 counters on that creature.
┬á
120.3e Damage dealt to a creature by a source with neither wither nor infect causes that much damage to be marked on that creature.
┬á
120.3f Damage dealt by a source with lifelink causes that sourceΓÇÖs controller to gain that much life, in addition to the damageΓÇÖs other results.
┬á
120.3g Combat damage dealt to a player by a creature with toxic causes that creatureΓÇÖs controller to give the player a number of poison counters equal to that creatureΓÇÖs total toxic value, in addition to the damageΓÇÖs other results. See rule 702.164, ΓÇ£Toxic.ΓÇ¥
┬á
120.3h Damage dealt to a battle causes that many defense counters to be removed from that battle.
┬á
120.4. Damage is processed in a four-part sequence.
┬á
120.4a First, if an effect thatΓÇÖs causing damage to be dealt states that excess damage that would be dealt to a permanent is dealt to another permanent or player instead, the damage event is modified accordingly. If the first permanent is a creature, the excess damage is the amount of damage in excess of what would be lethal damage, taking into account damage already marked on the creature and damage from other sources that would be dealt at the same time. (See rule 120.6.) Any amount of damage greater than 1 is excess damage if the source dealing that damage to a creature has deathtouch. (See rule 702.2.) If the first permanent is a planeswalker, the excess damage is the amount of damage in excess of that planeswalkerΓÇÖs loyalty, taking into account damage from other sources that would be dealt at the same time. If the first permanent is a battle, the excess damage is the amount of damage in excess of that battleΓÇÖs defense, taking into account damage from other sources that would be dealt at the same time. If the first permanent has multiple card types from among the list of creature, planeswalker, and battle, the excess damage is the greatest of the calculated amounts for each of the card types it has.
┬á
120.4b Second, damage is dealt, as modified by replacement and prevention effects that interact with damage. (See rule 614, ΓÇ£Replacement Effects,ΓÇ¥ and rule 615, ΓÇ£Prevention Effects.ΓÇ¥) Abilities that trigger when damage is dealt trigger now and wait to be put on the stack.
┬á
120.4c Third, damage thatΓÇÖs been dealt is processed into its results, as modified by replacement effects that interact with those results (such as life loss or counters).
┬á
120.4d Finally, the damage event occurs.
Example: A player who controls Boon Reflection, an enchantment that says ΓÇ£If you would gain life, you gain twice that much life instead,ΓÇ¥ attacks with a 3/3 creature with wither and lifelink. ItΓÇÖs blocked by a 2/2 creature, and the defending player casts a spell that prevents the next 2 damage that would be dealt to the blocking creature. The damage event starts out as [3 damage is dealt to the 2/2 creature, 2 damage is dealt to the 3/3 creature]. The prevention effect is applied, so the damage event becomes [1 damage is dealt to the 2/2 creature, 2 damage is dealt to the 3/3 creature]. ThatΓÇÖs processed into its results, so the damage event is now [one -1/-1 counter is put on the 2/2 creature, the active player gains 1 life, 2 damage is marked on the 3/3 creature]. Boon ReflectionΓÇÖs effect is applied, so the damage event becomes [one -1/-1 counter is put on the 2/2 creature, the active player gains 2 life, 2 damage is marked on the 3/3 creature]. Then the damage event occurs.
Example: The defending player controls a creature and Worship, an enchantment that says ΓÇ£If you control a creature, damage that would reduce your life total to less than 1 reduces it to 1 instead.ΓÇ¥ That player is at 2 life, and is being attacked by two unblocked 5/5 creatures. The player casts Awe Strike, which says ΓÇ£The next time target creature would deal damage this turn, prevent that damage. You gain life equal to the damage prevented this way,ΓÇ¥ targeting one of the attackers. The damage event starts out as [10 damage is dealt to the defending player]. Awe StrikeΓÇÖs effect is applied, so the damage event becomes [5 damage is dealt to the defending player, the defending player gains 5 life]. ThatΓÇÖs processed into its results, so the damage event is now [the defending player loses 5 life, the defending player gains 5 life]. WorshipΓÇÖs effect sees that the damage event would not reduce the playerΓÇÖs life total to less than 1, so WorshipΓÇÖs effect is not applied. Then the damage event occurs.
┬á
120.5. Damage dealt to a creature, planeswalker, or battle doesnΓÇÖt destroy it. Likewise, the source of that damage doesnΓÇÖt destroy it. Rather, state-based actions may destroy a creature or otherwise put a permanent into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard, due to the results of the damage dealt to that permanent. See rule 704.
Example: A player casts Lightning Bolt, an instant that says ΓÇ£Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to any target,ΓÇ¥ targeting a 2/2 creature. After Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to that creature, the creature is destroyed as a state-based action. Neither Lightning Bolt nor the damage dealt by Lightning Bolt destroyed that creature.
┬á
120.6. Damage marked on a creature remains until the cleanup step, even if that permanent stops being a creature. If the total damage marked on a creature is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed as a state-based action (see rule 704). All damage marked on a permanent is removed when it regenerates (see rule 701.19, ΓÇ£RegenerateΓÇ¥) and during the cleanup step (see rule 514.2).
┬á
120.7. The source of damage is the object that dealt it. If an effect requires a player to choose a source of damage, they may choose a permanent; a spell on the stack (including a permanent spell); any object referred to by an object on the stack, by a prevention or replacement effect thatΓÇÖs waiting to apply, or by a delayed triggered ability thatΓÇÖs waiting to trigger (even if that object is no longer in the zone it used to be in); or a face-up object in the command zone. A source doesnΓÇÖt need to be capable of dealing damage to be a legal choice. See rule 609.7, ΓÇ£Sources of Damage.ΓÇ¥
┬á
120.8. If a source would deal 0 damage, it does not deal damage at all. That means abilities that trigger on damage being dealt wonΓÇÖt trigger. It also means that replacement effects that would increase the damage dealt by that source, or would have that source deal that damage to a different object or player, have no event to replace, so they have no effect.
┬á
120.9. If an ability triggers on damage being dealt by a specific source or sources, and the effect refers to the ΓÇ£damage dealt,ΓÇ¥ it refers only to the damage dealt by the specified sources and not to any damage dealt at the same time by other sources.
┬á
120.10. Some triggered abilities check whether a permanent has been dealt excess damage. These abilities check after the permanent has been dealt damage by one or more sources. If those sources together dealt an amount of damage to a creature greater than lethal damage, excess damage equal to the difference was dealt to that creature. If those sources together dealt an amount of damage to a planeswalker greater than that planeswalkerΓÇÖs loyalty before the damage was dealt, excess damage equal to the difference was dealt to that planeswalker. If those sources together dealt an amount of damage to a battle greater than that battleΓÇÖs defense before the damage was dealt, excess damage equal to the difference was dealt to that battle. If a permanent has multiple card types from among the list of creature, planeswalker, and battle, the excess damage dealt to that permanent is the greatest of the calculated amounts for each of the card types it has.
┬á
121. Drawing a Card
┬á
121.1. A player draws a card by putting the top card of their library into their hand. This is done as a turn-based action during each playerΓÇÖs draw step. It may also be done as part of a cost or effect of a spell or ability.
┬á
121.2. Cards may only be drawn one at a time. If a player is instructed to draw multiple cards, that player performs that many individual card draws.
┬á
121.2a An instruction to draw multiple cards can be modified by replacement effects that refer to the number of cards drawn. This modification occurs before considering any of the individual card draws. See rule 616.1g.
┬á
121.2b Some effects say that a player canΓÇÖt draw more than one card each turn. Such an effect applies to individual card draws. Instructions to draw multiple cards may still be partially carried out. However, if an effect offers the player a choice to draw multiple cards, the affected player canΓÇÖt choose to do so. Similarly, the player canΓÇÖt pay a cost that includes drawing multiple cards.
┬á
121.2c If more than one player is instructed to draw cards, the active player performs all of their draws first, then each other player in turn order does the same.
┬á
121.2d If more than one player is instructed to draw cards in a game thatΓÇÖs using the shared team turns option (such as a Two-Headed Giant game), first each player on the active team, in whatever order that team likes, performs their draws, then each player on each nonactive team in turn order does the same.
┬á
121.3. If there are no cards in a playerΓÇÖs library and an effect offers that player the choice to draw a card, that player can choose to do so. However, if an effect says that a player canΓÇÖt draw cards and another effect offers that player the choice to draw a card, that player canΓÇÖt choose to do so.
┬á
121.3a The same principles apply if the player whoΓÇÖs making the choice is not the player who would draw the card. If the latter player has no cards in their library, the choice can be taken. If an effect says that the latter player canΓÇÖt draw a card, the choice canΓÇÖt be taken.
┬á
121.4. A player who attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it loses the game the next time a player would receive priority. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.)
┬á
121.5. If an effect moves cards from a playerΓÇÖs library to that playerΓÇÖs hand without using the word ΓÇ£draw,ΓÇ¥ the player has not drawn those cards. This makes a difference for abilities that trigger on drawing cards and effects that replace card draws, as well as if the playerΓÇÖs library is empty.
┬á
121.6. Some effects replace card draws.
┬á
121.6a An effect that replaces a card draw is applied even if no cards could be drawn because there are no cards in the affected playerΓÇÖs library.
┬á
121.6b If an effect replaces a draw within a sequence of card draws, the replacement effect is completed before resuming the sequence.
┬á
121.6c Some effects perform additional actions on a card after itΓÇÖs drawn. If the draw is replaced, the additional action is not performed on any cards that are drawn as a result of that replacement effect or any subsequent replacement effects.
┬á
121.7. Some replacement effects and prevention effects result in one or more card draws. In such a case, if there are any parts of the original event that havenΓÇÖt been replaced, those parts occur first, then the card draws happen one at a time.
┬á
121.8. If a spell or ability causes a card to be drawn while another spell is being cast, the drawn card is kept face down until that spell becomes cast (see rule 601.2i) or until the casting process is reversed (see rule 733, ΓÇ£Handling Illegal ActionsΓÇ¥). The same is true with relation to another ability being activated. If an effect allows or instructs a player to reveal the card as itΓÇÖs being drawn, itΓÇÖs revealed after the spell becomes cast or the ability becomes activated. While face down, the drawn card is considered to have no characteristics and canΓÇÖt be used to pay any part of the cost of the spell or ability that would require the card to have specific characteristics.
┬á
121.9. If an effect gives a player the option to reveal a card as they draw it, that player may look at that card as they draw it before choosing whether to reveal it.
┬á
122. Counters
┬á
122.1. A counter is a marker placed on an object or player that modifies its characteristics and/or interacts with a rule, ability, or effect. Counters are not objects and have no characteristics. Notably, a counter is not a token, and a token is not a counter. Counters with the same name or description are interchangeable.
┬á
122.1a A +X/+Y counter on a creature or on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield, where X and Y are numbers, adds X to that objectΓÇÖs power and Y to that objectΓÇÖs toughness. Similarly, -X/-Y counters subtract from power and toughness. See rule 613.4c.
┬á
122.1b A keyword counter on a permanent or on a card in a zone other than the battlefield causes that object to gain that keyword. The keywords that a keyword counter can be are flying, first strike, double strike, deathtouch, decayed, exalted, haste, hexproof, indestructible, lifelink, menace, reach, shadow, trample, and vigilance, as well as any variants of those keywords. See rule 613.1f.
┬á
122.1c One or more shield counters on a permanent create a single replacement effect and a single prevention effect that protect the permanent. These effects are ΓÇ£If this permanent would be destroyed as the result of an effect, instead remove a shield counter from itΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£If damage would be dealt to this permanent, prevent that damage and remove a shield counter from it.ΓÇ¥ See rule 614, ΓÇ£Replacement Effects,ΓÇ¥ and rule 615, ΓÇ£Prevention Effects.ΓÇ¥
┬á
122.1d One or more stun counters on a permanent create a single replacement effect that stops the permanent from untapping. That effect is ΓÇ£If a permanent with a stun counter on it would become untapped, instead remove a stun counter from it.ΓÇ¥
┬á
122.1e The number of loyalty counters on a planeswalker on the battlefield indicates how much loyalty it has. A planeswalker with 0 loyalty is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard as a state-based action. See rule 704.
┬á
122.1f If a player has ten or more poison counters, that player loses the game as a state-based action. See rule 704. A player is ΓÇ£poisonedΓÇ¥ if they have one or more poison counters. (See rule 810 for additional rules for Two-Headed Giant games.)
┬á
122.1g The number of defense counters on a battle on the battlefield indicates how much defense it has. A battle with 0 defense is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard if it isnΓÇÖt the source of an ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack. This state-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack. See rule 704.
┬á
122.1h One or more finality counters on a permanent create a single replacement effect that stops the permanent from going to the graveyard. That effect is ΓÇ£If this permanent would be put into a graveyard from the battlefield, exile it instead.ΓÇ¥
┬á
122.1i One or more rad counters on a player cause a triggered ability to trigger at the beginning of that playerΓÇÖs precombat main phase. See rule 728, ΓÇ£Rad Counters.ΓÇ¥
┬á
122.1j A hone counter on an Equipment gives +1/+0 to any creature that Equipment is attached to.
┬á
122.2. Counters on an object are not retained if that object moves from one zone to another. The counters are not ΓÇ£removedΓÇ¥; they simply cease to exist. See rule 400.7.
┬á
122.3. If a permanent has both a +1/+1 counter and a -1/-1 counter on it, N +1/+1 and N -1/-1 counters are removed from it as a state-based action, where N is the smaller of the number of +1/+1 and -1/-1 counters on it. See rule 704.
┬á
122.4. If a permanent with an ability that says it canΓÇÖt have more than N counters of a certain kind on it has more than N counters of that kind on it, all but N of those counters are removed from it as a state-based action. See rule 704.
┬á
122.5. If an effect says to ΓÇ£moveΓÇ¥ a counter, it means to remove that counter from the object itΓÇÖs currently on and put it onto a second object. If either of these actions isnΓÇÖt possible, itΓÇÖs not possible to move a counter, and no counter is removed from or put onto anything. This may occur if the first and second objects are the same object; if the first object doesnΓÇÖt have the appropriate kind of counter on it; if the second object canΓÇÖt have counters put onto it; or if either object is no longer in the correct zone.
┬á
122.6. Some spells and abilities refer to counters being put on an object. This refers to putting counters on that object while itΓÇÖs on the battlefield and also to an object thatΓÇÖs given counters as it enters the battlefield.
┬á
122.6a If an object enters the battlefield with counters on it, the effect causing the object to be given counters may specify which player puts those counters on it. If the effect doesnΓÇÖt specify a player, the objectΓÇÖs controller puts those counters on it.
┬á
122.7. An ability that triggers ΓÇ£When/Whenever the Nth [kind] counterΓÇ¥ is put on an object triggers when one or more counters of the appropriate kind are put on the object such that the object had fewer than N counters on it before the counters were put on it and N or more counters on it after.
┬á
122.8. If a triggered ability instructs a player to put one objectΓÇÖs counters on another object and that abilityΓÇÖs trigger condition or effect checks that the object with those counters left the battlefield, the player doesnΓÇÖt move counters from one object to the other. Rather, the player puts the same number of each kind of counter the first object had onto the second object. If the ability specifies what kind(s) of counters to place, the player puts the same number of each of those kinds of counter the first object had onto the second object.
┬á
122.9. If an activated ability of an object instructs a player to put its counters on another object and sacrificing the object with those counters is a cost to activate that ability, the player doesnΓÇÖt move counters from one object to the other. Rather, the player puts the same number of each kind of counter the first object had onto the second object. If the ability specified what kind(s) of counters to place, the player puts the same number of each of those kinds of counters the first object had onto the second object.
┬á
123. Stickers
┬á
123.1. A sticker is a marker placed on an object that modifies its characteristics and/or interacts with a rule, ability, or effect. Stickers are not objects. Notably, a sticker is not a counter or a token. Changes to an object from stickers are not part of its copiable values. There are four kinds of stickers: name stickers; ability stickers; power and toughness stickers; and art stickers.
┬á
123.2. Stickers are found in boosters of the Unfinity expansion on numbered inserts. Each insert has a predetermined combination of stickers. Any rule that refers to a sticker sheet refers to the specific combination of stickers found on one of those inserts. Sticker sheets are not cards and have no characteristics. Each sticker sheet can be found at Gatherer.Wizards.com.
┬á
123.2a In constructed play, a player who chooses to play with stickers must start the game with at least ten sticker sheets selected before play begins, and each of their sticker sheets must be unique. There is no maximum number of sticker sheets a player may start the game with. Each player playing with sticker sheets reveals all of their sticker sheets and chooses three of them at random. See rule 103, ΓÇ£Starting the Game.ΓÇ¥
┬á
123.2b In limited play, each player chooses up to three sticker sheets from among those in the sealed products they opened and reveals them. See rule 103, ΓÇ£Starting the Game.ΓÇ¥
┬á
123.2c Each player has access to only the stickers on the chosen sheets during the game, and those sticker sheets remain revealed.
┬á
123.3. If an effect instructs a player to put a sticker on an object, that player chooses a sticker that is not currently on any objects they own from among the stickers they have access to and puts it on that object.
┬á
123.3a Each sticker a player has access to is discrete and is distinct from each other sticker they have access to. Two stickers are never considered to be the same sticker, even if they have the same text or information on them.
┬á
123.3b A player canΓÇÖt put a sticker on an object that they donΓÇÖt own. If an effect would cause them to do so, that part of the effect does nothing.
┬á
123.3c A sticker may have a ticket cost represented by a number inside a ticket symbol (see rule 107.17a). In order to put a sticker with a ticket cost on an object, the player who owns that object must pay that much {TK}. If they donΓÇÖt have that much {TK}, they canΓÇÖt put that sticker on an object.
┬á
123.3d If a sticker that is already on an object is moved to another object, that stickerΓÇÖs ticket cost does not need to be paid again.
┬á
123.4. Some rules and effects refer to a ΓÇ£stickeredΓÇ¥ object. An object is ΓÇ£stickeredΓÇ¥ if it currently has any kind of sticker on it. An object without any stickers on it is not a stickered object, even if it previously had stickers on it.
┬á
123.5. Stickers on an object are not retained as that object moves to a hidden zone. Stickers are retained as that object moves to a public zone and continue to apply to the new object it becomes in that zone; this is an exception to rule 400.7.
┬á
123.5a If one or more cards with stickers on them enter the battlefield as part of a melded permanent, all of those stickers are on the permanent that object becomes on the battlefield. They maintain their relative timestamp order.
┬á
123.5b If an object with a sticker on it becomes a component of a merged permanent on the battlefield, that sticker is on that merged permanent.
┬á
123.5c If a melded or merged permanent with one or more stickers on it moves from the battlefield to another public zone, only one of the objects it becomes will retain those stickers. Its owner chooses which of the objects it becomes in its new zone retains any stickers that are on it. Effects from those stickers will continue to apply to only that object.
┬á
123.6. A name sticker consists only of one or more words. A name sticker on a permanent or on a card in a zone other than the battlefield causes the word on that sticker to be added to the text of that objectΓÇÖs name. This is a text-changing effect. See rule 613.1c and rule 612, ΓÇ£Text-Changing Effects.ΓÇ¥
┬á
123.6a For the purposes of rules and effects related to name stickers, a ΓÇ£wordΓÇ¥ in an objectΓÇÖs name is any series of non-space characters that are separated from other non-space characters by one or more spaces. Hyphenated words and words with punctuation are considered to be one word. Blank lines, such as the one in ΓÇ£Wolf in ________ Clothing,ΓÇ¥ are not considered words in a cardΓÇÖs name.
┬á
123.6b As a name sticker is placed on an object, that objectΓÇÖs controller chooses a position in that objectΓÇÖs name for the word in the name sticker to be added, then announces that objectΓÇÖs new name. That word can be added at the beginning of the objectΓÇÖs name or after any number of the other words that are currently in its name. The new name can be further modified by other name stickers. If that object has no name, its name becomes the word added by the name sticker. Name stickers never modify or remove any of the other words in that name.
Example: As a player puts a name sticker with the word ΓÇ£DarkΓÇ¥ printed on it onto a creature named Bear Cub, that creatureΓÇÖs controller chooses whether its new name is ΓÇ£Dark Bear Cub,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£Bear Dark Cub,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£Bear Cub Dark.ΓÇ¥ They then announce the new name to all players.
┬á
123.6c The text that a name sticker is modifying may change due to other effects and/or a permanentΓÇÖs face-down status (see rule 708, ΓÇ£Face-Down Spells and PermanentsΓÇ¥). To determine the name of an object with one or more name stickers, start with the objectΓÇÖs copiable values, then apply each name stickerΓÇÖs effect and each other text-changing effect in timestamp order. The position of each name sticker will continue to be after the number of words that were before it in the objectΓÇÖs name when it was placed. If there are fewer words in the objectΓÇÖs current name, the word on that sticker is added at the end of its name instead. The position and timestamp order of each name sticker on an object is remembered as the object that sticker is on moves from one public zone to another, and it continues to apply to the new object it becomes in that zone (see rule 123.5). This is an exception to rule 400.7.
Example: Fae of Wishes, an adventurer card, is in exile with a name sticker on it adding the word ΓÇ£ManaΓÇ¥ after its second word, so its name is ΓÇ£Fae of Mana Wishes.ΓÇ¥ An effect allows that player to cast Granted, its Adventure, from exile. The name of that spell on the stack is ΓÇ£Granted Mana.ΓÇ¥ After that card is exiled as the Adventure resolves, the stickerΓÇÖs position (after the second word) is remembered, so the name of the exiled card is once again ΓÇ£Fae of Mana Wishes.ΓÇ¥
Example: A player owns a creature named It That Betrays on the battlefield. Using name stickers, they add the word ΓÇ£EldraziΓÇ¥ to its name after the third word, such that its new name is ΓÇ£It That Betrays Eldrazi.ΓÇ¥ Later, that creature becomes a copy of a creature named Seeker of the Way. The name sticker continues to apply after the third word, so its new name is ΓÇ£Seeker of the Eldrazi Way.ΓÇ¥
Example: A creature with a name sticker on it becomes enchanted by Witness Protection, an Aura that changes the creatureΓÇÖs name to ΓÇ£Legitimate Businessperson.ΓÇ¥ Since Witness Protection is also a text-changing effect, and it has a later timestamp than the name sticker, the word on that name sticker is not part of the creatureΓÇÖs name. Its name is ΓÇ£Legitimate Businessperson.ΓÇ¥
┬á
123.6d Some effects refer to the number of one or more specific letters on a name sticker. A lowercase letter and its uppercase equivalent are the same letter.
┬á
123.6e Some effects refer to the number of ΓÇ£unique vowelsΓÇ¥ on a name sticker. These count the number of different vowels that appear on that sticker, even if one or more of them appear more than once. The vowels are A, E, I, O, U, and Y. A lowercase letter and its uppercase equivalent are the same letter.
┬á
123.7. An ability sticker is a sticker with one or more abilities printed on it. An ability sticker on a permanent or on a card in a zone other than the battlefield causes that object to gain the ability that is printed on that sticker. See rule 613.1f.
┬á
123.7a If an effect refers to an ability of an ability sticker, it refers to the ability that sticker grants to the object it is on, even if the object it is on doesnΓÇÖt currently have that ability due to another effect.
┬á
123.8. A power and toughness sticker is a sticker that has two numbers and a slash printed on it, resembling the power and toughness of a creature card. A power and toughness sticker on a creature or on a creature or Vehicle card in a zone other than the battlefield sets that objectΓÇÖs power and toughness to the values printed on that sticker (see rule 613.4b). If more than one power and toughness sticker is on a creature, use timestamp order to determine which one takes precedence (see rule 613.7).
┬á
123.8a An effect that refers to the power and/or toughness of a sticker refers only to the printed power and/or toughness values on a power and toughness sticker. It does not refer to any printed value on any other stickers.
┬á
123.9. An art sticker on a permanent has no effect on game play other than to act as a marker that other spells and abilities can identify.

2. Parts of a Card
┬á
200. General
┬á
200.1. The parts of a card are name, mana cost, illustration, color indicator, type line, expansion symbol, text box, power and toughness, loyalty, defense, hand modifier, life modifier, illustration credit, legal text, and collector number. Some cards may have more than one of any or all of these parts.
┬á
200.2. Some parts of a card are also characteristics of the object that has them. See rule 109.3.
┬á
200.3. Some objects that arenΓÇÖt cards (tokens, copies of cards, and copies of spells) have some of the parts of a card, but only the ones that are also characteristics. See rule 111 and rule 707.
┬á
201. Name
┬á
201.1. The name of a card is printed on its upper left corner.
┬á
201.2. A cardΓÇÖs name is always considered to be the English version of its name, regardless of printed language.
┬á
201.2a Two or more objects have the same name if they have at least one name in common, even if one or more of those objects have additional names. An object with no name doesnΓÇÖt have the same name as any other object, including another object with no name.
┬á
201.2b Some spells and abilities refer to two or more objects with different names. Those objects have different names only if each of them has at least one name and no two objects in that group have a name in common.
Example: A player controls LilianaΓÇÖs Contract, which says, in part, ΓÇ£At the beginning of your upkeep, if you control four or more Demons with different names, you win the game.ΓÇ¥ That player controls three Demons with different names and a face-down creature with no name, with an effect making it a Demon. Because the four creatures include one with no name, those four creatures donΓÇÖt count as four Demons with different names. The ability of LilianaΓÇÖs Contract wonΓÇÖt trigger.
┬á
201.2c Some spells or abilities check if one object has a different name than a second object or group of objects. The first object has a different name than those objects if the first object has at least one name and has no names in common with any of the other objects, even if one or more of the other objects have no names. If the first object has no name, it does not have a different name than any of the other objects, even if those other objects themselves have names.
┬á
201.3. Some cards with different English names are treated as though they had the same English name. Pairs of cards with this property have names that are interchangeable.
┬á
201.3a For the purposes of all rules, abilities, and effects that refer to a cardΓÇÖs name, objects with interchangeable names have the same name. (See rules 201.2aΓÇôb.)
┬á
201.3b For the purposes of deck construction and format legality, cards with interchangeable names have the same name.
┬á
201.3c If a card has later printings with interchangeable names, the later printings will have an interchangeable names indicator in the bottom left-hand corner referring to the original printingΓÇÖs three-letter set code and collector number (see rule 213.1d).
┬á
201.4. If an effect instructs a player to choose a card name, the player must choose the name of a card in the Oracle card reference. (See rule 108.1.) A player may not choose the name of a token unless itΓÇÖs also the name of a card.
┬á
201.4a If a player is instructed to choose a card name with certain characteristics, the player must choose the name of a card whose Oracle text matches those characteristics. (See rule 108.1.)
Example: Dispossess reads, in part, ΓÇ£Choose an artifact card name.ΓÇ¥ The player can choose the name of any artifact card, even one thatΓÇÖs not legal in the format of the current game. The player canΓÇÖt choose Island, even if an Island on the battlefield has been turned into artifact by some effect.
┬á
201.4b If a player wants to choose the name of a split card, the player must choose the name of one of its halves, but not both. (See rule 709.) If a player is instructed to choose a card name with certain characteristics, use only that halfΓÇÖs characteristics to determine if this name can be chosen.
┬á
201.4c If a player wants to choose a flip cardΓÇÖs alternative name, the player may do so. (See rule 710.) If a player is instructed to choose a card name with certain characteristics, use the cardΓÇÖs characteristics as modified by its alternative characteristics to determine if this name can be chosen.
┬á
201.4d If a player wants to choose the name of the back face of a double-faced card, the player may do so. (See rule 712.) If a player is instructed to choose a card name with certain characteristics, use only the characteristics of the back face to determine if this name can be chosen.
┬á
201.4e If a player wants to choose the name of the combined back face of a meld pair, the player may do so. (See rule 713.) If a player is instructed to choose a card name with certain characteristics, use only the characteristics of the combined back face to determine if this name can be chosen.
┬á
201.4f If a player wants to choose an adventurer cardΓÇÖs alternative name, the player may do so. (See rule 715.) If a player is instructed to choose a card name with certain characteristics, use the cardΓÇÖs characteristics as modified by its alternative characteristics to determine if this name can be chosen.
┬á
201.4g Some cards have interchangeable names (see rule 201.3). For all game purposes, these cards have the same name. If a player chooses the name of a card which has interchangeable names, the name of each of those cards has been chosen.
┬á
201.5. Text that refers to the object itΓÇÖs on by name means just that particular object and not any other objects with that name, regardless of any name changes caused by game effects.
┬á
201.5a If an abilityΓÇÖs effect grants another ability to an object, and that second ability refers to that first abilityΓÇÖs source by name, the name refers only to the specific object which is that first abilityΓÇÖs source. The second ability does not refer to any other object with the same name as the first abilityΓÇÖs source. However, if the second ability also moved the first abilityΓÇÖs source to a different public zone, the name refers to the object the source became in its new zone. This is also true if the second ability is copied onto a new object.
Example: Gutter Grime has an ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever a nontoken creature you control dies, put a slime counter on this enchantment, then create a green Ooze creature token with ΓÇÿThis tokenΓÇÖs power and toughness are each equal to the number of slime counters on Gutter Grime.ΓÇÖΓÇ¥ The ability granted to the token only looks at the Gutter Grime that created the token, not at any other Gutter Grime on the battlefield. A copy of that token would also have an ability that referred only to the Gutter Grime that created the original token.
┬á
201.5b If an ability of an object refers to that object by name, and an object with a different name gains that ability, each instance of the first name in the gained ability that refers to the first object by name should be treated as the second name.
Example: Quicksilver Elemental says, in part, ΓÇ£{U}: This creature gains all activated abilities of target creature until end of turn.ΓÇ¥ If it gains an ability that says ΓÇ£{BB}: Regenerate Skithiryx,ΓÇ¥ activating that ability will regenerate Quicksilver Elemental, not the Skithiryx, the Blight Dragon it gained the ability from.
Example: Glacial Ray is an instant with splice onto Arcane that says ΓÇ£Glacial Ray deals 2 damage to any target.ΓÇ¥ If itΓÇÖs spliced onto a KodamaΓÇÖs Reach, that KodamaΓÇÖs Reach deals 2 damage to the target.
Example: The Ever-Changing ΓÇÖDane says ΓÇ£{1}, Sacrifice another creature: The Ever-Changing ΓÇÖDane becomes a copy of the sacrificed creature, except it has this ability.ΓÇ¥ Its ability is activated sacrificing a Runeclaw Bear. The Ever-Changing ΓÇÖDane becomes a copy of Runeclaw Bear and gains an ability that should be treated as saying ΓÇ£{1}, Sacrifice another creature: Runeclaw Bear becomes a copy of the sacrificed creature, except it has this ability.ΓÇ¥
┬á
201.5c Text printed on some cards refers to that card by a shortened version of its name. Instances of a cardΓÇÖs shortened name used in this manner are treated as though they used the cardΓÇÖs full name.
┬á
201.6. Promotional or alternate-art versions of some cards feature a secondary title bar below the name line. The cardΓÇÖs name as listed in the Oracle card reference is displayed in the secondary title bar, and an alternate name appears in the upper left corner. For the purposes of deck construction, game rules, and effects, these cards have only the card name specified in the secondary title bar. Rules text may also refer to a cardΓÇÖs alternate name; instances of the alternate name that are present in rules text refer to the name specified in the secondary title bar. The alternate name has no effect on game play.
┬á
202. Mana Cost and Color
┬á
202.1. A cardΓÇÖs mana cost is indicated by mana symbols near the top of the card. (See rule 107.4.) On most cards, these symbols are printed in the upper right corner. Some cards from the Future Sight set have alternate frames in which the mana symbols appear to the left of the illustration.
┬á
202.1a The mana cost of an object represents what a player must spend from their mana pool to cast that card. Unless an objectΓÇÖs mana cost includes Phyrexian mana symbols (see rule 107.4f), paying that mana cost requires matching the type of any colored or colorless mana symbols as well as paying the generic mana indicated in the cost.
┬á
202.1b Some objects have no mana cost. This normally includes all land cards, any other cards that have no mana symbols where their mana cost would appear, tokens (unless the effect that creates them specifies otherwise), and nontraditional Magic cards. Having no mana cost represents an unpayable cost (see rule 118.6). Note that lands are played without paying any costs (see rule 305, ΓÇ£LandsΓÇ¥).
┬á
202.2. An object is the color or colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost, regardless of the color of its frame.
┬á
202.2a The five colors are white, blue, black, red, and green. The white mana symbol is represented by {W}, blue by {U}, black by {B}, red by {R}, and green by {G}.
Example: An object with a mana cost of {2}{W} is white, an object with a mana cost of {2} is colorless, and one with a mana cost of {2}{W}{B} is both white and black.
┬á
202.2b Objects with no colored mana symbols in their mana costs are colorless.
┬á
202.2c An object with two or more different colored mana symbols in its mana cost is each of the colors of those mana symbols. Most multicolored cards are printed with a gold frame, but this is not a requirement for a card to be multicolored.
┬á
202.2d An object with one or more hybrid mana symbols and/or Phyrexian mana symbols in its mana cost is all of the colors of those mana symbols, in addition to any other colors the object might be. (Most cards with hybrid mana symbols in their mana costs are printed in a two-tone frame. See rule 107.4e.)
┬á
202.2e An object may have a color indicator printed to the left of the type line. That object is each color denoted by that color indicator. (See rule 204.)
┬á
202.2f Effects may change an objectΓÇÖs color, give a color to a colorless object, or make a colored object become colorless; see rule 105.3.
┬á
202.3. The mana value of an object is a number equal to the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color.
Example: A mana cost of {3}{U}{U} translates to a mana value of 5.
┬á
202.3a The mana value of an object with no mana cost is 0, unless that object is the back face of a nonmodal double-faced permanent or spell, or it is a melded permanent.
┬á
202.3b The mana value of the back face of a nonmodal double-faced permanent or spellΓÇÖs back face is calculated as though it had the mana cost of its front face. If a permanent or spell is a copy of the back face of a nonmodal double-faced object (even if the card representing that copy is itself a double-faced card), the mana value of the copy is 0.
Example: Huntmaster of the Fells is a nonmodal double-faced card with mana cost {2}{R}{G}. Its mana value is 4. After it transforms to its other face (Ravager of the Fells), its mana value remains 4.
Example: A Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of Ravager of the Fells. Its mana value is 0.
Example: Insectile Aberration is the back face of a nonmodal double-faced card whose front face has mana cost {U}. It becomes a copy of Ravager of the Fells. Its mana value becomes 0.
┬á
202.3c The mana value of a melded permanent is calculated as though it had the combined mana cost of the front faces of each card that represents it. If a permanent is a copy of a melded permanent (even if that copy is represented by two other meld cards), the mana value of the copy is 0.
┬á
202.3d The mana value of a split card not on the stack or of a fused split spell on the stack is determined from the combined mana costs of its halves. Otherwise, while a split card is on the stack, the mana value of the spell is determined by the mana cost of the half that was chosen to be cast. See rule 709, ΓÇ£Split Cards.ΓÇ¥
┬á
202.3e When calculating the mana value of an object with an {X} in its mana cost, X is treated as 0 while the object is not on the stack, and X is treated as the number chosen for it while the object is on the stack.
┬á
202.3f When calculating the mana value of an object with a hybrid mana symbol in its mana cost, use the largest component of each hybrid symbol.
Example: The mana value of a card with mana cost {1}{W/U}{W/U} is 3.
Example: The mana value of a card with mana cost {2/B}{2/B}{2/B} is 6.
┬á
202.3g Each Phyrexian mana symbol in a cardΓÇÖs mana cost contributes 1 to its mana value.
Example: The mana value of a card with mana cost {1}{W/P}{W/P} is 3.
┬á
202.4. Any additional cost listed in an objectΓÇÖs rules text or imposed by an effect isnΓÇÖt part of the mana cost. (See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥) Such costs are paid at the same time as the spellΓÇÖs other costs.
┬á
203. Illustration
┬á
203.1. The illustration is printed on the upper half of a card and has no effect on game play. For example, a creature doesnΓÇÖt have the flying ability unless stated in its rules text, even if itΓÇÖs depicted as flying.
┬á
204. Color Indicator
┬á
204.1. The color indicator is printed to the left of the type line directly below the illustration. It consists of a circular symbol filled in with one or more colors. A color indicator is usually found on nonland cards without a mana cost.
┬á
204.2. An object with a color indicator is each color denoted by that color indicator.
┬á
205. Type Line
┬á
205.1. The type line is printed directly below the illustration. It contains the cardΓÇÖs card type(s). It also contains the cardΓÇÖs subtype(s) and supertype(s), if applicable.
┬á
205.1a Some effects set an objectΓÇÖs card type. In most such cases, the new card type(s) replaces any existing card types. However, an object with either the instant or sorcery card type retains that type. Counters, stickers, effects, and damage marked on the object remain with it, even if they are meaningless to the new card type. Similarly, when an effect sets one or more of an objectΓÇÖs subtypes, the new subtype(s) replaces any existing subtypes from the appropriate set (creature types, land types, artifact types, enchantment types, planeswalker types, or spell types). If an objectΓÇÖs card type is removed, the subtypes correlated with that card type will remain if they are also the subtypes of a card type the object currently has; otherwise, they are also removed for the entire time the objectΓÇÖs card type is removed. Removing an objectΓÇÖs subtype doesnΓÇÖt affect its card types at all.
┬á
205.1b Some effects change an objectΓÇÖs card type, supertype, or subtype but specify that the object retains a prior card type, supertype, or subtype. In such cases, all the objectΓÇÖs prior card types, supertypes, and subtypes are retained. This rule applies to effects that use phrases such as ΓÇ£in addition to its other typesΓÇ¥ or that state that something is ΓÇ£still a [type, supertype, or subtype].ΓÇ¥ Some effects state that an object becomes an ΓÇ£artifact creatureΓÇ¥; these effects also allow the object to retain all of its prior card types and subtypes. Some effects state that an object becomes a ΓÇ£[creature type or types] artifact creatureΓÇ¥; these effects also allow the object to retain all of its prior card types and subtypes other than creature types, but replace any existing creature types.
Example: An ability reads, ΓÇ£All lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands.ΓÇ¥ The affected lands now have two card types: creature and land. If there were any lands that were also artifacts before the abilityΓÇÖs effect applied to them, those lands would become ΓÇ£artifact land creatures,ΓÇ¥ not just ΓÇ£creatures,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£land creatures.ΓÇ¥ The effect allows them to retain both the artifact and land card types. In addition, each land affected by the ability retains any land types and supertypes it had before the ability took effect.
Example: An ability reads, ΓÇ£All artifacts are 1/1 artifact creatures.ΓÇ¥ If a permanent is both an artifact and an enchantment, it will become an artifact enchantment creature.
┬á
205.2. Card Types
┬á
205.2a The card types are artifact, battle, conspiracy, creature, dungeon, enchantment, instant, kindred, land, phenomenon, plane, planeswalker, scheme, sorcery, and vanguard. See section 3, ΓÇ£Card Types.ΓÇ¥
┬á
205.2b Some objects have more than one card type (for example, an artifact creature). Such objects satisfy the criteria for any effect that applies to any of their card types.
┬á
205.2c Tokens have card types even though they arenΓÇÖt cards. The same is true of copies of spells and copies of cards.
┬á
205.3. Subtypes
┬á
205.3a A card can have one or more subtypes printed on its type line.
┬á
205.3b Subtypes of each card type except creature and plane are always single words and are listed after a long dash. Each word after the dash is a separate subtype. Subtypes of creature cards are one or two words and are listed after a long dash. Each word or two-word phrase, as listed in rule 205.3m, is a separate subtype. Objects other than planes may have multiple subtypes. Subtypes of planes are also listed after a long dash, but may be multiple words; all words after the dash are, collectively, a single subtype.
Example: ΓÇ£Basic Land ΓÇö MountainΓÇ¥ means the card is a land with the subtype Mountain. ΓÇ£Creature ΓÇö Goblin WizardΓÇ¥ means the card is a creature with the subtypes Goblin and Wizard. ΓÇ£Artifact ΓÇö EquipmentΓÇ¥ means the card is an artifact with the subtype Equipment.
┬á
205.3c If a card with multiple card types has one or more subtypes, each subtype is correlated to its appropriate card type.
Example: Dryad ArborΓÇÖs type line says ΓÇ£Land Creature ΓÇö Forest Dryad.ΓÇ¥ Forest is a land type, and Dryad is a creature type.
┬á
205.3d An object canΓÇÖt gain a subtype that doesnΓÇÖt correspond to one of that objectΓÇÖs types.
┬á
205.3e If an effect instructs a player to choose a subtype, that player must choose one, and only one, existing subtype, and the subtype must be for the appropriate card type. For example, the player canΓÇÖt choose a land type if an instruction requires choosing a creature type.
Example: When choosing a creature type, ΓÇ£MerfolkΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£WizardΓÇ¥ is acceptable, but ΓÇ£Merfolk WizardΓÇ¥ is not. Words like ΓÇ£artifact,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£opponent,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£Swamp,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£truckΓÇ¥ canΓÇÖt be chosen because they arenΓÇÖt creature types.
┬á
205.3f Many cards were printed with subtypes that are now obsolete. Many cards have retroactively received subtypes. Use the Oracle card reference to determine what a cardΓÇÖs subtypes are. (See rule 108.1.)
┬á
205.3g Artifacts have their own unique set of subtypes; these subtypes are called artifact types. The artifact types are Attraction (see rule 717), Blood, Bobblehead, Book, Clue, Contraption, Equipment (see rule 301.5), Food, Fortification (see rule 301.6), Gold, Incubator, Infinity, Junk, Lander, Map, Mutagen, Powerstone, Spacecraft, Stone, Treasure, Vehicle (see rule 301.7), and Vibranium.
┬á
205.3h Enchantments have their own unique set of subtypes; these subtypes are called enchantment types. The enchantment types are Aura (see rule 303.4), Background, Cartouche, Case (see rule 719), Class (see rule 716), Curse, Plan, Role (see rule 303.7), Room, Rune, Saga (see rule 714), Shard, and Shrine.
┬á
205.3i Lands have their own unique set of subtypes; these subtypes are called land types. The land types are Cave, Desert, Forest, Gate, Island, Lair, Locus, Mine, Mountain, Plains, Planet, Power-Plant, Sphere, Swamp, Tower, Town, and UrzaΓÇÖs. Of that list, Forest, Island, Mountain, Plains, and Swamp are the basic land types. See rule 305.6.
┬á
205.3j Planeswalkers have their own unique set of subtypes; these subtypes are called planeswalker types. The planeswalker types are Ajani, Aminatou, Angrath, Arlinn, Ashiok, Bahamut, Basri, Bolas, Calix, Chandra, Comet, Dack, Dakkon, Daretti, Davriel, Dellian, Dihada, Domri, Dovin, Ellywick, Elminster, Elspeth, Estrid, Freyalise, Garruk, Gideon, Grist, Guff, Huatli, Jace, Jared, Jaya, Jeska, Kaito, Karn, Kasmina, Kaya, Kiora, Koth, Liliana, Lolth, Lukka, Minsc, Mordenkainen, Nahiri, Narset, Niko, Nissa, Nixilis, Oko, Quintorius, Ral, Rowan, Saheeli, Samut, Sarkhan, Serra, Sivitri, Sorin, Szat, Tamiyo, Tasha, Teferi, Teyo, Tezzeret, Tibalt, Tyvar, Ugin, Urza, Venser, Vivien, Vraska, Vronos, Will, Windgrace, Wrenn, Xenagos, Yanggu, Yanling, and Zariel.
┬á
205.3k Instants and sorceries share their lists of subtypes; these subtypes are called spell types. The spell types are Adventure, Arcane, Lesson, Omen, and Trap.
┬á
205.3m Creatures and kindreds share their lists of subtypes; these subtypes are called creature types. One creature type is two words long: Time Lord. All other creature types are one word long: Advisor, Aetherborn, Alien, Ally, Angel, Antelope, Ape, Archer, Archon, Armadillo, Army, Artificer, Assassin, Assembly-Worker, Astartes, Atog, Aurochs, Avatar, Azra, Badger, Balloon, Barbarian, Bard, Basilisk, Bat, Bear, Beast, Beaver, Beeble, Beholder, Berserker, Bird, Bison, Blinkmoth, Boar, Bringer, Brushwagg, Camarid, Camel, Capybara, Caribou, Carrier, Cat, Centaur, Child, Chimera, Citizen, Cleric, Clown, Cockatrice, Construct, Coward, Coyote, Crab, Crocodile, CΓÇÖtan, Custodes, Cyberman, Cyclops, Dalek, Dauthi, Demigod, Demon, Deserter, Detective, Devil, Dinosaur, Djinn, Doctor, Dog, Dragon, Drake, Dreadnought, Drix, Drone, Druid, Dryad, Dwarf, Echidna, Efreet, Egg, Elder, Eldrazi, Elemental, Elephant, Elf, Elk, Employee, Eternal, Eye, Faerie, Ferret, Fish, Flagbearer, Fox, Fractal, Frog, Fungus, Gamer, Gamma, Gargoyle, Germ, Giant, Giraffe, Gith, Glimmer, Gnoll, Gnome, Goat, Goblin, God, Golem, Gorgon, Graveborn, Gremlin, Griffin, Guest, Hag, Halfling, Hamster, Harpy, Hedgehog, Hellion, Hero, Hippo, Hippogriff, Homarid, Homunculus, Horror, Horse, Human, Hydra, Hyena, Illusion, Imp, Incarnation, Inhuman, Inkling, Inquisitor, Insect, Jackal, Jellyfish, Juggernaut, Kangaroo, Kavu, Kirin, Kithkin, Knight, Kobold, Kor, Kraken, Kree, Llama, Lamia, Lammasu, Leech, Lemur, Leviathan, Lhurgoyf, Licid, Lizard, Lobster, Nightmare, Nightstalker, Ninja, Noble, Noggle, Nomad, Nymph, Octopus, Ogre, Ooze, Orb, Orc, Orgg, Otter, Ouphe, Ox, Oyster, Pangolin, Peasant, Pegasus, Pentavite, Performer, Pest, Phelddagrif, Skeleton, Skrull, Skunk, Slith, Sliver, Sloth, Slug, Snail, Snake, Soldier, Soltari, Sorcerer, Spawn, Specter, Spellshaper, Sphinx, Spider, Spike, Spirit, Splinter, Sponge, Spy, Squid, Squirrel, Varmint, Vedalken, Villain, Volver, Wall, Walrus, Warlock, Warrior, Weasel, Weird, Werewolf, Whale, Wizard, Wolf, Wolverine, Wombat, Worm, Wraith, Wurm, Yeti, Zombie, and Zubera.
┬á
205.3n Planes have their own unique set of subtypes; these subtypes are called planar types. 205.4. Supertypes
┬á
205.4a An object can have one or more supertypes. A cardΓÇÖs supertypes are printed directly before its card types. The supertypes are basic, legendary, ongoing, snow, and world.
┬á
205.4b An objectΓÇÖs supertype is independent of its card type and subtype, even though some supertypes are closely identified with specific card types. Changing an objectΓÇÖs card types or subtypes wonΓÇÖt change its supertypes. Changing an objectΓÇÖs supertypes wonΓÇÖt change its card types or subtypes. When an object gains or loses a supertype, it retains any other supertypes it had.
Example: An ability reads, ΓÇ£All lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands.ΓÇ¥ If any of the affected lands were legendary, they are still legendary.
┬á
205.4c Any land with the supertype ΓÇ£basicΓÇ¥ is a basic land. Any land that doesnΓÇÖt have this supertype is a nonbasic land, even if it has a basic land type.ΓÇ¿┬á┬á┬á┬á Cards printed in sets prior to the Eighth Edition core set didnΓÇÖt use the word ΓÇ£basicΓÇ¥ to indicate a basic land. Cards from those sets with the following names are basic lands and have received errata in the Oracle card reference accordingly: Forest, Island, Mountain, Plains, Swamp, Snow-Covered Forest, Snow-Covered Island, Snow-Covered Mountain, Snow-Covered Plains, and Snow-Covered Swamp.

205.4d Any permanent with the supertype ΓÇ£legendaryΓÇ¥ is subject to the state-based action for legendary permanents, also called the ΓÇ£legend ruleΓÇ¥ (see rule 704.5j).
┬á
205.4e Any instant or sorcery spell with the supertype ΓÇ£legendaryΓÇ¥ is subject to a casting restriction. A player canΓÇÖt cast a legendary instant or sorcery spell unless that player controls a legendary creature or a legendary planeswalker.
┬á
205.4f Any permanent with the supertype ΓÇ£worldΓÇ¥ is subject to the state-based action for world permanents, also called the ΓÇ£world ruleΓÇ¥ (see rule 704.5k).
┬á
205.4g Any permanent with the supertype ΓÇ£snowΓÇ¥ is a snow permanent. Any permanent that doesnΓÇÖt have this supertype is a nonsnow permanent, regardless of its name.
┬á
205.4h Any scheme card with the supertype ΓÇ£ongoingΓÇ¥ is exempt from the state-based action for schemes (see rule 704.6e).
