207. Text Box
┬á
207.1. The text box is printed on the lower half of the card. It usually contains rules text defining the cardΓÇÖs abilities.
┬á
207.2. The text box may also contain italicized text that has no game function.
┬á
207.2a Reminder text is italicized text within parentheses that summarizes a rule that applies to that card. It usually appears on the same line as the ability itΓÇÖs relevant to, but it may appear on its own line if it applies to an aspect of the card other than an ability.
┬á
207.2b Flavor text is italicized text that, like the illustration, adds artistic appeal to the game. It usually appears below the rules text.
┬á
207.2c An ability word appears in italics at the beginning of some abilities. Ability words are similar to keywords in that they tie together cards that have similar functionality, but they have no special rules meaning and no individual entries in the Comprehensive Rules. The ability words are adamant, addendum, alliance, battalion, bloodrush, celebration, channel, chroma, cohort, constellation, converge, councilΓÇÖs dilemma, coven, delirium, descend 4, descend 8, disappear, domain, eerie, eminence, enrage, fateful hour, fathomless descent, ferocious, flurry, formidable, grandeur, hellbent, heroic, imprint, infusion, inspired, join forces, kinship, landfall, lieutenant, magecraft, metalcraft, morbid, opus, pack tactics, paradox, parley, radiance, raid, rally, renew, repartee, revolt, secret council, spell mastery, strive, survival, sweep, tempting offer, threshold, undergrowth, valiant, vivid, void, and will of the council.
┬á
207.2d Similar to ability words, flavor words appear in italics at the beginning of some abilities. Flavor words provide a flavorful description of abilities, but they have no special rules meaning and are not listed in the Comprehensive Rules. While an ability word ties together several abilities with similar functionality, each flavor word is tailored to the specific ability it appears with.
┬á
207.3. Some cards have decorative icons in the background of their text boxes. For example, a guild icon appears in the text box of many cards associated with the guilds of Ravnica, and a faction icon appears in the text box of most Scars of MirrodinΓäó block cards. Similarly, many promotional cards include decorative icons. These icons have no effect on game play.
┬á
207.4. The chaos symbol appears in the text box of each plane card to the left of a triggered ability that triggers whenever chaos ensues. The symbol itself has no special rules meaning. See rule 901, ΓÇ£Planechase.ΓÇ¥
┬á
207.5. One card (Cryptic Spires) has a set of symbols below the text box that represent each color and an ability that instructs a player to circle two of those colors as they create their deck. To circle a color, the player circles (or otherwise clearly indicates) that colorΓÇÖs symbol. The mana symbol of each circled color is considered part of that cardΓÇÖs printed rules text (see rule 613.1) and affects that cardΓÇÖs color identity (see rule 903.4).
┬á
208. Power/Toughness
┬á
208.1. A creature card has two numbers separated by a slash printed in its lower right corner. The first number is its power (the amount of damage it deals in combat); the second is its toughness (the amount of damage needed to destroy it). For example, 2/3 means the object has power 2 and toughness 3. Power and toughness can be modified or set to particular values by effects.
┬á
208.2. Rather than a fixed number, some creature cards have power and/or toughness that includes a star (*).
┬á
208.2a The card may have a characteristic-defining ability that sets its power and/or toughness according to some stated condition. (See rule 604.3.) Such an ability is worded ΓÇ£[This creatureΓÇÖs] [power or toughness] is equal to . . .ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£[This creatureΓÇÖs] power and toughness are each equal to . . .ΓÇ¥ This ability functions everywhere, even outside the game. If the ability needs to use a number that canΓÇÖt be determined, including inside a calculation, use 0 instead of that number.
Example: Lost Order of Jarkeld has power and toughness each equal to 1+*. It has the abilities ΓÇ£As this creature enters, choose an opponentΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£Lost Order of JarkeldΓÇÖs power and toughness are each equal to 1 plus the number of creatures the chosen player controls.ΓÇ¥ While Lost Order of Jarkeld isnΓÇÖt on the battlefield, there wonΓÇÖt be a chosen player. Its power and toughness will each be equal to 1 plus 0, so itΓÇÖs 1/1.
┬á
208.2b The card may have a static ability that creates a replacement effect that sets the creatureΓÇÖs power and toughness to one of a number of specific values as it enters the battlefield or is turned face up. (See rule 614, ΓÇ£Replacement Effects.ΓÇ¥) Such an ability is worded ΓÇ£As [this creature] enters . . . ,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£As [this creature] is turned face up . . . ,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£[This creature] enters as . . .ΓÇ¥ and lists two or more specific power and toughness values (and may also list additional characteristics). The characteristics chosen or determined with these effects affect the creatureΓÇÖs copiable values. (See rule 707.2.) While the card isnΓÇÖt on the battlefield, its power and toughness are each considered to be 0.
┬á
208.3. A noncreature permanent has no power or toughness, even if itΓÇÖs a card with a power and toughness printed on it (such as a Vehicle). A noncreature object not on the battlefield has power or toughness only if it has a power and toughness printed on it.
┬á
208.3a If an effect would be created that sets the base power and/or toughness of a noncreature permanent, or otherwise modifies its power and/or toughness, that effect is created even though it doesnΓÇÖt do anything unless that permanent becomes a creature.
Example: Veteran Motorist has the ability ΓÇ£Whenever this creature crews a Vehicle, that Vehicle gets +1/+1 until end of turn,ΓÇ¥ and itΓÇÖs tapped to pay the crew cost of a Vehicle. This triggered ability resolves while the Vehicle it crewed isnΓÇÖt yet a creature. The continuous effect is created and will apply to the Vehicle once it becomes a creature.
┬á
208.4. Some effects refer to a creatureΓÇÖs ΓÇ£base power,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£base toughness,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£base power and toughness.ΓÇ¥
┬á
208.4a Effects that set a creatureΓÇÖs power and/or toughness to specific values may refer to base power and/or toughness. Other continuous effects may further modify the creatureΓÇÖs power and toughness. See rule 613, ΓÇ£Interaction of Continuous Effects.ΓÇ¥
┬á
208.4b Some effects check a creatureΓÇÖs base power and/or toughness. These effects see that creatureΓÇÖs characteristics after applying any characteristic-defining abilities and abilities that set power and/or toughness, ignoring any effects and counters that modify power and/or toughness without setting them. See rule 613, ΓÇ£Interaction of Continuous Effects.ΓÇ¥
┬á
208.5. If a creature somehow has no value for its power, its power is 0. The same is true for toughness.
┬á
209. Loyalty
┬á
209.1. Each planeswalker card has a loyalty number printed in its lower right corner. This indicates its loyalty while itΓÇÖs not on the battlefield, and it also indicates that the planeswalker enters the battlefield with that many loyalty counters on it (see rule 306.5b).
┬á
209.2. An activated ability with a loyalty symbol in its cost is a loyalty ability. Loyalty abilities follow special rules: A player may activate a loyalty ability of a permanent they control any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn, but only if none of that permanentΓÇÖs loyalty abilities have been activated that turn. See rule 606, ΓÇ£Loyalty Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
210. Defense
┬á
210.1. Each battle card has a defense number printed in its lower right corner. This indicates its defense while itΓÇÖs not on the battlefield, and it also indicates that the battle enters the battlefield with that many defense counters on it (see rule 310.4b).
┬á
211. Hand Modifier
┬á
211.1. Each vanguard card has a hand modifier printed in its lower left corner. This is a number preceded by a plus sign, a number preceded by a minus sign, or a zero. This modifier is applied as the starting hand size and the maximum hand size of the vanguard cardΓÇÖs owner are determined. See rule 103.5.
┬á
212. Life Modifier
┬á
212.1. Each vanguard card has a life modifier printed in its lower right corner. This is a number preceded by a plus sign, a number preceded by a minus sign, or a zero. This modifier is applied as the starting life total of the vanguard cardΓÇÖs owner is determined. See rule 103.4.
┬á
213. Information Below the Text Box
┬á
213.1. Each card features text printed below the text box that has no effect on game play. Not all card sets were printed with all of the information listed below on each card.
┬á
213.1a Most card sets feature collector numbers. This information is printed in the form [card number]/[total cards in the set] or simply [card number]. Some cards, such as unique cards in Planeswalker Decks┬«, have card numbers that exceed the listed total number of cards.
┬á
213.1b A cardΓÇÖs rarity is indicated with a single letter following the collector number.
┬á
213.1c Some promotional cards include information to indicate the specific promotion the card is associated with.
┬á
213.1d Some cards with interchangeable names include information about a specific version of a card with that interchangeable name. See rule 201.3.
┬á
213.1e The three-character code representing the set in which a card is printed and the two-character code representing the language in which a card is printed are separated by a bullet point. If a card is premium, these codes are instead separated by a star.
┬á
213.1f The illustration credit for a card follows the paintbrush icon or, on older cards, the abbreviation ΓÇ£Illus.ΓÇ¥
┬á
213.1g Legal text (the fine print at the bottom or bottom-right of the card) lists the trademark and copyright information.

3. Card Types
┬á
300. General
┬á
300.1. The card types are artifact, battle, conspiracy, creature, dungeon, enchantment, instant, kindred, land, phenomenon, plane, planeswalker, scheme, sorcery, and vanguard.
┬á
300.2. Some objects have more than one card type (for example, an artifact creature). Such objects combine the aspects of each of those card types, and are subject to spells and abilities that affect either or all of those card types.
┬á
300.2a An object thatΓÇÖs both a land and another card type (for example, an artifact land) can only be played as a land. It canΓÇÖt be cast as a spell.
┬á
300.2b Each kindred card has another card type. Casting and resolving a kindred card follow the rules for casting and resolving a card of the other card type.
┬á
301. Artifacts
┬á
301.1. A player who has priority may cast an artifact card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty. Casting an artifact as a spell uses the stack. (See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
301.2. When an artifact spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control.
┬á
301.3. Artifact subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: ΓÇ£Artifact ΓÇö Equipment.ΓÇ¥ Artifact subtypes are also called artifact types. Artifacts may have multiple subtypes. See rule 205.3g for the complete list of artifact types.
┬á
301.4. Artifacts have no characteristics specific to their card type. Most artifacts have no colored mana symbols in their mana costs, and are therefore colorless. However, there is no correlation between being colorless and being an artifact: artifacts may be colored, and colorless objects may be card types other than artifact.
┬á
301.5. Some artifacts have the subtype ΓÇ£Equipment.ΓÇ¥ An Equipment can be attached to a creature. It canΓÇÖt legally be attached to anything that isnΓÇÖt a creature.
┬á
301.5a The creature an Equipment is attached to is called the ΓÇ£equipped creature.ΓÇ¥ The Equipment is attached to, or ΓÇ£equips,ΓÇ¥ that creature.
┬á
301.5b Equipment spells are cast like other artifact spells. Equipment enter the battlefield like other artifacts. They donΓÇÖt enter the battlefield attached to a creature. The equip keyword ability attaches the Equipment to a creature you control (see rule 702.6, ΓÇ£EquipΓÇ¥). Control of the creature matters only when the equip ability is activated and when it resolves. Spells and other abilities may also attach an Equipment to a creature. If an effect attempts to attach an Equipment to an object that canΓÇÖt be equipped by it, the Equipment doesnΓÇÖt move.
┬á
301.5c An Equipment thatΓÇÖs also a creature canΓÇÖt equip a creature unless that Equipment has reconfigure (see rule 702.151, ΓÇ£ReconfigureΓÇ¥). An Equipment that loses the subtype ΓÇ£EquipmentΓÇ¥ canΓÇÖt equip a creature. An Equipment canΓÇÖt equip itself. An Equipment that equips an illegal or nonexistent permanent becomes unattached from that permanent but remains on the battlefield. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.) An Equipment canΓÇÖt equip more than one creature. If a spell or ability would cause an Equipment to equip more than one creature, the EquipmentΓÇÖs controller chooses which creature it equips.
┬á
301.5d An EquipmentΓÇÖs controller is separate from the equipped creatureΓÇÖs controller; the two need not be the same. Changing control of the creature doesnΓÇÖt change control of the Equipment, and vice versa. Only the EquipmentΓÇÖs controller can activate its abilities. However, if the Equipment grants an ability to the equipped creature (with ΓÇ£gainsΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£hasΓÇ¥), the equipped creatureΓÇÖs controller is the only one who can activate that ability.
┬á
301.5e If an effect attempts to put an Equipment that isnΓÇÖt also an Aura (see rule 303.4i) onto the battlefield attached to either an object it canΓÇÖt legally equip or an object that is undefined, the Equipment enters the battlefield unattached. If the Equipment is a token, itΓÇÖs created and enters the battlefield unattached.
┬á
301.5f An ability of a permanent that refers to the ΓÇ£equipped creatureΓÇ¥ refers to whatever creature that permanent is attached to, even if the permanent with the ability isnΓÇÖt an Equipment.
┬á
301.6. Some artifacts have the subtype ΓÇ£Fortification.ΓÇ¥ A Fortification can be attached to a land. It canΓÇÖt legally be attached to an object that isnΓÇÖt a land. FortificationΓÇÖs analog to the equip keyword ability is the fortify keyword ability. Rules 301.5aΓÇôf apply to Fortifications in relation to lands just as they apply to Equipment in relation to creatures, with one clarification relating to rule 301.5c: a Fortification thatΓÇÖs also a creature (not a land) canΓÇÖt fortify a land. (See rule 702.67, ΓÇ£Fortify.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
301.7. Some artifacts have the subtype ΓÇ£Vehicle.ΓÇ¥ Most Vehicles have a crew ability which allows them to become artifact creatures. See rule 702.122, ΓÇ£Crew.ΓÇ¥
┬á
301.7a Each Vehicle has a printed power and toughness, but it has these characteristics only if itΓÇÖs also a creature. See rule 208.3.
┬á
301.7b If a Vehicle becomes a creature, it immediately has its printed power and toughness. Other effects, including the effect that makes it a creature, may modify these values or set them to different values.
┬á
302. Creatures
┬á
302.1. A player who has priority may cast a creature card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty. Casting a creature as a spell uses the stack. (See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
302.2. When a creature spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control.
┬á
302.3. Creature subtypes are usually a single word long and are listed after a long dash: ΓÇ£Creature ΓÇö Human Soldier,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£Artifact Creature ΓÇö Golem,ΓÇ¥ and so on. Creature subtypes are also called creature types. Creatures may have multiple subtypes. See rule 205.3m for the complete list of creature types.
Example: ΓÇ£Creature ΓÇö Goblin WizardΓÇ¥ means the card is a creature with the subtypes Goblin and Wizard.
┬á
302.4. Power and toughness are characteristics only creatures have.
┬á
302.4a A creatureΓÇÖs power is the amount of damage it deals in combat.
┬á
302.4b A creatureΓÇÖs toughness is the amount of damage needed to destroy it.
┬á
302.4c To determine a creatureΓÇÖs power and toughness, start with the numbers printed in its lower right corner, then apply any applicable continuous effects. (See rule 613, ΓÇ£Interaction of Continuous Effects.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
302.5. Creatures can attack and block. (See rule 508, ΓÇ£Declare Attackers Step,ΓÇ¥ and rule 509, ΓÇ£Declare Blockers Step.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
302.6. A creatureΓÇÖs activated ability with the tap symbol or the untap symbol in its activation cost canΓÇÖt be activated unless the creature has been under its controllerΓÇÖs control continuously since their most recent turn began. A creature canΓÇÖt attack unless it has been under its controllerΓÇÖs control continuously since their most recent turn began. This rule is informally called the ΓÇ£summoning sicknessΓÇ¥ rule.
┬á
302.7. Damage dealt to a creature by a source with neither wither nor infect is marked on that creature (see rule 120.3). If the total damage marked on that creature is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed as a state-based action (see rule 704). All damage marked on a creature is removed when it regenerates (see rule 701.19, ΓÇ£RegenerateΓÇ¥) and during the cleanup step (see rule 514.2).
┬á
303. Enchantments
┬á
303.1. A player who has priority may cast an enchantment card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty. Casting an enchantment as a spell uses the stack. (See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
303.2. When an enchantment spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control.
┬á
303.3. Enchantment subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: ΓÇ£Enchantment ΓÇö Shrine.ΓÇ¥ Each word after the dash is a separate subtype. Enchantment subtypes are also called enchantment types. Enchantments may have multiple subtypes. See rule 205.3h for the complete list of enchantment types.
┬á
303.4. Some enchantments have the subtype ΓÇ£Aura.ΓÇ¥ An Aura enters the battlefield attached to an object or player. What an Aura can be attached to is defined by its enchant keyword ability (see rule 702.5, ΓÇ£EnchantΓÇ¥). Other effects can limit what a permanent can be enchanted by.
┬á
303.4a An Aura spell requires a target, which is defined by its enchant ability.
┬á
303.4b The object or player an Aura is attached to is called enchanted. The Aura is attached to, or ΓÇ£enchants,ΓÇ¥ that object or player.
┬á
303.4c If an Aura is enchanting an illegal object or player as defined by its enchant ability and other applicable effects, the object it was attached to no longer exists, or the player it was attached to has left the game, the Aura is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.)
┬á
303.4d An Aura canΓÇÖt enchant itself. If this occurs somehow, the Aura is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. An Aura thatΓÇÖs also a creature canΓÇÖt enchant anything. If this occurs somehow, the Aura becomes unattached, then is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. (These are state-based actions. See rule 704.) An Aura canΓÇÖt enchant more than one object or player. If a spell or ability would cause an Aura to become attached to more than one object or player, the AuraΓÇÖs controller chooses which object or player it becomes attached to.
┬á
303.4e An AuraΓÇÖs controller is separate from the enchanted objectΓÇÖs controller or the enchanted player; the two need not be the same. If an Aura enchants an object, changing control of the object doesnΓÇÖt change control of the Aura, and vice versa. Only the AuraΓÇÖs controller can activate its abilities. However, if the Aura grants an ability to the enchanted object (with ΓÇ£gainsΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£hasΓÇ¥), the enchanted objectΓÇÖs controller is the only one who can activate that ability.
┬á
303.4f If an Aura is entering the battlefield under a playerΓÇÖs control by any means other than by resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesnΓÇÖt specify the object or player the Aura will enchant, that player chooses what it will enchant as the Aura enters the battlefield. The player must choose a legal object or player according to the AuraΓÇÖs enchant ability and any other applicable effects.
┬á
303.4g If an Aura is entering the battlefield and there is no legal object or player for it to enchant, the Aura remains in its current zone, unless that zone is the stack. In that case, the Aura is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard instead of entering the battlefield. If the Aura is a token, it isnΓÇÖt created.
┬á
303.4h If an effect attempts to put a permanent that isnΓÇÖt an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification onto the battlefield attached to an object or player, it enters the battlefield unattached.
┬á
303.4i If an effect attempts to put an Aura onto the battlefield attached to either an object or player it canΓÇÖt legally enchant or an object or player that is undefined, the Aura remains in its current zone, unless that zone is the stack. In that case, the Aura is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard instead of entering the battlefield. If the Aura is a token, it isnΓÇÖt created.
┬á
303.4j If an effect attempts to attach an Aura on the battlefield to an object or player it canΓÇÖt legally enchant, the Aura doesnΓÇÖt move.
┬á
303.4k If an effect allows an Aura thatΓÇÖs being turned face up to become attached to an object or player, the AuraΓÇÖs controller considers the characteristics of that Aura as it would exist if it were face up to determine what it may be attached to, and they must choose a legal object or player according to the AuraΓÇÖs enchant ability and any other applicable effects.
┬á
303.4m An ability of a permanent that refers to the ΓÇ£enchanted [object or player]ΓÇ¥ refers to whatever object or player that permanent is attached to, even if the permanent with the ability isnΓÇÖt an Aura.
┬á
303.5. Some enchantments have the subtype ΓÇ£Saga.ΓÇ¥ See rule 714 for more information about Saga cards.
┬á
303.6. Some enchantments have the subtype ΓÇ£Class.ΓÇ¥ See rule 716 for more information about Class cards.
┬á
303.7. Some Aura enchantments also have the subtype ΓÇ£Role.ΓÇ¥
┬á
303.7a If a permanent has more than one Role controlled by the same player attached to it, each of those Roles except the one with the most recent timestamp is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. This is a state-based action. See rule 704.
┬á
304. Instants
┬á
304.1. A player who has priority may cast an instant card from their hand. Casting an instant as a spell uses the stack. (See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
304.2. When an instant spell resolves, the actions stated in its rules text are followed. Then itΓÇÖs put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard.
┬á
304.3. Instant subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: ΓÇ£Instant ΓÇö Arcane.ΓÇ¥ Each word after the dash is a separate subtype. The set of instant subtypes is the same as the set of sorcery subtypes; these subtypes are called spell types. Instants may have multiple subtypes. See rule 205.3k for the complete list of spell types.
┬á
304.4. Instants canΓÇÖt enter the battlefield. If an instant would enter the battlefield, it remains in its previous zone instead.
┬á
304.5. If text states that a player may do something ΓÇ£any time they could cast an instantΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£only as an instant,ΓÇ¥ it means only that the player must have priority. The player doesnΓÇÖt need to have an instant card they could cast. Effects that would preclude that player from casting an instant spell donΓÇÖt affect the playerΓÇÖs capability to perform that action (unless the action is actually casting an instant spell).

305. Lands
┬á
305.1. A player who has priority may play a land card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty. Playing a land is a special action; it doesnΓÇÖt use the stack (see rule 116). Rather, the player simply puts the land onto the battlefield. Since the land doesnΓÇÖt go on the stack, it is never a spell, and players canΓÇÖt respond to it with instants or activated abilities.
┬á
305.2. A player can normally play one land during their turn; however, continuous effects may increase this number.
┬á
305.2a To determine whether a player can play a land, compare the number of lands the player can play this turn with the number of lands they have already played this turn (including lands played as special actions and lands played during the resolution of spells and abilities). If the number of lands the player can play is greater, the play is legal.
┬á
305.2b A player canΓÇÖt play a land, for any reason, if the number of lands the player can play this turn is equal to or less than the number of lands they have already played this turn. Ignore any part of an effect that instructs a player to do so.
┬á
305.3. A player canΓÇÖt play a land, for any reason, if it isnΓÇÖt their turn. Ignore any part of an effect that instructs a player to do so.
┬á
305.4. Effects may also allow players to ΓÇ£putΓÇ¥ lands onto the battlefield. This isnΓÇÖt the same as ΓÇ£playing a landΓÇ¥ and doesnΓÇÖt count as a land played during the current turn.
┬á
305.5. Land subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash. Land subtypes are also called land types. Lands may have multiple subtypes. See rule 205.3i for the complete list of land types.
Example: ΓÇ£Basic Land ΓÇö MountainΓÇ¥ means the card is a land with the subtype Mountain.
┬á
305.6. The basic land types are Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest. If an object uses the words ΓÇ£basic land type,ΓÇ¥ itΓÇÖs referring to one of these subtypes. An object with the land card type and a basic land type has the intrinsic ability ΓÇ£{T}: Add [mana symbol],ΓÇ¥ even if the text box doesnΓÇÖt actually contain that text or the object has no text box. For Plains, [mana symbol] is {W}; for Islands, {U}; for Swamps, {B}; for Mountains, {R}; and for Forests, {G}. See rule 107.4a. See also rule 605, ΓÇ£Mana Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
305.7. If an effect sets a landΓÇÖs subtype to one or more of the basic land types, the land no longer has its old land type. It loses all abilities generated from its rules text, its old land types, and any copiable effects affecting that land, and it gains the appropriate mana ability for each new basic land type. Note that this doesnΓÇÖt remove any abilities that were granted to the land by other effects. Setting a landΓÇÖs subtype doesnΓÇÖt add or remove any card types (such as creature) or supertypes (such as basic, legendary, and snow) the land may have. If a land gains one or more land types in addition to its own, it keeps its land types and rules text, and it gains the new land types and mana abilities.
┬á
305.8. Any land with the supertype ΓÇ£basicΓÇ¥ is a basic land. Any land that doesnΓÇÖt have this supertype is a nonbasic land, even if it has a basic land type.
┬á
305.9. If an object is both a land and another card type, it can be played only as a land. It canΓÇÖt be cast as a spell.
┬á
306. Planeswalkers
┬á
306.1. A player who has priority may cast a planeswalker card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty. Casting a planeswalker as a spell uses the stack. (See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
306.2. When a planeswalker spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control.
┬á
306.3. Planeswalker subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: ΓÇ£Planeswalker ΓÇö Jace.ΓÇ¥ Each word after the dash is a separate subtype. Planeswalker subtypes are also called planeswalker types. Planeswalkers may have multiple subtypes. See rule 205.3j for the complete list of planeswalker types.
┬á
306.4. Previously, planeswalkers were subject to a ΓÇ£planeswalker uniqueness ruleΓÇ¥ that stopped a player from controlling two planeswalkers of the same planeswalker type. This rule has been removed and planeswalker cards printed before this change have received errata in the Oracle card reference to have the legendary supertype. Like other legendary permanents, they are subject to the ΓÇ£legend ruleΓÇ¥ (see rule 704.5j).
┬á
306.5. Loyalty is a characteristic only planeswalkers have.
┬á
306.5a The loyalty of a planeswalker card not on the battlefield is equal to the number printed in its lower right corner.
┬á
306.5b A planeswalker has the intrinsic ability ΓÇ£This permanent enters with a number of loyalty counters on it equal to its printed loyalty number.ΓÇ¥ This ability creates a replacement effect (see rule 614.1c).
┬á
306.5c The loyalty of a planeswalker on the battlefield is equal to the number of loyalty counters on it.
┬á
306.5d Each planeswalker has a number of loyalty abilities, which are activated abilities with loyalty symbols in their costs. Loyalty abilities follow special rules: A player may activate a loyalty ability of a permanent they control any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn, but only if none of that permanentΓÇÖs loyalty abilities have been activated that turn. See rule 606, ΓÇ£Loyalty Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
306.6. Planeswalkers can be attacked. (See rule 508, ΓÇ£Declare Attackers Step.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
306.7. Previously, planeswalkers were subject to a redirection effect that allowed a player to have noncombat damage that would be dealt to an opponent be dealt to a planeswalker under that opponentΓÇÖs control instead. This rule has been removed and certain cards have received errata in the Oracle card reference to deal damage directly to planeswalkers.
┬á
306.8. Damage dealt to a planeswalker results in that many loyalty counters being removed from it.
┬á
306.9. If a planeswalkerΓÇÖs loyalty is 0, itΓÇÖs put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.)

307. Sorceries
┬á
307.1. A player who has priority may cast a sorcery card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty. Casting a sorcery as a spell uses the stack. (See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
307.2. When a sorcery spell resolves, the actions stated in its rules text are followed. Then itΓÇÖs put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard.
┬á
307.3. Sorcery subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: ΓÇ£Sorcery ΓÇö Arcane.ΓÇ¥ Each word after the dash is a separate subtype. The set of sorcery subtypes is the same as the set of instant subtypes; these subtypes are called spell types. Sorceries may have multiple subtypes. See rule 205.3k for the complete list of spell types.
┬á
307.4. Sorceries canΓÇÖt enter the battlefield. If a sorcery would enter the battlefield, it remains in its previous zone instead.
┬á
307.5. If a spell, ability, or effect states that a player can do something only ΓÇ£any time they could cast a sorceryΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£only as a sorcery,ΓÇ¥ it means only that the player must have priority, it must be during the main phase of their turn, and the stack must be empty. The player doesnΓÇÖt need to have a sorcery card they could cast. Effects that would preclude that player from casting a sorcery spell donΓÇÖt affect the playerΓÇÖs capability to perform that action (unless the action is actually casting a sorcery spell).
┬á
307.5a Similarly, if an effect checks to see if a spell was cast ΓÇ£any time a sorcery couldnΓÇÖt have been cast,ΓÇ¥ itΓÇÖs checking only whether the spellΓÇÖs controller cast it without having priority, during a phase other than their main phase, or while another object was on the stack.

308. Kindreds
┬á
308.1. Each kindred card has another card type. Casting and resolving a kindred card follows the rules for casting and resolving a card of the other card type.
┬á
308.2. Kindred subtypes are usually a single word long and are listed after a long dash: ΓÇ£Kindred Enchantment ΓÇö Merfolk.ΓÇ¥ The set of kindred subtypes is the same as the set of creature subtypes; these subtypes are called creature types. Kindreds may have multiple subtypes. See rule 205.3m for the complete list of creature types.
┬á
308.3. Some older kindred cards were printed with the ΓÇ£tribalΓÇ¥ card type. Cards printed with that type have received errata in the Oracle card reference.

309. Dungeons
┬á
309.1. Dungeon is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards.
┬á
309.2. Dungeon cards begin outside the game. Dungeon cards arenΓÇÖt part of a playerΓÇÖs deck or sideboard. They are brought into the game using the venture into the dungeon keyword action. See rule 701.49, ΓÇ£Venture into the Dungeon.ΓÇ¥
┬á
309.2a If a player ventures into the dungeon while they donΓÇÖt own a dungeon card in the command zone, they choose a dungeon card they own from outside the game and put it into the command zone.
┬á
309.2b A dungeon card thatΓÇÖs brought into the game is put into the command zone until it leaves the game.
┬á
309.2c Dungeon cards are not permanents. They canΓÇÖt be cast. Dungeon cards canΓÇÖt leave the command zone except as they leave the game.
┬á
309.2d If an effect other than a venture into the dungeon keyword action would bring a dungeon card into the game from outside the game, it doesnΓÇÖt; that card remains outside the game.
┬á
309.3. A player can own only one dungeon card in the command zone at a time, and they canΓÇÖt bring a dungeon card into the game if a dungeon card they own is in the command zone.
┬á
309.4. Each dungeon card has a series of rooms connected to one another with arrows. A player uses a venture marker placed on the dungeon card they own to indicate which room they are currently in.
┬á
309.4a As a player puts a dungeon they own into the command zone, they put their venture marker on the topmost room.
┬á
309.4b Each room has a name. These names are considered flavor text and do not affect game play.
┬á
309.4c Each room has a triggered ability called a room ability whose effect is printed on the card. They all have the same trigger condition not printed on the card. The full text of each room ability is ΓÇ£When you move your venture marker into this room, [effect.]ΓÇ¥ As long as a dungeon card is in the command zone, its abilities may trigger. Each room ability is controlled by the player who owns the dungeon card that is that abilityΓÇÖs source.
┬á
309.5. The venture into the dungeon keyword action allows players to move their venture marker down the rooms of a dungeon card.
┬á
309.5a If a player ventures into the dungeon while they own a dungeon card in the command zone and their venture marker isnΓÇÖt on that dungeonΓÇÖs bottommost room, they move their venture marker from the room it is on to the next room, following the direction of an arrow pointing away from the room their venture marker is on. If there are multiple arrows pointing away from the room the playerΓÇÖs venture marker is on, they choose one of them to follow.
┬á
309.5b If a player ventures into the dungeon while they own a dungeon card in the command zone and their venture marker is on that dungeon cardΓÇÖs bottommost room, they remove that dungeon card from the game. They then choose a dungeon card they own from outside the game and put it into the command zone. They put their venture marker on the topmost room.
┬á
309.6. If a playerΓÇÖs venture marker is on the bottommost room of a dungeon card, and that dungeon card isnΓÇÖt the source of a room ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, the dungeon cardΓÇÖs owner removes it from the game. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.)
┬á
309.7. A player completes a dungeon as that dungeon card is removed from the game.
┬á
310. Battles
┬á
310.1. A player who has priority may cast a battle card from their hand during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty. Casting a battle as a spell uses the stack. (See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
310.2. When a battle spell resolves, its controller puts it onto the battlefield under their control.
┬á
310.3. Battle subtypes are always a single word and are listed after a long dash: ΓÇ£Battle ΓÇö Siege.ΓÇ¥ Battle subtypes are also called battle types. See rule 205.3q for the complete list of battle types.
┬á
310.4. Defense is a characteristic that battles have.
┬á
310.4a The defense of a battle card not on the battlefield is equal to the number printed in its lower right corner.
┬á
310.4b A battle has the intrinsic ability ΓÇ£This permanent enters with a number of defense counters on it equal to its printed defense number.ΓÇ¥ This ability creates a replacement effect (see rule 614.1c).
┬á
310.4c The defense of a battle on the battlefield is equal to the number of defense counters on it.
┬á
310.5. Battles can be attacked. (See rule 508, ΓÇ£Declare Attackers Step.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
310.6. Damage dealt to a battle results in that many defense counters being removed from it.
┬á
310.7. If a Siege battleΓÇÖs defense is 0 and it isnΓÇÖt the source of an ability which has triggered but not yet left the stack, itΓÇÖs put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.)
┬á
310.8. If a non-Siege battleΓÇÖs defense is 0, itΓÇÖs put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.)
┬á
310.9. Each battle has a player designated as its protector.
┬á
310.9a As a battle enters the battlefield, its controller chooses a player to be its protector. Which players may be chosen as its protector are determined by its battle type (see rule 310.12). If it has no battle types, only its controller can be its protector.
┬á
310.9b A battleΓÇÖs protector can never attack it. A battle can be attacked by any attacking player for whom its protector is a defending player. Notably, a Siege battle can be attacked by its own controller.
┬á
310.9c A battleΓÇÖs protector may block creatures attacking that battle with creatures they control. Creatures controlled by other players canΓÇÖt block those attackers.
┬á
310.9d If a battleΓÇÖs protector is a different player than its controller, all rules and effects that refer to the ΓÇ£defending playerΓÇ¥ relative to a battle that is being attacked refer to that battleΓÇÖs protector rather than its controller. See rule 508.5.
┬á
310.9e If a rule or effect refers to the player who protects a battle, it means the player who is that battleΓÇÖs protector.
┬á
310.9f A battle can have only one protector at a time. A battleΓÇÖs protector stops being its protector if another player becomes its protector.
┬á
310.9g A battleΓÇÖs protector doesnΓÇÖt change if it stops being a battle or it becomes a copy of another battle.
┬á
310.10. A battle canΓÇÖt be attached to players or permanents, even if it is also an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification. If a battle is somehow attached to a permanent, it becomes unattached. This is a state-based action (see rule 704).
┬á
310.11. If a battle that isnΓÇÖt being attacked has no player designated as its protector, or its protector is a player who canΓÇÖt be its protector, its controller chooses an appropriate player to be its protector. If no player can be chosen this way, the battle is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. This is a state-based action (see rule 704).
┬á
310.12. Some battles have the subtype Siege. Sieges are subject to special rules.
┬á
310.12a As a Siege enters the battlefield, its controller must choose its protector from among their opponents. Only an opponent of a SiegeΓÇÖs controller can be its protector.
┬á
310.12b Sieges have the intrinsic ability ΓÇ£When the last defense counter is removed from this permanent, exile it, then you may cast it transformed without paying its mana cost.ΓÇ¥
┬á
311. Planes
┬á
311.1. Plane is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards. Only the Planechase casual variant uses plane cards. See rule 901, ΓÇ£Planechase.ΓÇ¥
┬á
311.2. Plane cards remain in the command zone throughout the game, both while theyΓÇÖre part of a planar deck and while theyΓÇÖre face up. TheyΓÇÖre not permanents. They canΓÇÖt be cast. If a plane card would leave the command zone, it remains in the command zone.
┬á
311.3. Plane subtypes are listed after a long dash, and may be multiple words: ΓÇ£Plane ΓÇö SerraΓÇÖs Realm.ΓÇ¥ All words after the dash are, collectively, a single subtype. Planar subtypes are called planar types. A plane can have only one subtype. See rule 205.3n for the complete list of planar types.
┬á
311.4. A plane card may have any number of static, triggered, and/or activated abilities. As long as a plane card is face up in the command zone, its static abilities affect the game, its triggered abilities may trigger, and its activated abilities may be activated.
┬á
311.5. The controller of a face-up plane card is the player designated as the planar controller. Normally, the planar controller is whoever the active player is. However, if the current planar controller would leave the game, instead the next player in turn order that wouldnΓÇÖt leave the game becomes the planar controller, then the old planar controller leaves the game. The new planar controller retains that designation until they leave the game or a different player becomes the active player, whichever comes first.
┬á
311.6. A face-up plane card thatΓÇÖs turned face down becomes a new object.
┬á
311.7. Each plane card has a triggered ability that triggers ΓÇ£Whenever chaos ensues.ΓÇ¥ These are called chaos abilities. Each one is indicated by a chaos symbol to the left of the ability, though the symbol itself has no special rules meaning. This ability triggers if the chaos symbol is rolled on the planar die (see rule 901.9b), if a resolving spell or ability says that chaos ensues, or if a resolving spell or ability states that chaos ensues for a particular object. In the last case, the chaos ability can trigger even if that plane card is still in the planar deck but revealed. A chaos ability is controlled by the current planar controller.
┬á
312. Phenomena
┬á
312.1. Phenomenon is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards. Only the Planechase casual variant uses phenomenon cards. See rule 901, ΓÇ£Planechase.ΓÇ¥
┬á
312.2. Phenomenon cards remain in the command zone throughout the game, both while theyΓÇÖre part of a planar deck and while theyΓÇÖre face up. TheyΓÇÖre not permanents. They canΓÇÖt be cast. If a phenomenon card would leave the command zone, it remains in the command zone.
┬á
312.3. Phenomenon cards have no subtypes.
┬á
312.4. The controller of a face-up phenomenon card is the player designated as the planar controller. Normally, the planar controller is whoever the active player is. However, if the current planar controller would leave the game, instead the next player in turn order that wouldnΓÇÖt leave the game becomes the planar controller, then the old planar controller leaves the game. The new planar controller retains that designation until they leave the game or a different player becomes the active player, whichever comes first.
┬á
312.5. Each phenomenon card has a triggered ability that triggers when you encounter it. ΓÇ£When you encounter [this phenomenon]ΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£When you move this card off a planar deck and turn it face up.ΓÇ¥
┬á
312.6. A face-up phenomenon card thatΓÇÖs turned face down becomes a new object.
┬á
312.7. If a phenomenon card is face up in the command zone, and it isnΓÇÖt the source of a triggered ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, the planar controller planeswalks the next time a player would receive priority. (This is a state-based action; see rule 704. See also rule 701.31, ΓÇ£Planeswalk.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
313. Vanguards
┬á
313.1. Vanguard is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards. Only the Vanguard casual variant uses vanguard cards. See rule 902, ΓÇ£Vanguard.ΓÇ¥
┬á
313.2. Vanguard cards remain in the command zone throughout the game. TheyΓÇÖre not permanents. They canΓÇÖt be cast. If a vanguard card would leave the command zone, it remains in the command zone.
┬á
313.3. Vanguard cards have no subtypes.
┬á
313.4. A vanguard card may have any number of static, triggered, and/or activated abilities. As long as a vanguard card is in the command zone, its static abilities affect the game, its triggered abilities may trigger, and its activated abilities may be activated.
┬á
313.5. The owner of a vanguard card is the player who started the game with it in the command zone. The controller of a face-up vanguard card is its owner.
┬á
313.6. Each vanguard card has a hand modifier printed in its lower left corner. This is a number preceded by a plus sign, a number preceded by a minus sign, or a zero. This modifier is applied to the starting hand size and maximum hand size of the vanguard cardΓÇÖs owner (normally seven). The resulting number is both how many cards that player draws at the beginning of the game and their maximum hand size. See rule 103.5.
┬á
313.7. Each vanguard card has a life modifier printed in its lower right corner. This is a number preceded by a plus sign, a number preceded by a minus sign, or a zero. This modifier is applied as the starting life total of the vanguard cardΓÇÖs owner (normally 20) to is determined. See rule 103.4.
┬á
314. Schemes
┬á
314.1. Scheme is a card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards. Only the Archenemy casual variant uses scheme cards. See rule 904, ΓÇ£Archenemy.ΓÇ¥
┬á
314.2. Scheme cards remain in the command zone throughout the game, both while theyΓÇÖre part of a scheme deck and while theyΓÇÖre face up. TheyΓÇÖre not permanents. They canΓÇÖt be cast. If a scheme card would leave the command zone, it remains in the command zone.
┬á
314.3. Scheme cards have no subtypes.
┬á
314.4. A scheme card may have any number of static, triggered, and/or activated abilities. As long as a scheme card is face up in the command zone, its static abilities affect the game, its triggered abilities may trigger, and its activated abilities may be activated.
┬á
314.5. The owner of a scheme card is the player who started the game with it in the command zone. The controller of a face-up scheme card is its owner.
┬á
314.6. If a non-ongoing scheme card is face up in the command zone, and no triggered abilities of any scheme are on the stack or waiting to be put on the stack, that scheme card is turned face down and put on the bottom of its ownerΓÇÖs scheme deck the next time a player would receive priority. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.)
┬á
314.7. If an ability of a scheme card includes the text ΓÇ£this scheme,ΓÇ¥ it means the scheme card in the command zone thatΓÇÖs the source of that ability. This is an exception to rule 109.2.
┬á
315. Conspiracies
┬á
315.1. Conspiracy cards are used only in limited play, particularly in the Conspiracy Draft variant (see rule 905). Conspiracy cards arenΓÇÖt used in constructed play.
┬á
315.2. At the start of a game, before decks are shuffled, each player may put any number of conspiracy cards from their sideboard into the command zone. Conspiracy cards with hidden agenda are put into the command zone face down. (See rule 702.106, ΓÇ£Hidden Agenda.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
315.3. Conspiracy cards remain in the command zone throughout the game. TheyΓÇÖre not permanents. They canΓÇÖt be cast or included in a deck. If a conspiracy card would leave the command zone, it remains in the command zone. Conspiracy cards that arenΓÇÖt in the game canΓÇÖt be brought into the game.
┬á
315.4. Conspiracy cards have no subtypes.
┬á
315.5. Conspiracy cards may have any number of static or triggered abilities. As long as a conspiracy card is face up in the command zone, its static abilities affect the game, and its triggered abilities may trigger.
┬á
315.5a Abilities of conspiracy cards may affect the start-of-game procedure.
┬á
315.5b Face-down conspiracy cards have no characteristics.
┬á
315.6. The owner of a conspiracy card is the player who put it into the command zone at the start of the game. The controller of a conspiracy card is its owner.
┬á
315.7. At any time, you may look at a face-down conspiracy card you control. You canΓÇÖt look at face-down conspiracy cards controlled by other players.

4. Zones
┬á
400. General
┬á
400.1. A zone is a place where objects can be during a game. There are normally seven zones: library, hand, battlefield, graveyard, stack, exile, and command. Some older cards also use the ante zone. Each player has their own library, hand, and graveyard. The other zones are shared by all players.
┬á
400.2. Public zones are zones in which all players can see the cardsΓÇÖ faces, except for those cards that some rule or effect specifically allow to be face down. Graveyard, battlefield, stack, exile, ante, and command are public zones. Hidden zones are zones in which not all players can be expected to see the cardsΓÇÖ faces. Library and hand are hidden zones, even if all the cards in one such zone happen to be revealed.
┬á
400.3. If an object would go to any library, graveyard, or hand other than its ownerΓÇÖs, it goes to its ownerΓÇÖs corresponding zone.
┬á
400.4. Cards with certain card types canΓÇÖt enter certain zones.
┬á
400.4a If an instant or sorcery card would enter the battlefield, it remains in its previous zone.
┬á
400.4b If a conspiracy, phenomenon, plane, scheme, or vanguard card would leave the command zone, it remains in the command zone.
┬á
400.5. The order of objects in a library, in a graveyard, or on the stack canΓÇÖt be changed except when effects or rules allow it. The same is true for objects arranged in face-down piles in other zones. Other objects in other zones can be arranged however their owners wish, although who controls those objects, whether theyΓÇÖre tapped or flipped, and what other objects are attached to them must remain clear to all players.
┬á
400.6. If an object would move from one zone to another, determine what event is moving the object. If the object is moving to a public zone and its owner will be able to look at it in that zone, its owner looks at it to see if it has any abilities that would affect the move. If the object is moving to the battlefield, each other player who will be able to look at it in that zone does so. Then any appropriate replacement effects, whether they come from that object or from elsewhere, are applied to that event. If any effects or rules try to do two or more contradictory or mutually exclusive things to a particular object, that objectΓÇÖs controllerΓÇöor its owner if it has no controllerΓÇöchooses which effect to apply, and what that effect does. (Note that multiple instances of the same thing may be mutually exclusive; for example, two simultaneous ΓÇ£destroyΓÇ¥ effects.) Then the event moves the object.
Example: Exquisite Archangel has an ability which reads ΓÇ£If you would lose the game, instead exile this creature and your life total becomes equal to your starting life total.ΓÇ¥ A spell deals 5 damage to a player with 5 life and 5 damage to an Exquisite Archangel under that playerΓÇÖs control. As state-based actions are performed, that playerΓÇÖs life total becomes equal to their starting life total, and that player chooses whether Exquisite Archangel moves to its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard or to exile.
┬á
400.7. An object that moves from one zone to another becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence. This rule has the following exceptions.
┬á
400.7a Effects from spells, activated abilities, and triggered abilities that change the characteristics or controller of a permanent spell on the stack continue to apply to the permanent that spell becomes.
┬á
400.7b Effects from static abilities that grant an ability to a permanent spell that functions on the battlefield continue to apply to the permanent that spell becomes (see rule 611.3d).
┬á
400.7c Prevention effects that apply to damage from a permanent spell on the stack continue to apply to damage from the permanent that spell becomes.
┬á
400.7d An ability of a permanent can reference information about the spell that became that permanent as it resolved, including what costs were paid to cast that spell or what mana was spent to pay those costs.
┬á
400.7e Abilities that trigger when an object moves from one zone to another (for example, ΓÇ£When this Aura is put into a graveyard from the battlefieldΓÇ¥) can find the new object that it became in the zone it moved to when the ability triggered, if that zone is a public zone.
┬á
400.7f Abilities that trigger when an enchanted permanent leaves the battlefield can find the new object that each Aura enchanting that permanent became in its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard if it was put into that graveyard at the same time the enchanted permanent left the battlefield. It can also find the new object that each Aura enchanting it became in its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard as a result of being put there as a state-based action for not being attached to a permanent. (See rule 704.5m.)
┬á
400.7g If an effect grants a nonland card an ability that allows it to be cast, that ability will continue to apply to the new object that card became after it moved to the stack as a result of being cast this way.
┬á
400.7h If an effect allows a nonland card to be cast, other parts of that effect can find the new object that card becomes after it moves to the stack as a result of being cast this way.
┬á
400.7i If an effect allows a land card to be played, other parts of that effect can find the new object that land card becomes after it moves to the battlefield as a result of being played this way.
┬á
400.7j If an effect causes an object to move to a public zone, other parts of that effect can find that object. If the cost of a spell or ability causes an object to move to a public zone, that spell or abilityΓÇÖs effects can find that object.
┬á
400.7k After resolving a madness triggered ability (see rule 702.35), if the exiled card wasnΓÇÖt cast and was moved to a public zone, effects referencing the discarded card can find that object.
┬á
400.7m Stickers on an object in a public zone are retained as it moves to another public zone (see rule 123.5). Any effects from stickers continue to apply to the new object it becomes in that zone.
┬á
400.8. If an object in the exile zone is exiled, it doesnΓÇÖt change zones, but it becomes a new object that has just been exiled.
┬á
400.9. If a face-up object in the command zone is turned face down, it becomes a new object.
┬á
400.10. If an object in the command zone is put into the command zone, it doesnΓÇÖt change zones, but it becomes a new object that has just entered the command zone.
┬á
400.11. An object is outside the game if it isnΓÇÖt in any of the gameΓÇÖs zones. Outside the game is not a zone.
┬á
400.11a Cards in a playerΓÇÖs sideboard are outside the game. See rule 100.4.
┬á
400.11b Some effects bring cards into a game from outside the game. Those cards remain in the game until the game ends, their owner leaves the game, or a rule or effect removes them from the game, whichever comes first.
┬á
400.11c Cards outside the game canΓÇÖt be affected by spells or abilities, except for characteristic-defining abilities printed on them (see rule 604.3) and spells and abilities that allow those cards to be brought into the game.
┬á
400.12. Some effects instruct a player to do something to a zone (such as ΓÇ£Shuffle your hand into your libraryΓÇ¥). That action is performed on all cards in that zone. The zone itself is not affected.
┬á
401. Library
┬á
401.1. When a game begins, each playerΓÇÖs deck becomes their library.
┬á
401.2. Each library must be kept in a single face-down pile. Players canΓÇÖt look at or change the order of cards in a library.
┬á
401.3. Any player may count the number of cards remaining in any playerΓÇÖs library at any time.
┬á
401.4. If an effect puts two or more cards in a specific position in a library at the same time, the owner of those cards may arrange them in any order. That libraryΓÇÖs owner doesnΓÇÖt reveal the order in which the cards go into the library.
┬á
401.5. Some effects tell a player to play with the top card of their library revealed, or say that a player may look at the top card of their library. If the top card of the playerΓÇÖs library changes while a spell is being cast, the new top card wonΓÇÖt be revealed and canΓÇÖt be looked at until the spell becomes cast (see rule 601.2i). The same is true with relation to an ability being activated. If the top card of the playerΓÇÖs library changes while a player is taking a special action (see rule 116, ΓÇ£Special ActionsΓÇ¥), the new card wonΓÇÖt be revealed and canΓÇÖt be looked at until the player has finished taking that special action.
┬á
401.6. If an effect causes a player to play with the top card of their library revealed, and that particular card stops being revealed for any length of time before being revealed again, it becomes a new object.
┬á
401.7. If an effect causes a player to put a card into a library ΓÇ£Nth from the top,ΓÇ¥ and that library has fewer than N cards in it, the player puts that card on the bottom of that library.
┬á
402. Hand
┬á
402.1. The hand is where a player holds cards that have been drawn. Cards can be put into a playerΓÇÖs hand by other effects as well. At the beginning of the game, each player draws a number of cards equal to that playerΓÇÖs starting hand size, normally seven. (See rule 103, ΓÇ£Starting the Game.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
402.2. Each player has a maximum hand size, which is normally seven cards. A player may have any number of cards in their hand, but as part of their cleanup step, the player must discard excess cards down to the maximum hand size.
┬á
402.3. A player may arrange their hand in any convenient fashion and look at it at any time. A player canΓÇÖt look at the cards in another playerΓÇÖs hand but may count those cards at any time.
┬á
403. Battlefield
┬á
403.1. Most of the area between the players represents the battlefield. The battlefield starts out empty. Permanents a player controls are normally kept in front of them on the battlefield, though there are some cases (such as an Aura attached to another playerΓÇÖs permanent) when a permanent one player controls is kept closer to a different player.
┬á
403.2. A spell or ability affects and checks only the battlefield unless it specifically mentions a player or another zone.
┬á
403.3. Permanents exist only on the battlefield. Every object on the battlefield is a permanent. See rule 110, ΓÇ£Permanents.ΓÇ¥
┬á
403.4. Whenever a permanent enters the battlefield, it becomes a new object and has no relationship to any previous permanent represented by the same card, except for the cases listed in rule 400.7. (This is also true for any objects entering any zone.)
┬á
403.5. Previously, the battlefield was called the ΓÇ£in-play zone.ΓÇ¥ Cards that were printed with text that contains the phrases ΓÇ£in play,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£from play,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£into play,ΓÇ¥ or the like are referring to the battlefield. Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference.
┬á
404. Graveyard
┬á
404.1. A playerΓÇÖs graveyard is their discard pile. Any object thatΓÇÖs countered, discarded, destroyed, or sacrificed is put on top of its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard, as is any instant or sorcery spell thatΓÇÖs finished resolving. Each playerΓÇÖs graveyard starts out empty.
┬á
404.2. Each graveyard is kept in a single face-up pile. A player can examine the cards in any graveyard at any time but normally canΓÇÖt change their order. Additional rules applying to sanctioned tournaments may allow a player to change the order of cards in their graveyard.
┬á
404.3. If an effect or rule puts two or more cards into the same graveyard at the same time, the owner of those cards may arrange them in any order.
┬á
405. Stack
┬á
405.1. When a spell is cast, the physical card is put on the stack (see rule 601.2a). When an ability is activated or triggers, it goes on top of the stack without any card associated with it (see rules 602.2a and 603.3).
┬á
405.2. The stack keeps track of the order that spells and/or abilities were added to it. Each time an object is put on the stack, itΓÇÖs put on top of all objects already there.
┬á
405.3. If an effect puts two or more objects on the stack at the same time, those controlled by the active player are put on lowest, followed by each other playerΓÇÖs objects in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). If a player controls more than one of these objects, that player chooses their relative order on the stack.
┬á
405.4. Each spell has all the characteristics of the card associated with it. Each activated or triggered ability thatΓÇÖs on the stack has the text of the ability that created it and no other characteristics. The controller of a spell is the player who cast it. The controller of an activated ability is the player who activated it. The controller of a triggered ability is the player who controlled the abilityΓÇÖs source when it triggered, unless itΓÇÖs a delayed triggered ability. To determine the controller of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7dΓÇôf.
┬á
405.5. When all players pass in succession, the top (last-added) spell or ability on the stack resolves. If the stack is empty when all players pass, the current step or phase ends and the next begins.
┬á
405.6. Some things that happen during the game donΓÇÖt use the stack.
┬á
405.6a Effects donΓÇÖt go on the stack; theyΓÇÖre the result of spells and abilities resolving. Effects may create delayed triggered abilities, however, and these may go on the stack when they trigger (see rule 603.7).
┬á
405.6b Static abilities continuously generate effects and donΓÇÖt go on the stack. (See rule 604, ΓÇ£Handling Static Abilities.ΓÇ¥) This includes characteristic-defining abilities such as ΓÇ£[This object] is redΓÇ¥ (see rule 604.3).
┬á
405.6c Mana abilities resolve immediately. If a mana ability both produces mana and has another effect, the mana is produced and the other effect happens immediately. If a player had priority before a mana ability was activated, that player gets priority after it resolves. (See rule 605, ΓÇ£Mana Abilities.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
405.6d Special actions donΓÇÖt use the stack; they happen immediately. See rule 116, ΓÇ£Special Actions.ΓÇ¥
┬á
405.6e Turn-based actions donΓÇÖt use the stack; they happen automatically when certain steps or phases begin. TheyΓÇÖre dealt with before a player would receive priority (see rule 117.3a). Turn-based actions also happen automatically when each step and phase ends; no player receives priority afterward. See rule 703.
┬á
405.6f State-based actions donΓÇÖt use the stack; they happen automatically when certain conditions are met. See rule 704. They are dealt with before a player would receive priority. See rule 117.5.
┬á
405.6g A player may concede the game at any time. That player leaves the game immediately. See rule 104.3a.
┬á
405.6h If a player leaves a multiplayer game, objects may leave the game, cease to exist, change control, or be exiled as a result. These actions happen immediately. See rule 800.4a.
┬á
406. Exile
┬á
406.1. The exile zone is essentially a holding area for objects. Some spells and abilities exile an object without any way to return that object to another zone. Other spells and abilities exile an object only temporarily.
┬á
406.2. To exile an object is to put it into the exile zone from whatever zone itΓÇÖs currently in. An exiled card is a card thatΓÇÖs been put into the exile zone.
┬á
406.3. Exiled cards are, by default, kept face up and may be examined by any player at any time. Cards ΓÇ£exiled face downΓÇ¥ canΓÇÖt be examined by any player except when instructions allow it. However, if a player is instructed to look at a card and then exile it face down, or once a player is allowed to look at a card exiled face down, that player may continue to look at that card until it leaves the exile zone or is part of a pile of cards that are shuffled, even if the instruction allowing the player to do so no longer applies.
┬á
406.3a A card exiled face down has no characteristics, but the spell or ability that exiled it may allow it to be played from exile. Unless that card is being cast face down (see rule 708.4), the card is turned face up just before the player announces that they are playing the card (see rule 601.2).
┬á
406.3b Some spells and abilities allow a player to cast spells with certain qualities from among face-down cards in exile. A player may cast such a spell only if they are allowed to look at the face-down card in exile and if the resulting spell has the specified qualities.
┬á
406.4. Face-down cards in exile should be kept in separate piles based on when they were exiled and how they were exiled. If a player is instructed to choose an exiled card, the player may choose a specific face-down card only if the player is allowed to look at that card. Otherwise, they may choose a pile of face-down exiled cards, and then a card is chosen at random from within that pile. If choosing such a card is part of casting a spell or activating an ability, the chosen card isnΓÇÖt revealed until after that cost is fully paid. (See rule 601.2i.)
┬á
406.5. Exiled cards that might return to the battlefield or any other zone should be kept in separate piles to keep track of their respective ways of returning. Exiled cards that may have an impact on the game due to their own abilities (such as cards with haunt) or the abilities of the cards that exiled them should likewise be kept in separate piles.
┬á
406.6. An object may have one ability printed on it that causes one or more cards to be exiled, and another ability that refers either to ΓÇ£the exiled cardsΓÇ¥ or to cards ΓÇ£exiled with [this object].ΓÇ¥ These abilities are linked: the second refers only to cards that have been exiled due to the first. See rule 607, ΓÇ£Linked Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
406.7. If an object in the exile zone becomes exiled, it doesnΓÇÖt change zones, but it becomes a new object that has just been exiled.
┬á
406.8. Previously, the exile zone was called the ΓÇ£removed-from-the-game zone.ΓÇ¥ Cards that were printed with text that ΓÇ£removes [an object] from the gameΓÇ¥ exiles that object. The same is true for cards printed with text that ΓÇ£sets [an object] aside.ΓÇ¥ Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference.
┬á
407. Ante
┬á
407.1. Earlier versions of the Magic rules included an ante rule as a way of playing ΓÇ£for keeps.ΓÇ¥ Playing Magic games for ante is now considered an optional variation on the game, and itΓÇÖs allowed only where itΓÇÖs not forbidden by law or by other rules. Playing for ante is strictly forbidden under the Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules (WPN.Wizards.com/en/rules-documents).
┬á
407.2. When playing for ante, each player puts one random card from their deck into the ante zone after determining which player goes first but before players draw any cards. Cards in the ante zone may be examined by any player at any time. At the end of the game, the winner becomes the owner of all the cards in the ante zone.
┬á
407.3. A few cards have the text ΓÇ£Remove this card from your deck before playing if youΓÇÖre not playing for ante.ΓÇ¥ These are the only cards that can add or remove cards from the ante zone or change a cardΓÇÖs owner. When not playing for ante, players canΓÇÖt include these cards in their decks or sideboards, and these cards canΓÇÖt be brought into the game from outside the game.
┬á
407.4. To ante an object is to put that object into the ante zone from whichever zone itΓÇÖs currently in. The owner of an object is the only player who can ante that object.
┬á
408. Command
┬á
408.1. The command zone is a game area reserved for certain specialized objects that have an overarching effect on the game, yet are not permanents and cannot be destroyed.
┬á
408.2. Emblems may be created in the command zone. See rule 114, ΓÇ£Emblems.ΓÇ¥
┬á
408.3. In the Planechase, Vanguard, Commander, Archenemy, and Conspiracy Draft casual variants, nontraditional Magic cards and/or specially designated cards start the game in the command zone. Each variant has its own rules regarding such cards. See section 9, ΓÇ£Casual Variants.ΓÇ¥
┬á

5. Turn Structure
┬á
500. General
┬á
500.1. A turn consists of five phases, in this order: beginning, precombat main, combat, postcombat main, and ending. Each of these phases takes place every turn, even if nothing happens during the phase. The beginning, combat, and ending phases are further broken down into steps, which proceed in order.
┬á
500.2. A phase or step in which players receive priority ends when the stack is empty and all players pass in succession. Simply having the stack become empty doesnΓÇÖt cause such a phase or step to end; all players have to pass in succession with the stack empty. Because of this, each player gets a chance to add new things to the stack before that phase or step ends.
┬á
500.3. A step in which no players receive priority ends when all specified actions that take place during that step are completed. The only such steps are the untap step (see rule 502) and certain cleanup steps (see rule 514).
┬á
500.4. As a step or phase begins, if there are effects that last until that step or phase, those effects expire.
┬á
500.5. As a step or phase ends, if there are effects that last until the end of that step or phase, those effects expire. Then any unspent mana left in a playerΓÇÖs mana pool empties. This is a turn-based action that doesnΓÇÖt use the stack (see rule 703.4q).
┬á
500.5a Effects that last ΓÇ£until end of combatΓÇ¥ expire at the end of the combat phase, not at the beginning of the end of combat step.
┬á
500.5b Effects that last ΓÇ£until end of turnΓÇ¥ are subject to special rules; see rule 514.2.
┬á
500.6. When a phase or step begins, any abilities that trigger ΓÇ£at the beginning ofΓÇ¥ that phase or step trigger. They are put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority. (See rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and Priority.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
500.7. Some effects can give a player extra turns. They do this by adding the turns directly after the specified turn. If a player is given multiple extra turns, the extra turns are added one at a time. If multiple players are given extra turns, the extra turns are added one at a time, in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). The most recently created turn will be taken first.
┬á
500.8. Some effects can add phases to a turn. They do this by adding the phases directly after the specified phase. If multiple extra phases are created after the same phase, the most recently created phase will occur first.
┬á
500.9. Some effects can add steps to a phase. They do this by adding the steps directly after a specified step or directly before a specified step. If multiple extra steps are created after the same step, the most recently created step will occur first.
┬á
500.10. Some effects add a step after a particular phase. In that case, that effect first creates the phase which normally contains that step directly after the specified phase. Any other steps that phase would normally have are skipped (see rule 500.11).
Example: Obeka, Splitter of Seconds says, in part, ΓÇ£Whenever Obeka deals combat damage to a player, you get that many additional upkeep steps after this phase.ΓÇ¥ After that ability resolves, its controller adds that many beginning phases after this phase. Those new beginning phases have only an upkeep step. The untap steps and draw steps of those phases are skipped.
┬á
500.10a If an effect that says ΓÇ£you getΓÇ¥ an additional step or phase would add a step or phase to a turn other than its controllerΓÇÖs, no steps or phases are added.
┬á
500.11. Some effects can cause a step, phase, or turn to be skipped. To skip a step, phase, or turn is to proceed past it as though it didnΓÇÖt exist. See rule 614.10.
┬á
500.12. No game events can occur between steps, phases, or turns.
┬á
501. Beginning Phase
┬á
501.1. The beginning phase consists of three steps, in this order: untap, upkeep, and draw.
┬á
502. Untap Step
┬á
502.1. First, all phased-in permanents with phasing that the active player controls phase out, and all phased-out permanents that the active player controlled when they phased out phase in. This all happens simultaneously. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack. See rule 702.26, ΓÇ£Phasing.ΓÇ¥
┬á
502.2. Second, if itΓÇÖs day and the previous turnΓÇÖs active player didnΓÇÖt cast any spells during that turn, it becomes night. If itΓÇÖs night and the previous turnΓÇÖs active player cast two or more spells during that turn, it becomes day. If itΓÇÖs neither day nor night, this check doesnΓÇÖt happen and it remains neither. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack. See rule 731, ΓÇ£Day and Night.ΓÇ¥
┬á
502.2a Multiplayer games using the shared team turns option use a modified rule. If itΓÇÖs day and no player on the previous turnΓÇÖs active team cast a spell during that turn, it becomes night. If itΓÇÖs night and any player on the previous turnΓÇÖs active team cast two or more spells during the previous turn, it becomes day. If itΓÇÖs neither day nor night, this check doesnΓÇÖt happen and it remains neither. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack.
┬á
502.3. Third, the active player determines which permanents they control will untap. Then they untap them all simultaneously. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack. Normally, all of a playerΓÇÖs permanents untap, but effects can keep one or more of a playerΓÇÖs permanents from untapping.
┬á
502.4. No player receives priority during the untap step, so no spells can be cast or resolve and no abilities can be activated or resolve. Any ability that triggers during this step will be held until the next time a player would receive priority, which is usually during the upkeep step. (See rule 503, ΓÇ£Upkeep Step.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
503. Upkeep Step
┬á
503.1. The upkeep step has no turn-based actions. Once it begins, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and Priority.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
503.1a Any abilities that triggered during the untap step and any abilities that triggered at the beginning of the upkeep are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority; the order in which they triggered doesnΓÇÖt matter. (See rule 603, ΓÇ£Handling Triggered Abilities.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
503.2. If a spell states that it may be cast only ΓÇ£after [a playerΓÇÖs] upkeep step,ΓÇ¥ and the turn has multiple upkeep steps, that spell may be cast any time after the first upkeep step ends.
┬á
504. Draw Step
┬á
504.1. First, the active player draws a card. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack.
┬á
504.2. Second, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and Priority.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
505. Main Phase
┬á
505.1. There are two main phases in a turn. In each turn, the first main phase (also known as the precombat main phase) and the second main phase (also known as the postcombat main phase) are separated by the combat phase (see rule 506, ΓÇ£Combat PhaseΓÇ¥). The precombat and postcombat main phases are individually and collectively known as the main phase.
┬á
505.1a Only the first main phase of the turn is a precombat main phase. All other main phases are postcombat main phases. This includes the second main phase of a turn in which the combat phase has been skipped. It is also true of a turn in which an effect has caused an additional combat phase and an additional main phase to be created.
┬á
505.1b Phrases such as ΓÇ£first main phase,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£second main phase,ΓÇ¥ and so on count the number of main phases that have occurred only in the current turn unless that text specifies otherwise.
┬á
505.2. The main phase has no steps, so a main phase ends when all players pass in succession while the stack is empty. (See rule 500.2.)
┬á
505.3. First, but only if the players are playing an Archenemy game (see rule 904), the active player is the archenemy, and itΓÇÖs the active playerΓÇÖs precombat main phase, the active player sets the top card of their scheme deck in motion (see rule 701.32). This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack.
┬á
505.4. Second, if the active player controls one or more Saga enchantments and itΓÇÖs the active playerΓÇÖs precombat main phase, the active player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control with one or more chapter abilities. (See rule 714, ΓÇ£Saga Cards.ΓÇ¥) This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack.
┬á
505.5. Third, if the active player controls one or more Attractions and itΓÇÖs the active playerΓÇÖs precombat main phase, the active player rolls to visit their Attractions. (See rule 701.52, ΓÇ£Roll to Visit Your Attractions.ΓÇ¥) This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack.
┬á
505.6. Fourth, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and Priority.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
505.6a The main phase is the only phase in which a player can normally cast artifact, creature, enchantment, planeswalker, and sorcery spells. The active player may cast these spells.
┬á
505.6b During either main phase, the active player may play one land card from their hand if the stack is empty, if the player has priority, and if they havenΓÇÖt played a land this turn (unless an effect states the player may play additional lands). This action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack. Neither the land nor the action of playing the land is a spell or ability, so it canΓÇÖt be countered, and players canΓÇÖt respond to it with instants or activated abilities. (See rule 305, ΓÇ£Lands.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
506. Combat Phase
┬á
506.1. The combat phase has five steps, which proceed in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat. The declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped if no creatures are declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking (see rule 508.8). There are two combat damage steps if any attacking or blocking creature has first strike (see rule 702.7) or double strike (see rule 702.4).
