506.2. During the combat phase, the active player is the attacking player; creatures that player controls may attack. During the combat phase of a two-player game, the nonactive player is the defending player; that player, planeswalkers they control, and battles they protect may be attacked.
┬á
506.2a During the combat phase of a multiplayer game, there may be one or more defending players, depending on the variant being played and the options chosen for it. Unless all the attacking playerΓÇÖs opponents automatically become defending players during the combat phase, the attacking player chooses one of their opponents as a turn-based action during the beginning of combat step. (Note that the choice may be dictated by the variant being played or the options chosen for it.) That player becomes the defending player. See rule 802, ΓÇ£Attack Multiple Players Option,ΓÇ¥ rule 803, ΓÇ£Attack Left and Attack Right Options,ΓÇ¥ and rule 809, ΓÇ£Emperor Variant.ΓÇ¥
┬á
506.2b In multiplayer games using the shared team turns option, the active team is the attacking team and the nonactive team is the defending team. See rule 805, ΓÇ£Shared Team Turns Option.ΓÇ¥
┬á
506.3. Only a creature can attack or block. Only a player, a planeswalker, or a battle can be attacked.
┬á
506.3a If an effect would put a noncreature permanent onto the battlefield attacking or blocking, the permanent does enter the battlefield but itΓÇÖs never considered to be an attacking or blocking permanent.
┬á
506.3b If an effect would put a creature onto the battlefield attacking under the control of any player except an attacking player, that creature does enter the battlefield, but itΓÇÖs never considered to be an attacking creature.
┬á
506.3c If an effect would put a creature onto the battlefield attacking either a player not in the game or a permanent thatΓÇÖs no longer on the battlefield or isnΓÇÖt either a planeswalker or a battle, that creature does enter the battlefield, but itΓÇÖs never considered to be an attacking creature. See rule 508.4a.
┬á
506.3d If an effect puts a creature onto the battlefield attacking during the declare blockers step, combat damage step, or end of combat step, that creature enters the battlefield unblocked. See rule 508.4d.
┬á
506.3e If an effect would put a creature onto the battlefield blocking but the creature it would block isnΓÇÖt attacking the entering creatureΓÇÖs controller, a planeswalker that player controls, or a battle that player protects, that creature does enter the battlefield, but itΓÇÖs never considered to be a blocking creature.
┬á
506.3f If an effect would put a creature thatΓÇÖs also a battle onto the battlefield attacking or blocking, that permanent enters the battlefield but itΓÇÖs never considered to be an attacking or blocking creature.
┬á
506.3g If a resolving spell or ability would cause a battle to become an attacking or blocking creature, that part of the effect does nothing.
┬á
506.4. A permanent is removed from combat if it leaves the battlefield, if its controller or protector changes, if it phases out, if an effect specifically removes it from combat, if itΓÇÖs a planeswalker thatΓÇÖs being attacked and stops being a planeswalker, if itΓÇÖs a battle thatΓÇÖs being attacked and stops being a battle, or if itΓÇÖs an attacking or blocking creature that regenerates (see rule 701.19), stops being a creature, or becomes a battle. A creature thatΓÇÖs removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature. A planeswalker or battle thatΓÇÖs removed from combat stops being attacked.
┬á
506.4a Once a creature has been declared as an attacking or blocking creature, spells or abilities that would have kept that creature from attacking or blocking donΓÇÖt remove the creature from combat.
┬á
506.4b Tapping or untapping a creature thatΓÇÖs already been declared as an attacker or blocker doesnΓÇÖt remove it from combat and doesnΓÇÖt prevent its combat damage.

506.4c If a creature is attacking a planeswalker or battle, removing that planeswalker or battle from combat doesnΓÇÖt remove that creature from combat. It continues to be an attacking creature, although it is not attacking any player, planeswalker, or battle. It may be blocked. If it is unblocked, it will deal no combat damage.
┬á
506.4d A permanent thatΓÇÖs both a blocking creature and a planeswalker thatΓÇÖs being attacked is removed from combat if it stops being both a creature and a planeswalker. If it stops being one of those card types but continues to be the other, it continues to be either a blocking creature or a planeswalker thatΓÇÖs being attacked, whichever is appropriate.
┬á
506.4e A permanent thatΓÇÖs being attacked that is both a planeswalker and a battle is removed from combat if it stops being both a planeswalker and a battle. If it stops being a battle but is still a planeswalker, it is removed from combat only if it is not controlled by its protector. If it stops being a planeswalker but is still a battle, it is not removed from combat. It continues to be a battle thatΓÇÖs being attacked.
┬á
506.5. A creature attacks alone if itΓÇÖs the only creature declared as an attacker during the declare attackers step. A creature is attacking alone if itΓÇÖs attacking but no other creatures are. A creature blocks alone if itΓÇÖs the only creature declared as a blocker during the declare blockers step. A creature is blocking alone if itΓÇÖs blocking but no other creatures are.
┬á
506.6. Some abilities check to see whether or not a creature ΓÇ£had to attackΓÇ¥ during a particular combat phase. A creature had to attack if one or more effects were requiring that creature to attack at the time attackers were declared in that combat. A creature did not ΓÇ£have to attackΓÇ¥ if there were no such effects that required it to attack, even if there were no other legal attacks that could have been declared. (See rule 508.)
┬á
506.7. Some spells state that they may be cast ΓÇ£only [before/after] [a particular point in the combat phase],ΓÇ¥ in which that point may be ΓÇ£attackers are declared,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£blockers are declared,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£the combat damage step,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£the end of combat step,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£the combat phase,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£combat.ΓÇ¥
┬á
506.7a A spell that states it may be cast ΓÇ£only before (or after) attackers are declaredΓÇ¥ is referring to the turn-based action of declaring attackers. It may be cast only before (or after) the declare attackers step begins, regardless of whether any attackers are actually declared. (See rule 508.)

506.7b A spell that states it may be cast ΓÇ£only before (or after) blockers are declaredΓÇ¥ is referring to the turn-based action of declaring blockers. It may be cast only before (or after) the declare blockers step begins, regardless of whether any blockers are actually declared. (See rule 509.)
┬á
506.7c Some spells state that they may be cast only ΓÇ£during combatΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£during a certain playerΓÇÖs combat phaseΓÇ¥ in addition to the criteria described in rule 506.7. If a turn has multiple combat phases, such spells may be cast at an appropriate time during any of them.
┬á
506.7d Some spells state that they may be cast ΓÇ£only before (or after) [a particular point in the combat phase],ΓÇ¥ but donΓÇÖt meet the additional criteria described in rule 506.7c. If a turn has multiple combat phases, such spells may be cast that turn only before (or after) the stated point of the first combat phase.
┬á
506.7e If a spell states that it may be cast ΓÇ£only before [a particular point in the combat phase],ΓÇ¥ but the stated point doesnΓÇÖt exist within the relevant combat phase because the declare blockers step and the combat damage step are skipped (see rule 508.8), then the spell may be cast only before the declare attackers step ends. If the stated point doesnΓÇÖt exist because the relevant combat phase has been skipped, then the spell may be cast only before the precombat main phase ends.
┬á
506.7f If a spell states that it may be cast ΓÇ£only during combat after blockers are declared,ΓÇ¥ but the declare blockers step is skipped that combat phase (see rule 508.8), then the spell may not be cast during that combat phase.
┬á
506.7g Rules 506.7 and 506.7aΓÇôf apply to abilities that state that they may be activated only at certain times with respect to combat just as they apply to spells that state that they may be cast only at certain times with respect to combat.
┬á
507. Beginning of Combat Step
┬á
507.1. First, if the game being played is a multiplayer game in which the active playerΓÇÖs opponents donΓÇÖt all automatically become defending players, the active player chooses one of their opponents. That player becomes the defending player. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack. (See rule 506.2.)
┬á
507.2. Second, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and Priority.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
508. Declare Attackers Step
┬á
508.1. First, the active player declares attackers. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack. To declare attackers, the active player follows the steps below, in order. If at any point during the declaration of attackers, the active player is unable to comply with any of the steps listed below, the declaration is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the declaration (see rule 733, ΓÇ£Handling Illegal ActionsΓÇ¥).

508.1a The active player chooses which creatures that they control, if any, will attack. The chosen creatures must be untapped, they canΓÇÖt also be battles, and each one must either have haste or have been controlled by the active player continuously since the turn began.
┬á
508.1b If the defending player controls any planeswalkers, is the protector of any battles, or the game allows the active player to attack multiple other players, the active player announces which player, planeswalker, or battle each of the chosen creatures is attacking.
┬á
508.1c The active player checks each creature they control to see whether itΓÇÖs affected by any restrictions (effects that say a creature canΓÇÖt attack, or that it canΓÇÖt attack unless some condition is met). If any restrictions are being disobeyed, the declaration of attackers is illegal.
Example: A player controls two creatures, each with a restriction that states ΓÇ£This creature canΓÇÖt attack alone.ΓÇ¥ ItΓÇÖs legal to declare both as attackers.
┬á
508.1d The active player checks each creature they control to see whether itΓÇÖs affected by any requirements (effects that say a creature attacks if able, or that it attacks if some condition is met). If the number of requirements that are being obeyed is fewer than the maximum possible number of requirements that could be obeyed without disobeying any restrictions, the declaration of attackers is illegal. If a creature canΓÇÖt attack unless a player pays a cost, that player is not required to pay that cost, even if attacking with that creature would increase the number of requirements being obeyed. If a requirement that says a creature attacks if able during a certain turn refers to a turn with multiple combat phases, the creature attacks if able during each declare attackers step in that turn.
Example: A player controls two creatures: one that ΓÇ£attacks if ableΓÇ¥ and one with no abilities. An effect states ΓÇ£No more than one creature can attack each turn.ΓÇ¥ The only legal attack is for just the creature that ΓÇ£attacks if ableΓÇ¥ to attack. ItΓÇÖs illegal to attack with the other creature, attack with both, or attack with neither.

508.1e If any of the chosen creatures have banding or a ΓÇ£bands with otherΓÇ¥ ability, the active player announces which creatures, if any, are banded with which. (See rule 702.22, ΓÇ£Banding.ΓÇ¥)

508.1f The active player taps the chosen creatures. Tapping a creature when itΓÇÖs declared as an attacker isnΓÇÖt a cost; attacking simply causes creatures to become tapped.

508.1g If there are any optional costs to attack with the chosen creatures (expressed as costs a player may pay ΓÇ£asΓÇ¥ a creature attacks), the active player chooses which, if any, they will pay.
┬á
508.1h If any of the chosen creatures require paying costs to attack, or if any optional costs to attack were chosen, the active player determines the total cost to attack. Costs may include paying mana, tapping permanents, sacrificing permanents, discarding cards, and so on. Once the total cost is determined, it becomes ΓÇ£locked in.ΓÇ¥ If effects would change the total cost after this time, ignore this change.

508.1i If any of the costs require mana, the active player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, ΓÇ£Mana AbilitiesΓÇ¥).
┬á
508.1j Once the player has enough mana in their mana pool, they pay all costs in any order. Partial payments are not allowed.
┬á
508.1k Each chosen creature still controlled by the active player becomes an attacking creature. It remains an attacking creature until itΓÇÖs removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. See rule 506.4.
┬á
508.1m Any abilities that trigger on attackers being declared trigger.
┬á
508.2. Second, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and Priority.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
508.2a Abilities that trigger on a creature attacking trigger only at the point the creature is declared as an attacker. They will not trigger if a creature attacks and then that creatureΓÇÖs characteristics change to match the abilityΓÇÖs trigger condition.
Example: A permanent has the ability ΓÇ£Whenever a green creature attacks, destroy that creature at end of combat.ΓÇ¥ If a blue creature attacks and is later turned green, the ability will not trigger.
┬á
508.2b Any abilities that triggered on attackers being declared or that triggered during the process described in rules 508.1 are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority; the order in which they triggered doesnΓÇÖt matter. (See rule 603, ΓÇ£Handling Triggered Abilities.ΓÇ¥)

508.3. Triggered abilities that trigger on attackers being declared may have different trigger conditions.

508.3a An ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever [a creature] attacks, . . .ΓÇ¥ triggers if that creature is declared as an attacker. Similarly, ΓÇ£Whenever [a creature] attacks [a player, planeswalker, or battle], . . .ΓÇ¥ triggers if that creature is declared as an attacker attacking that player or permanent. Such abilities wonΓÇÖt trigger if a creature is put onto the battlefield attacking.

508.3b An ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever [a player, planeswalker, or battle] is attacked, . . .ΓÇ¥ triggers if one or more creatures are declared as attackers attacking that player or permanent. It wonΓÇÖt trigger if a creature is put onto the battlefield attacking that player or permanent.

┬á
508.3d An ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever [a player] attacks, . . .ΓÇ¥ triggers if one or more creatures that player controls are declared as attackers.
┬á
508.3e An ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever [a player] attacks [another player], . . .ΓÇ¥ triggers if one or more creatures the first player controls are declared as attackers attacking the second player. It wonΓÇÖt trigger if a creature is put onto the battlefield attacking or if a creature attacks a planeswalker or a battle.

508.3f An ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever [a creature] attacks and isnΓÇÖt blocked, . . .ΓÇ¥ triggers during the declare blockers step, not the declare attackers step. See rule 509.3g.
┬á
508.4. If a creature is put onto the battlefield attacking, its controller chooses which defending player, planeswalker a defending player controls, or battle a defending player protects itΓÇÖs attacking as it enters the battlefield (unless the effect that put it onto the battlefield specifies what itΓÇÖs attacking). Similarly, if an effect states that a creature is attacking, its controller chooses which defending player, planeswalker a defending player controls, or battle a defending player protects itΓÇÖs attacking (unless the effect has already specified). Such creatures are ΓÇ£attackingΓÇ¥ but, for the purposes of trigger events and effects, they never ΓÇ£attacked.ΓÇ¥ They remain attacking creatures until theyΓÇÖre removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first.

508.4c A creature thatΓÇÖs put onto the battlefield attacking or that is stated to be attacking isnΓÇÖt affected by requirements or restrictions that apply to the declaration of attackers.

If that creature is no longer attacking, the defending player itΓÇÖs referring to is the player that creature was attacking before it was removed from combat, the controller of the planeswalker that creature was attacking before it was removed from combat, or the protector of the battle that creature was attacking before it was removed from combat.

508.5a In a multiplayer game, any rule, object, or effect that refers to a ΓÇ£defending playerΓÇ¥ refers to one specific defending player, not to all of the defending players. If a spell or ability could apply to multiple attacking creatures, the appropriate defending player is individually determined for each of those attacking creatures. If there are multiple defending players that could be chosen, the controller of the spell or ability chooses one.

508.6. A player is ΓÇ£attacking [a player]ΓÇ¥ if the first player controls a creature that is attacking the second player. A player has ΓÇ£attacked [a player]ΓÇ¥ if the first player declared one or more creatures as attackers attacking the second player.

508.7. Some cards allow a player to reselect which player, planeswalker, or battle a creature is attacking.

508.7a The attacking creature isnΓÇÖt removed from combat and it isnΓÇÖt considered to have attacked a second time. That creature is attacking the reselected player or permanent, but itΓÇÖs still considered to have attacked the player or permanent chosen as it was declared as an attacker.

┬á
508.7e In a multiplayer game using the limited range of influence option (see rule 801), the reselected player, planeswalker, or battle must be within the range of influence of the attacking creatureΓÇÖs controller. In the case of a battle, the battleΓÇÖs protector must also be within the range of influence of the attacking creatureΓÇÖs controller.

508.8. If no creatures are declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking, skip the declare blockers and combat damage steps.

509. Declare Blockers Step
┬á
509.1. First, the defending player declares blockers. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack. To declare blockers, the defending player follows the steps below, in order. If at any point during the declaration of blockers, the defending player is unable to comply with any of the steps listed below, the declaration is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the declaration (see rule 733, ΓÇ£Handling Illegal ActionsΓÇ¥).
┬á
509.1a The defending player chooses which creatures they control, if any, will block. The chosen creatures must be untapped and they canΓÇÖt also be battles. For each of the chosen creatures, the defending player chooses one creature for it to block thatΓÇÖs attacking that player, a planeswalker they control, or a battle they protect.
┬á
509.1b The defending player checks each creature they control to see whether itΓÇÖs affected by any restrictions (effects that say a creature canΓÇÖt block, or that it canΓÇÖt block unless some condition is met). If any restrictions are being disobeyed, the declaration of blockers is illegal.ΓÇ¿┬á┬á┬á┬á A restriction may be created by an evasion ability (a static ability an attacking creature has that restricts what can block it). If an attacking creature gains or loses an evasion ability after a legal block has been declared, it doesnΓÇÖt affect that block. Different evasion abilities are cumulative.
Example: An attacking creature with flying and shadow canΓÇÖt be blocked by a creature with flying but without shadow.
┬á
509.1c The defending player checks each creature they control to see whether itΓÇÖs affected by any requirements (effects that say a creature must block, or that it must block if some condition is met). If the number of requirements that are being obeyed is fewer than the maximum possible number of requirements that could be obeyed without disobeying any restrictions, the declaration of blockers is illegal. If a creature canΓÇÖt block unless a player pays a cost, that player is not required to pay that cost, even if blocking with that creature would increase the number of requirements being obeyed. If a requirement that says a creature blocks if able during a certain turn refers to a turn with multiple combat phases, the creature blocks if able during each declare blockers step in that turn.
Example: A player controls one creature that ΓÇ£blocks if ableΓÇ¥ and another creature with no abilities. If a creature with menace attacks that player, the player must block with both creatures. Having only the first creature block violates the restriction created by menace (the attacking creature canΓÇÖt be blocked except by two or more creatures). Having only the second creature block violates both the menace restriction and the first creatureΓÇÖs blocking requirement. Having neither creature block fulfills the restriction but not the requirement.
┬á
509.1d If any of the chosen creatures require paying costs to block, the defending player determines the total cost to block. Costs may include paying mana, tapping permanents, sacrificing permanents, discarding cards, and so on. Once the total cost is determined, it becomes ΓÇ£locked in.ΓÇ¥ If effects would change the total cost after this time, ignore this change.
┬á
509.1e If any of the costs require mana, the defending player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, ΓÇ£Mana AbilitiesΓÇ¥).
┬á
509.1f Once the player has enough mana in their mana pool, they pay all costs in any order. Partial payments are not allowed.
┬á
509.1g Each chosen creature still controlled by the defending player becomes a blocking creature. Each one is blocking the attacking creatures chosen for it. It remains a blocking creature until itΓÇÖs removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. See rule 506.4.
┬á
509.1h An attacking creature with one or more creatures declared as blockers for it becomes a blocked creature; one with no creatures declared as blockers for it becomes an unblocked creature. This remains unchanged until the creature is removed from combat, an effect says that it becomes blocked or unblocked, or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first. A creature remains blocked even if all the creatures blocking it are removed from combat.
┬á
509.1i Any abilities that trigger on blockers being declared trigger. See rule 509.2a for more information.
┬á
509.2. Second, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and Priority.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
509.2a Any abilities that triggered on blockers being declared or that triggered during the process described in rule 509.1 are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority; the order in which they triggered doesnΓÇÖt matter. (See rule 603, ΓÇ£Handling Triggered Abilities.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
509.3. Triggered abilities that trigger on blockers being declared may have different trigger conditions.
┬á
509.3a An ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever [a creature] blocks, . . .ΓÇ¥ generally triggers only once each combat for that creature, even if it blocks multiple creatures. It triggers if the creature is declared as a blocker. It will also trigger if that creature becomes a blocker as the result of an effect, but only if it wasnΓÇÖt a blocking creature at that time. (See rule 509.1g.) It wonΓÇÖt trigger if the creature is put onto the battlefield blocking.
┬á
509.3b An ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever [a creature] blocks a creature, . . .ΓÇ¥ triggers once for each attacking creature the creature with the ability blocks. It triggers if the creature is declared as a blocker. It will also trigger if an effect causes that creature to block an attacking creature, but only if it wasnΓÇÖt already blocking that attacking creature at that time. It wonΓÇÖt trigger if the creature is put onto the battlefield blocking.
┬á
509.3c An ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever [a creature] becomes blocked, . . .ΓÇ¥ generally triggers only once each combat for that creature, even if itΓÇÖs blocked by multiple creatures. It will trigger if that creature becomes blocked by at least one creature declared as a blocker. It will also trigger if that creature becomes blocked by an effect or by a creature thatΓÇÖs put onto the battlefield as a blocker, but only if the attacking creature was an unblocked creature at that time. (See rule 509.1h.)
┬á
509.3d An ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever [a creature] becomes blocked by a creature, . . .ΓÇ¥ triggers once for each creature that blocks the specified creature. It triggers if a creature is declared as a blocker for the attacking creature. It will also trigger if an effect causes a creature to block the attacking creature, but only if it wasnΓÇÖt already blocking that attacking creature at that time. In addition, it will trigger if a creature is put onto the battlefield blocking that creature. It wonΓÇÖt trigger if the creature becomes blocked by an effect rather than a creature.
┬á
509.3e If an ability triggers when a creature blocks or becomes blocked by a particular number of creatures, the ability triggers if the creature blocks or is blocked by that many creatures when blockers are declared. Effects that add or remove blockers can also cause such abilities to trigger. This applies to abilities that trigger on a creature blocking or being blocked by at least a certain number of creatures as well.
┬á
509.3f If an ability triggers when a creature with certain characteristics blocks, it will trigger only if the creature has those characteristics at the point blockers are declared, or at the point an effect causes it to block. If an ability triggers when a creature with certain characteristics becomes blocked, it will trigger only if the creature has those characteristics at the point it becomes a blocked creature. If an ability triggers when a creature becomes blocked by a creature with certain characteristics, it will trigger only if the latter creature has those characteristics at the point it becomes a blocking creature. None of those abilities will trigger if the relevant creatureΓÇÖs characteristics change to match the abilityΓÇÖs trigger condition later on.
Example: A creature has the ability ΓÇ£Whenever this creature becomes blocked by a white creature, destroy that creature at end of combat.ΓÇ¥ If the creature becomes blocked by a black creature that is later turned white, the ability will not trigger.
┬á
509.3g An ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever [a creature] attacks and isnΓÇÖt blocked, . . .ΓÇ¥ triggers if no creatures are declared as blockers for that creature. It will trigger even if the creature was never declared as an attacker (for example, if it entered the battlefield attacking). It wonΓÇÖt trigger if the attacking creature is blocked and then all its blockers are removed from combat.
┬á
509.4. If a creature is put onto the battlefield blocking, its controller chooses which attacking creature itΓÇÖs blocking as it enters the battlefield (unless the effect that put it onto the battlefield specifies what itΓÇÖs blocking). A creature put onto the battlefield this way is ΓÇ£blockingΓÇ¥ but, for the purposes of trigger events and effects, it never ΓÇ£blocked.ΓÇ¥
┬á
509.4a If the effect that puts a creature onto the battlefield blocking specifies itΓÇÖs blocking a certain creature and that creature is no longer attacking, the creature is put onto the battlefield but is never considered a blocking creature. The same is true if the controller of the creature thatΓÇÖs put onto the battlefield blocking isnΓÇÖt a defending player for the specified attacking creature.
┬á
509.4b A creature thatΓÇÖs put onto the battlefield blocking isnΓÇÖt affected by requirements or restrictions that apply to the declaration of blockers.
┬á
510. Combat Damage Step
┬á
510.1. First, the active player announces how each attacking creature assigns its combat damage, then the defending player announces how each blocking creature assigns its combat damage. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack. A player assigns a creatureΓÇÖs combat damage according to the following rules:
┬á
510.1a Each attacking creature and each blocking creature assigns combat damage equal to its power. Creatures that would assign 0 or less damage this way donΓÇÖt assign combat damage at all.
┬á
510.1b An unblocked creature assigns its combat damage to the player, planeswalker, or battle itΓÇÖs attacking. If it isnΓÇÖt currently attacking anything (if, for example, it was attacking a planeswalker that has left the battlefield), it assigns no combat damage.
┬á
510.1c A blocked creature assigns its combat damage to the creatures blocking it. If no creatures are currently blocking it (if, for example, they were destroyed or removed from combat), it assigns no combat damage. If exactly one creature is blocking it, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature. If two or more creatures are blocking it, it assigns its combat damage to those creatures divided as its controller chooses among them.
Example: An attacking Elvish Regrower (a 4/3 creature) is blocked by Vampire Spawn (a 2/3 creature) and Helpful Hunter (a 1/1 creature). Elvish RegrowerΓÇÖs controller can assign all 4 damage to the Hunter, 1 damage to the Spawn and 3 damage to the Hunter, 2 damage to each creature, 3 damage to the Spawn and 1 damage to the Hunter, or all 4 damage to the Spawn.
┬á
510.1d A blocking creature assigns combat damage to the creatures itΓÇÖs blocking. If it isnΓÇÖt currently blocking any creatures (if, for example, they were destroyed or removed from combat), it assigns no combat damage. If itΓÇÖs blocking exactly one creature, it assigns all its combat damage to that creature. If itΓÇÖs blocking two or more creatures, it assigns its combat damage divided as its controller chooses among them.
┬á
510.1e Once a player has assigned combat damage from each attacking or blocking creature they control, the total damage assignment (not solely the damage assignment of any individual attacking or blocking creature) is checked to see if it complies with the above rules. If it doesnΓÇÖt, the combat damage assignment is illegal; the game returns to the moment before that player began to assign combat damage. (See rule 733, ΓÇ£Handling Illegal Actions.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
510.2. Second, all combat damage thatΓÇÖs been assigned is dealt simultaneously. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack. No player has the chance to cast spells or activate abilities between the time combat damage is assigned and the time itΓÇÖs dealt.
┬á
510.3. Third, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and Priority.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
510.3a Any abilities that triggered on damage being dealt or while state-based actions are performed afterward are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority; the order in which they triggered doesnΓÇÖt matter. (See rule 603, ΓÇ£Handling Triggered Abilities.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
510.4. If at least one attacking or blocking creature has first strike (see rule 702.7) or double strike (see rule 702.4) as the combat damage step begins, the only creatures that assign combat damage in that step are those with first strike or double strike. After that step, instead of proceeding to the end of combat step, the phase gets a second combat damage step. The only creatures that assign combat damage in that step are the remaining attackers and blockers that had neither first strike nor double strike as the first combat damage step began, as well as the remaining attackers and blockers that currently have double strike. After that step, the phase proceeds to the end of combat step.
┬á
511. End of Combat Step
┬á
511.1. The end of combat step has no turn-based actions. Once it begins, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and Priority.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
511.2. Abilities that trigger ΓÇ£at end of combatΓÇ¥ trigger as the end of combat step begins. Effects that last ΓÇ£until end of combatΓÇ¥ expire at the end of the combat phase.
┬á
511.3. As soon as the end of combat step ends, all creatures, battles, and planeswalkers are removed from combat. After the end of combat step ends, the combat phase is over and the postcombat main phase begins (see rule 505).
┬á
512. Ending Phase
┬á
512.1. The ending phase consists of two steps: end and cleanup.
┬á
513. End Step
┬á
513.1. The end step has no turn-based actions. Once it begins, the active player gets priority. (See rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and Priority.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
513.1a Previously, abilities that triggered at the beginning of the end step were printed with the trigger condition ΓÇ£at end of turn.ΓÇ¥ Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference to say ΓÇ£at the beginning of the end stepΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£at the beginning of the next end step.ΓÇ¥
┬á
513.2. If a permanent with an ability that triggers ΓÇ£at the beginning of the end stepΓÇ¥ enters the battlefield during this step, that ability wonΓÇÖt trigger until the next turnΓÇÖs end step. Likewise, if a delayed triggered ability that triggers ΓÇ£at the beginning of the next end stepΓÇ¥ is created during this step, that ability wonΓÇÖt trigger until the next turnΓÇÖs end step. In other words, the step doesnΓÇÖt ΓÇ£back upΓÇ¥ so those abilities can go on the stack. This rule applies only to triggered abilities; it doesnΓÇÖt apply to continuous effects whose durations say ΓÇ£until end of turnΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£this turn.ΓÇ¥ (See rule 514, ΓÇ£Cleanup Step.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
514. Cleanup Step
┬á
514.1. First, if the active playerΓÇÖs hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to reduce their hand size to that number. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack.
┬á
514.2. Second, the following actions happen simultaneously: all damage marked on permanents (including phased-out permanents) is removed and all ΓÇ£until end of turnΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£this turnΓÇ¥ effects end. This turn-based action doesnΓÇÖt use the stack.
┬á
514.3. Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated. However, this rule is subject to the following exception:
┬á
514.3a At this point, the game checks to see if any state-based actions would be performed and/or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack (including those that trigger ΓÇ£at the beginning of the next cleanup stepΓÇ¥). If so, those state-based actions are performed, then those triggered abilities are put on the stack, then the active player gets priority. Players may cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins.
┬á

6. Spells, Abilities, and Effects
┬á
600. General
┬á
601. Casting Spells
┬á
601.1. Previously, the action of casting a spell, or casting a card as a spell, was referred to on cards as ΓÇ£playingΓÇ¥ that spell or that card. Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference so they now refer to ΓÇ£castingΓÇ¥ that spell or that card.
┬á
601.1a Some effects still refer to ΓÇ£playingΓÇ¥ a card. ΓÇ£Playing a cardΓÇ¥ means playing that card as a land or casting that card as a spell, whichever is appropriate.
┬á
601.2. To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2aΓÇôd) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2fΓÇôh). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, ΓÇ£Handling Illegal ActionsΓÇ¥).
┬á
601.2a To propose the casting of a spell, a player first moves that card (or that copy of a card) from where it is to the stack. It becomes the topmost object on the stack. It has all the characteristics of the card (or the copy of a card) associated with it, and that player becomes its controller. Any continuous effects that modify the characteristics of the spell as you start casting it begin as it is put on the stack (see rule 611.2f). Any one-shot effects that cause the spell to gain abilities as you cast it apply as it is put on the stack (see rule 610.5). The spell remains on the stack until it resolves, itΓÇÖs countered, or a rule or effect moves it elsewhere.
┬á
601.2b If the spell is modal, the player announces the mode choice (see rule 700.2). If the player wishes to splice any cards onto the spell (see rule 702.47), they reveal those cards in their hand. If the spell has alternative or additional costs that will be paid as itΓÇÖs being cast such as buyback or kicker costs (see rules 118.8 and 118.9), the player announces their intentions to pay any or all of those costs (see rule 601.2f). A player canΓÇÖt apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. If the spell has a variable cost that will be paid as itΓÇÖs being cast (such as an {X} in its mana cost; see rule 107.3), the player announces the value of that variable. If the value of that variable is defined in the text of the spell by a choice that player would make later in the announcement or resolution of the spell, that player makes that choice at this time instead of that later time. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes hybrid mana symbols, the player announces the nonhybrid equivalent cost they intend to pay. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes Phyrexian mana symbols, the player announces whether they intend to pay 2 life or a corresponding colored mana cost for each of those symbols. Previously made choices (such as choosing to cast a spell with flashback from a graveyard or choosing to cast a creature with morph face down) may restrict the playerΓÇÖs options when making these choices.
┬á
601.2c The player announces their choice of an appropriate object or player for each target the spell requires. A spell may require some targets only if an alternative or additional cost (such as a kicker cost) or a particular mode was chosen for it; otherwise, the spell is cast as though it did not require those targets. Similarly, a spell may require alternative targets only if an alternative or additional cost was chosen for it. If the spell has a variable number of targets, the player announces how many targets they will choose before they announce those targets. In some cases, the number of targets will be defined by the spellΓÇÖs text. Once the number of targets the spell has is determined, that number doesnΓÇÖt change, even if the information used to determine the number of targets does. The same target canΓÇÖt be chosen multiple times for any one instance of the word ΓÇ£targetΓÇ¥ on the spell. However, if the spell uses the word ΓÇ£targetΓÇ¥ in multiple places, the same object or player can be chosen once for each instance of the word ΓÇ£targetΓÇ¥ (as long as it fits the targeting criteria). If any effects say that an object or player must be chosen as a target, the player chooses targets so that they obey the maximum possible number of such effects without violating any rules or effects that say that an object or player canΓÇÖt be chosen as a target. The chosen objects and/or players each become a target of that spell. (Any abilities that trigger when those objects and/or players become the target of a spell trigger at this point; theyΓÇÖll wait to be put on the stack until the spell has finished being cast.)
Example: If a spell says ΓÇ£Tap two target creatures,ΓÇ¥ then the same creature canΓÇÖt be chosen twice; the spell requires two different legal targets. A spell that says ΓÇ£Destroy target artifact and target land,ΓÇ¥ however, can target the same artifact land twice because it uses the word ΓÇ£targetΓÇ¥ in multiple places.
┬á
601.2d If the spell requires the player to divide or distribute an effect (such as damage or counters) among one or more targets, the player announces the division. Each of these targets must receive at least one of whatever is being divided.
┬á
601.2e The game checks to see if the proposed spell can legally be cast. If the proposed spell is illegal, the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, ΓÇ£Handling Illegal ActionsΓÇ¥).
┬á
601.2f The player determines the total cost of the spell. Usually this is just the mana cost. Some spells have additional or alternative costs. Some effects may increase or reduce the cost to pay, or may provide other alternative costs. Costs may include paying mana, tapping permanents, sacrificing permanents, discarding cards, and so on. The total cost is the mana cost or alternative cost (as determined in rule 601.2b), plus all additional costs and cost increases, and minus all cost reductions. If multiple cost reductions apply, the player may apply them in any order. If the mana component of the total cost is reduced to nothing by cost reduction effects, it is considered to be {0}. It canΓÇÖt be reduced to less than {0}. Once the total cost is determined, any effects that directly affect the total cost are applied. Then the resulting total cost becomes ΓÇ£locked in.ΓÇ¥ If effects would change the total cost after this time, they have no effect.
┬á
601.2g If the total cost includes a mana payment, the player then has a chance to activate mana abilities (see rule 605, ΓÇ£Mana AbilitiesΓÇ¥). Mana abilities must be activated before costs are paid.
┬á
601.2h The player pays the total cost. First, they pay all costs that donΓÇÖt involve random elements or moving objects from the library to a public zone, in any order. Then they pay all remaining costs in any order. Partial payments are not allowed. Unpayable costs canΓÇÖt be paid.
Example: You cast AltarΓÇÖs Reap, which costs {1}{B} and has an additional cost of sacrificing a creature. You sacrifice Thunderscape Familiar, whose effect makes your black spells cost {1} less to cast. Because a spellΓÇÖs total cost is ΓÇ£locked inΓÇ¥ before payments are actually made, you pay {B}, not {1}{B}, even though youΓÇÖre sacrificing the Familiar.
┬á
601.2i Once the steps described in 601.2aΓÇôh are completed, effects that modify the characteristics of the spell as itΓÇÖs cast are applied, then the spell becomes cast. Any abilities that trigger when a spell is cast or put onto the stack trigger at this time. If the spellΓÇÖs controller had priority before casting it, they get priority.
┬á
601.3. A player can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows that player to cast it and no rule or effect prohibits that player from casting it.
┬á
601.3a If an effect prohibits a player from casting a spell with certain qualities, that player may consider any choices to be made during that spellΓÇÖs proposal that may cause those qualities to change. If any such choices could cause that effect to no longer prohibit that player from casting that spell, the player may begin to cast the spell, ignoring the effect.
Example: A player controls Void Winnower, which reads, in part, ΓÇ£Your opponents canΓÇÖt cast spells with even mana values.ΓÇ¥ That playerΓÇÖs opponent may begin to cast Rolling Thunder, a card whose mana cost is {X}{R}{R}, because the chosen value of X may cause the spellΓÇÖs mana value to become odd.
┬á
601.3b If an effect allows a player to cast a spell with certain qualities as though it had flash, that player may consider any choices to be made during that spellΓÇÖs proposal that may cause that spellΓÇÖs qualities to change. If any such choices could cause that effect to apply, that player may begin to cast that spell as though it had flash.
Example: An effect says that you may cast Aura spells as though they had flash, and you have a creature card with bestow in your hand. Because choosing the bestow abilityΓÇÖs alternative cost causes that spell to become an Aura spell, you may legally begin to cast that spell as though it had flash.
┬á
601.3c If an effect allows a player to cast a spell as though it had flash only if an alternative or additional cost is paid, that player may begin to cast that spell as though it had flash.
┬á
601.3d If a spell would have flash only if certain conditions are met, its controller may begin to cast that spell as though it had flash if those conditions are met.
┬á
601.3e Some rules and effects state that an alternative set of characteristics or a subset of characteristics are considered to determine if a card or copy of a card is legal to cast. These alternative characteristics replace the objectΓÇÖs characteristics for this determination. Continuous effects that would apply to that object once it has those characteristics are also considered.
Example: GarrukΓÇÖs Horde says, in part, ΓÇ£You may cast creature spells from the top of your library.ΓÇ¥ If you control GarrukΓÇÖs Horde and the top card of your library is a noncreature card with morph, you may cast it using its morph ability.
Example: Melek, Izzet Paragon says, in part, ΓÇ£You may cast instant and sorcery spells from the top of your library.ΓÇ¥ If you control Melek, Izzet Paragon and the top card of your library is Giant Killer, an adventurer creature card whose Adventure is an instant named Chop Down, you may cast Chop Down but not Giant Killer. If instead you control GarrukΓÇÖs Horde and the top card of your library is Giant Killer, you may cast Giant Killer but not Chop Down.
┬á
601.3f Some effects allow a player to cast a spell with certain qualities from among face-down cards in exile. A player may begin to cast such a spell only if they can look at the face-down card in exile.
┬á
601.4. While announcing the choices of any modes, alternative costs, and/or additional costs as described in rule 601.2b, some options may be available to a player only if other choices are made that would normally be made later in that ruleΓÇÖs instructions. In that case, the spellΓÇÖs controller may consider any other choices to be made in that step. If any such choices could allow them to choose a particular mode, alternative cost, or additional cost, they may do so.
Example: Inscription of Abundance is a modal spell with kicker and the text ΓÇ£Choose one. If this spell was kicked, choose any number instead.ΓÇ¥ When announcing the chosen modes for the spell, its controller may choose any number of modes, even though choosing to pay the kicker cost is normally done later in the announcement process.
┬á
601.5. While announcing the choices of any targets and/or the division or distribution of any effects as described in rules 601.2cΓÇôd, some options may be available to a player only if other choices are made later in spellcasting process. In that case, the spellΓÇÖs controller may consider any other choices to be made during that process, including the choice of any objects that may be used to pay costs for that spell.
┬á
601.6. If a player is no longer allowed to cast a spell after completing its proposal (see rules 601.2aΓÇôd), the casting of the spell is illegal and the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, ΓÇ£Handling Illegal ActionsΓÇ¥). It doesnΓÇÖt matter if a rule or effect would make the casting of the spell illegal while determining and paying that spellΓÇÖs costs (see rules 601.2fΓÇôh) or any time after the spell has been cast.
┬á
601.6a Once a player has begun casting a spell that had flash because certain conditions were met or that could be cast as though it had flash because certain conditions were met (see 601.3d), they may continue to cast that spell as though it had flash even if those conditions stop being met.
┬á
601.7. Some spells specify that one of their controllerΓÇÖs opponents does something the controller would normally do while itΓÇÖs being cast, such as choose a mode or choose targets. In these cases, the opponent does so when the spellΓÇÖs controller normally would do so.
┬á
601.7a If there is more than one opponent who could make such a choice, the spellΓÇÖs controller decides which of those opponents will make the choice.
┬á
601.7b If the spell instructs its controller and another player to do something at the same time as the spell is being cast, the spellΓÇÖs controller goes first, then the other player. This is an exception to rule 101.4.
┬á
601.8. Casting a spell that alters costs wonΓÇÖt affect spells and abilities that are already on the stack.
┬á
602. Activating Activated Abilities
┬á
602.1. Activated abilities have a cost and an effect. They are written as ΓÇ£[Cost]: [Effect.] [Activation instructions (if any).]ΓÇ¥
┬á
602.1a The activation cost is everything before the colon (:). An abilityΓÇÖs activation cost must be paid by the player who is activating it.
Example: The activation cost of an ability that reads ΓÇ£{2}, {T}: You gain 1 lifeΓÇ¥ is two mana of any type plus tapping the permanent that has the ability.
┬á
602.1b Some text after the colon of an activated ability states instructions that must be followed while activating that ability. Such text may state which players can activate that ability, may restrict when a player can activate the ability, or may define some aspect of the activation cost. This text is not part of the abilityΓÇÖs effect. It functions at all times. If an activated ability has any activation instructions, they appear last, after the abilityΓÇÖs effect.
┬á
602.1c An activated ability is the only kind of ability that can be activated. If an object or rule refers to activating an ability without specifying what kind, it must be referring to an activated ability.
┬á
602.1d Previously, the action of using an activated ability was referred to on cards as ΓÇ£playingΓÇ¥ that ability. Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference so they now refer to ΓÇ£activatingΓÇ¥ that ability.
┬á
602.1e If a spell or ability that refers to the ΓÇ£activation costΓÇ¥ of an ability modifies how a player may pay that cost, that modification applies to the total cost of that ability, even if that cost is increased and/or decreased by other effects. See rules 602.2b and 601.2f.
┬á
602.2. To activate an ability is to put it onto the stack and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Only an objectΓÇÖs controller (or its owner, if it doesnΓÇÖt have a controller) can activate its activated ability unless the object specifically says otherwise. Activating an ability follows the steps listed below, in order. If, at any point during the activation of an ability, a player is unable to comply with any of those steps, the activation is illegal; the game returns to the moment before that ability started to be activated (see rule 733, ΓÇ£Handling Illegal ActionsΓÇ¥). Announcements and payments canΓÇÖt be altered after theyΓÇÖve been made.
┬á
602.2a The player announces that they are activating the ability. If an activated ability is being activated from a hidden zone, the card that has that ability is revealed (see rule 701.20a). That ability is created on the stack as an object thatΓÇÖs not a card. It becomes the topmost object on the stack. It has the text of the ability that created it, and no other characteristics. Its controller is the player who activated the ability. The ability remains on the stack until itΓÇÖs countered, it resolves, or an effect moves it elsewhere.
┬á
602.2b The remainder of the process for activating an ability is identical to the process for casting a spell listed in rules 601.2bΓÇôi. Those rules apply to activating an ability just as they apply to casting a spell. An activated abilityΓÇÖs analog to a spellΓÇÖs mana cost (as referenced in rule 601.2f) is its activation cost.
┬á
602.3. Some abilities specify that one of their controllerΓÇÖs opponents does something the controller would normally do while itΓÇÖs being activated, such as choose a mode or choose targets. In these cases, the opponent does so when the abilityΓÇÖs controller normally would do so.
┬á
602.3a If there is more than one opponent who could make such a choice, the abilityΓÇÖs controller decides which of those opponents will make the choice.
┬á
602.3b If the ability instructs its controller and another player to do something at the same time as the ability is being activated, the abilityΓÇÖs controller goes first, then the other player. This is an exception to rule 101.4.
┬á
602.4. Activating an ability that alters costs wonΓÇÖt affect spells and abilities that are already on the stack.
┬á
602.5. A player canΓÇÖt begin to activate an ability thatΓÇÖs prohibited from being activated.
┬á
602.5a A creatureΓÇÖs activated ability with the tap symbol ({T}) or the untap symbol ({Q}) in its activation cost canΓÇÖt be activated unless the creature has been under its controllerΓÇÖs control since the start of their most recent turn. Ignore this rule for creatures with haste (see rule 702.10).
┬á
602.5b If an activated ability has a restriction on its use (for example, ΓÇ£Activate only once each turnΓÇ¥), the restriction continues to apply to that object even if its controller changes.
┬á
602.5c If an object acquires an activated ability with a restriction on its use from another object, that restriction applies only to that ability as acquired from that object. It doesnΓÇÖt apply to other, identically worded abilities.
┬á
602.5d Activated abilities that read ΓÇ£Activate only as a sorceryΓÇ¥ mean the player must follow the timing rules for casting a sorcery spell, though the ability isnΓÇÖt actually a sorcery. The player doesnΓÇÖt actually need to have a sorcery card that they could cast.
┬á
602.5e Activated abilities that read ΓÇ£Activate only as an instantΓÇ¥ mean the player must follow the timing rules for casting an instant spell, though the ability isnΓÇÖt actually an instant. The player doesnΓÇÖt actually need to have an instant card that they could cast.
┬á
603. Handling Triggered Abilities
┬á
603.1. Triggered abilities have a trigger condition and an effect. They are written as ΓÇ£[When/Whenever/At] [trigger condition or event], [effect]. [Instructions (if any).]ΓÇ¥
┬á
603.1a A triggered ability may include instructions after its effects that limit what the ability may target or state that it canΓÇÖt be countered. This text is not part of the abilityΓÇÖs effect. It functions while the ability is on the stack.
┬á
603.1b A triggered ability may have more than one trigger condition, and an instruction that refers to whether ΓÇ£allΓÇ¥ of those conditions have happened during a particular period. This refers to whether or not all of those conditions have occurred during that period, regardless of whether that ability has triggered based on those conditions.
┬á
603.2. Whenever a game event or game state matches a triggered abilityΓÇÖs trigger event, that ability automatically triggers. The ability doesnΓÇÖt do anything at this point.
┬á
603.2a Because they arenΓÇÖt cast or activated, triggered abilities can trigger even when it isnΓÇÖt legal to cast spells and activate abilities. Effects that preclude abilities from being activated donΓÇÖt affect them.
┬á
603.2b When a phase or step begins, all abilities that trigger ΓÇ£at the beginning ofΓÇ¥ that phase or step trigger.
┬á
603.2c An ability triggers only once each time its trigger event occurs. However, it can trigger repeatedly if one event contains multiple occurrences.
Example: A permanent has an ability whose trigger condition reads, ΓÇ£Whenever a land is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, . . . .ΓÇ¥ If someone casts a spell that destroys all lands, the ability will trigger once for each land put into the graveyard during the spellΓÇÖs resolution.
┬á
603.2d An ability may state that a triggered ability triggers additional times. In this case, rather than simply determining that such an ability has triggered, determine how many times it should trigger, then that ability triggers that many times. An effect that states that an ability triggers additional times doesnΓÇÖt invoke itself repeatedly and doesnΓÇÖt apply to other effects that affect how many times an ability triggers. An effect that states a triggered ability of an object triggers additional times refers only to triggered abilities that object has, not to any delayed or reflexive triggered abilities (see rule 603.7 and rule 603.12) that may be created by abilities the object has.
┬á
603.2e Some trigger events use the word ΓÇ£becomesΓÇ¥ (for example, ΓÇ£becomes attachedΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£becomes blockedΓÇ¥). These trigger only at the time the named event happensΓÇöthey donΓÇÖt trigger if that state already exists or retrigger if it persists. An ability that triggers when a permanent ΓÇ£becomes tappedΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£becomes untappedΓÇ¥ doesnΓÇÖt trigger if the permanent enters the battlefield in that state.
Example: An ability that triggers when a permanent ΓÇ£becomes tappedΓÇ¥ triggers only when the status of a permanent thatΓÇÖs already on the battlefield changes from untapped to tapped.
┬á
603.2f If a triggered abilityΓÇÖs trigger condition is met, but the object with that triggered ability is at no time visible to all players, the ability does not trigger.
┬á
603.2g An ability triggers only if its trigger event actually occurs. An event thatΓÇÖs prevented or replaced wonΓÇÖt trigger anything.
Example: An ability that triggers on damage being dealt wonΓÇÖt trigger if all the damage is prevented.
┬á
603.2h A triggered ability may have an instruction followed by ΓÇ£Do this only once each turn.ΓÇ¥ This ability triggers only if its sourceΓÇÖs controller has not yet taken the indicated action that turn.
┬á
603.3. Once an ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack as an object thatΓÇÖs not a card the next time a player would receive priority. See rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and Priority.ΓÇ¥ The ability becomes the topmost object on the stack. It has the text of the ability that created it, and no other characteristics. It remains on the stack until itΓÇÖs countered, it resolves, a rule causes it to be removed from the stack, or an effect moves it elsewhere.
┬á
603.3a A triggered ability is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered, unless itΓÇÖs a delayed triggered ability. To determine the controller of a delayed triggered ability, see rules 603.7dΓÇôf.
┬á
603.3b If multiple abilities have triggered since the last time a player received priority, the abilities are placed on the stack in a two-part process. First, each player, in APNAP order, puts each triggered ability they control with a trigger condition that isnΓÇÖt another ability triggering on the stack in any order they choose. (See rule 101.4.) Second, each player, in APNAP order, puts all remaining triggered abilities they control on the stack in any order they choose. Then the game once again checks for and performs state-based actions until none are performed, then abilities that triggered during this process go on the stack. This process repeats until no new state-based actions are performed and no abilities trigger. Then the appropriate player gets priority.
┬á
603.3c If a triggered ability is modal, its controller announces the mode choice when putting the ability on the stack. If one of the modes would be illegal (due to an inability to choose legal targets, for example), that mode canΓÇÖt be chosen. If no mode is chosen, the ability is removed from the stack. (See rule 700.2.)
┬á
603.3d The remainder of the process for putting a triggered ability on the stack is identical to the process for casting a spell listed in rules 601.2cΓÇôd. If a choice is required when the triggered ability goes on the stack but no legal choices can be made for it, or if a rule or a continuous effect otherwise makes the ability illegal, the ability is simply removed from the stack.
┬á
603.4. A triggered ability may read ΓÇ£When/Whenever/At [trigger event], if [condition], [effect].ΓÇ¥ When the trigger event occurs, the ability checks whether the stated condition is true. The ability triggers only if it is; otherwise it does nothing. If the ability triggers, it checks the stated condition again as it resolves. If the condition isnΓÇÖt true at that time, the ability is removed from the stack and does nothing. Note that this mirrors the check for legal targets. This rule is referred to as the ΓÇ£intervening ΓÇÿifΓÇÖ clauseΓÇ¥ rule. (The word ΓÇ£ifΓÇ¥ has only its normal English meaning anywhere else in the text of a card; this rule only applies to an ΓÇ£ifΓÇ¥ that immediately follows a trigger condition.)
Example: Felidar Sovereign reads, ΓÇ£At the beginning of your upkeep, if you have 40 or more life, you win the game.ΓÇ¥ Its controllerΓÇÖs life total is checked as that playerΓÇÖs upkeep begins. If that player has 39 or less life, the ability doesnΓÇÖt trigger at all. If that player has 40 or more life, the ability triggers and goes on the stack. As the ability resolves, that playerΓÇÖs life total is checked again. If that player has 39 or less life at this time, the ability is removed from the stack and has no effect. If that player has 40 or more life at this time, the ability resolves and that player wins the game.
┬á
603.5. Some triggered abilitiesΓÇÖ effects are optional (they contain ΓÇ£may,ΓÇ¥ as in ΓÇ£At the beginning of your upkeep, you may draw a cardΓÇ¥). These abilities go on the stack when they trigger, regardless of whether their controller intends to exercise the abilityΓÇÖs option or not. The choice is made when the ability resolves. Likewise, triggered abilities that have an effect ΓÇ£unlessΓÇ¥ something is true or a player chooses to do something will go on the stack normally; the ΓÇ£unlessΓÇ¥ part of the ability is dealt with when the ability resolves.
┬á
603.6. Trigger events that involve objects changing zones are called ΓÇ£zone-change triggers.ΓÇ¥ Many abilities with zone-change triggers attempt to do something to that object after it changes zones. During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to. If the object is unable to be found in the zone it went to, the part of the ability attempting to do something to the object will fail to do anything. The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponentΓÇÖs hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers.
┬á
603.6a Enters-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent enters the battlefield. These are written, ΓÇ£When [this object] enters, . . . ΓÇ£ or ΓÇ£Whenever a [type] enters, . . .ΓÇ¥ Each time an event puts one or more permanents onto the battlefield, all permanents on the battlefield (including the newcomers) are checked for any enters-the-battlefield triggers that match the event.
┬á
603.6b Continuous effects that modify characteristics of a permanent do so the moment the permanent is on the battlefield (and not before then). The permanent is never on the battlefield with its unmodified characteristics. Continuous effects donΓÇÖt apply before the permanent is on the battlefield, however (see rule 603.6d).
Example: If an effect reads ΓÇ£All lands are creaturesΓÇ¥ and a land card is played, the effect makes the land card into a creature the moment it enters the battlefield, so it would trigger abilities that trigger when a creature enters the battlefield. Conversely, if an effect reads ΓÇ£All creatures lose all abilitiesΓÇ¥ and a creature card with an enters-the-battlefield triggered ability enters the battlefield, that effect will cause it to lose its abilities the moment it enters the battlefield, so the enters-the-battlefield ability wonΓÇÖt trigger.
┬á
603.6c Leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent moves from the battlefield to another zone, or when a phased-in permanent leaves the game because its owner leaves the game. These are written as, but arenΓÇÖt limited to, ΓÇ£When [this object] leaves the battlefield, . . .ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£Whenever [something] is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, . . . .ΓÇ¥ (See also rule 603.10.) An ability that attempts to do something to the card that left the battlefield checks for it only in the first zone that it went to. An ability that triggers when a card is put into a certain zone ΓÇ£from anywhereΓÇ¥ is never treated as a leaves-the-battlefield ability, even if an object is put into that zone from the battlefield.
┬á
603.6d Some permanents have text that reads ΓÇ£[This permanent] enters with . . . ,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£As [this permanent] enters . . . ,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£[This permanent] enters as . . . ,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£[This permanent] enters tapped.ΓÇ¥ Such text is a static abilityΓÇönot a triggered abilityΓÇöwhose effect occurs as part of the event that puts the permanent onto the battlefield.
┬á
603.6e Some Auras have triggered abilities that trigger on the enchanted permanent leaving the battlefield. These triggered abilities can find the new object that permanent card became in the zone it moved to; they can also find the new object the Aura card became in its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard after state-based actions have been checked. See rule 400.7.
┬á
603.7. An effect may create a delayed triggered ability that can do something at a later time. A delayed triggered ability will contain ΓÇ£when,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£whenever,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£at,ΓÇ¥ although that word wonΓÇÖt usually begin the ability.
┬á
603.7a Delayed triggered abilities are created during the resolution of spells or abilities, as the result of a replacement effect being applied, or as a result of a static ability that allows a player to take an action. A delayed triggered ability wonΓÇÖt trigger until it has actually been created, even if its trigger event occurred just beforehand. Other events that happen earlier may make the trigger event impossible.
Example: Part of an effect reads ΓÇ£When this creature leaves the battlefield,ΓÇ¥ but the creature in question leaves the battlefield before the spell or ability creating the effect resolves. In this case, the delayed ability never triggers.
Example: If an effect reads ΓÇ£When this creature becomes untappedΓÇ¥ and the named creature becomes untapped before the effect resolves, the ability waits for the next time that creature untaps.
┬á
603.7b A delayed triggered ability will trigger only onceΓÇöthe next time its trigger event occursΓÇöunless it has a stated duration, such as ΓÇ£this turn.ΓÇ¥ If its trigger event occurs more than once simultaneously and the ability doesnΓÇÖt have a stated duration, the controller of the delayed triggered ability chooses which event causes the ability to trigger.
┬á
603.7c A delayed triggered ability that refers to a particular object still affects it even if the object changes characteristics. However, if that object is no longer in the zone itΓÇÖs expected to be in at the time the delayed triggered ability resolves, the ability wonΓÇÖt affect it. (Note that if that object left that zone and then returned, itΓÇÖs a new object and thus wonΓÇÖt be affected. See rule 400.7.)
Example: An ability that reads ΓÇ£Exile this creature at the beginning of the next end stepΓÇ¥ will exile the permanent even if itΓÇÖs no longer a creature during the next end step. However, it wonΓÇÖt do anything if the permanent left the battlefield before then.
┬á
603.7d If a spell creates a delayed triggered ability, the source of that delayed triggered ability is that spell. The controller of that delayed triggered ability is the player who controlled that spell as it resolved.
┬á
603.7e If an activated or triggered ability creates a delayed triggered ability, the source of that delayed triggered ability is the same as the source of that other ability. The controller of that delayed triggered ability is the player who controlled that other ability as it resolved.
┬á
603.7f If a static ability generates a replacement effect which causes a delayed triggered ability to be created, the source of that delayed triggered ability is the object with that static ability. The controller of that delayed triggered ability is the same as the controller of that object at the time the replacement effect was applied.
┬á
603.7g If a static ability allows a player to take an action and creates a delayed triggered ability if that player does so, the source of that delayed triggered ability is the object with that static ability. The controller of that delayed triggered ability is the same as the controller of that object at the time the action was taken.
┬á
603.7h An activated or triggered ability may create a delayed triggered ability that triggers when the ability that created it has resolved a certain number of times in a turn. In that case, that delayed triggered ability is created only once, during the appropriate resolution of that ability.
┬á
603.8. Some triggered abilities trigger when a game state (such as a player controlling no permanents of a particular card type) is true, rather than triggering when an event occurs. These abilities trigger as soon as the game state matches the condition. TheyΓÇÖll go onto the stack at the next available opportunity. These are called state triggers. (Note that state triggers arenΓÇÖt the same as state-based actions.) A state-triggered ability doesnΓÇÖt trigger again until the ability has resolved, has been countered, or has otherwise left the stack. Then, if the object with the ability is still in the same zone and the game state still matches its trigger condition, the ability will trigger again.
Example: A permanentΓÇÖs ability reads, ΓÇ£Whenever you have no cards in hand, draw a card.ΓÇ¥ If its controller plays the last card from their hand, the ability will trigger once and wonΓÇÖt trigger again until it has left the stack. If its controller casts a spell that reads ΓÇ£Discard your hand, then draw that many cards,ΓÇ¥ the ability will trigger during the spellΓÇÖs resolution because the playerΓÇÖs hand was momentarily empty.
┬á
603.9. Some triggered abilities trigger specifically when a player loses the game. These abilities trigger when a player loses or leaves the game, regardless of the reason, unless that player leaves the game as the result of a draw. See rule 104.3.
┬á
603.10. Normally, objects that exist immediately after an event are checked to see if the event matched any trigger conditions, and continuous effects that exist at that time are used to determine what the trigger conditions are and what the objects involved in the event look like. However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game ΓÇ£looks back in timeΓÇ¥ to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows:
┬á
603.10a Some zone-change triggers look back in time. These are leaves-the-battlefield abilities, abilities that trigger when a player sacrifices a permanent, abilities that trigger when a card leaves a graveyard, and abilities that trigger when an object that all players can see is put into a hand or library.
Example: Two creatures are on the battlefield along with an artifact that has the ability ΓÇ£Whenever a creature dies, you gain 1 life.ΓÇ¥ Someone casts a spell that destroys all artifacts, creatures, and enchantments. The artifactΓÇÖs ability triggers twice, even though the artifact goes to its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard at the same time as the creatures.
┬á
603.10b Abilities that trigger when a permanent phases out look back in time.
┬á
603.10c Abilities that trigger specifically when an object becomes unattached look back in time.
┬á
603.10d Abilities that trigger when a player loses control of an object or when a playerΓÇÖs opponent gains control of an object from that player look back in time.
┬á
603.10e Abilities that trigger when a spell is countered look back in time.
┬á
603.10f Abilities that trigger when a player loses the game look back in time.
┬á
603.10g Abilities that trigger when a player planeswalks away from a plane look back in time.
┬á
603.11. Some objects have a static ability thatΓÇÖs linked to one or more triggered abilities. (See rule 607, ΓÇ£Linked Abilities.ΓÇ¥) These objects combine the abilities into one paragraph, with the static ability first, followed by each triggered ability thatΓÇÖs linked to it. A very few objects have triggered abilities which are written with the trigger condition in the middle of the ability, rather than at the beginning.
Example: An ability that reads ΓÇ£Reveal the first card you draw each turn. Whenever you reveal a basic land card this way, draw a cardΓÇ¥ is a static ability linked to a triggered ability.
┬á
603.12. A resolving spell or ability may allow or instruct a player to take an action and create a triggered ability that triggers ΓÇ£when [a player] [does or doesnΓÇÖt]ΓÇ¥ take that action or ΓÇ£when [something happens] this way.ΓÇ¥ These reflexive triggered abilities follow the rules for delayed triggered abilities (see rule 603.7), except that theyΓÇÖre checked immediately after being created and trigger based on whether the trigger event or events occurred earlier during the resolution of the spell or ability that created them.
Example: Heart-Piercer Manticore has an ability that reads ΓÇ£When this creature enters, you may sacrifice another creature. When you do, this creature deals damage equal to that creatureΓÇÖs power to any target.ΓÇ¥ The reflexive triggered ability triggers only when you sacrifice another creature due to the original triggered ability, and not if you sacrifice a creature for any other reason.
┬á
603.12a Normally, if the trigger event or events occur multiple times during the resolution of the spell or ability that created it, the reflexive triggered ability will trigger once for each of those times. However, if a resolving spell or ability includes a choice to pay a cost multiple times and creates a triggered ability that triggers when that payment is made, paying that cost one or more times causes the reflexive triggered ability to trigger only once.
┬á
604. Handling Static Abilities
┬á
604.1. Static abilities do something all the time rather than being activated or triggered. They are written as statements, and theyΓÇÖre simply true.
┬á
604.2. Static abilities create continuous effects, some of which are prevention effects or replacement effects. These effects are active as long as the permanent with the ability remains on the battlefield and has the ability, or as long as the object with the ability remains in the appropriate zone, as described in rule 113.6.
┬á
604.3. Some static abilities are characteristic-defining abilities. A characteristic-defining ability conveys information about an objectΓÇÖs characteristics that would normally be found elsewhere on that object (such as in its mana cost, type line, or power/toughness box). Characteristic-defining abilities can add to or override information found elsewhere on that object. Characteristic-defining abilities function in all zones. They also function outside the game and before the game begins.
┬á
604.3a A static ability is a characteristic-defining ability if it meets the following criteria: (1) It defines an objectΓÇÖs colors, subtypes, power, or toughness; (2) it is printed on the card it affects, it was granted to the token it affects by the effect that created the token, or it was acquired by the object it affects as the result of a copy effect or text-changing effect; (3) it does not directly affect the characteristics of any other objects; (4) it is not an ability that an object grants to itself; and (5) it does not set the values of such characteristics only if certain conditions are met.
┬á
604.4. Many Auras, Equipment, and Fortifications have static abilities that modify the object theyΓÇÖre attached to, but those abilities donΓÇÖt target that object. If an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification is moved to a different object, the ability stops applying to the original object and starts modifying the new one.
┬á
604.5. Some static abilities apply while a spell is on the stack. These are often abilities that refer to countering the spell. Also, abilities that say ΓÇ£As an additional cost to cast . . . ,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£You may pay [cost] rather than pay [this object]ΓÇÖs mana cost,ΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£You may cast [this object] without paying its mana costΓÇ¥ work while a spell is on the stack.
┬á
604.6. Some static abilities apply while a card is in any zone that you could cast or play it from (usually your hand). These are limited to those that read, ΓÇ£You may [cast/play] [this card] . . . ,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£You canΓÇÖt [cast/play] [this card] . . . ,ΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£[Cast/Play] [this card] only . . . .ΓÇ¥
┬á
604.7. Unlike spells and other kinds of abilities, static abilities canΓÇÖt use an objectΓÇÖs last known information for purposes of determining how their effects are applied.
┬á
605. Mana Abilities
┬á
605.1. Some activated abilities and some triggered abilities are mana abilities, which are subject to special rules. Only abilities that meet either of the following two sets of criteria are mana abilities, regardless of what other effects they may generate or what timing restrictions (such as ΓÇ£Activate only as an instantΓÇ¥) they may have.
┬á
605.1a An activated ability is a mana ability if it meets all of the following criteria: it doesnΓÇÖt require a target (see rule 115.6), it could add mana to a playerΓÇÖs mana pool when it resolves, itΓÇÖs not a loyalty ability (see rule 606, ΓÇ£Loyalty AbilitiesΓÇ¥), and its cost and effect donΓÇÖt move any card to or from a library. Do not take into account replacement effects that may apply, other than self-replacement effects, when evaluating these criteria.
┬á
605.1b A triggered ability is a mana ability if it meets all of the following criteria: it doesnΓÇÖt require a target (see rule 115.6), it triggers from the activation or resolution of an activated mana ability (see rule 605.1a) or from mana being added to a playerΓÇÖs mana pool, and it could add mana to a playerΓÇÖs mana pool when it resolves.
┬á
605.2. A mana ability remains a mana ability even if the game state doesnΓÇÖt allow it to produce mana.
Example: A permanent has an ability that reads ΓÇ£{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control.ΓÇ¥ The ability is still a mana ability even if you control no creatures or if the permanent is already tapped.
┬á
605.3. Activating an activated mana ability follows the rules for activating any other activated ability (see rule 602.2), with the following exceptions:
┬á
605.3a A player may activate an activated mana ability whenever they have priority, whenever they are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment, or whenever a rule or effect asks for a mana payment, even if itΓÇÖs in the middle of casting or resolving a spell or activating or resolving an ability.
┬á
605.3b An activated mana ability doesnΓÇÖt go on the stack, so it canΓÇÖt be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after it is activated. (See rule 405.6c.)
┬á
605.3c Once a player begins to activate a mana ability, that ability canΓÇÖt be activated again until it has resolved.
┬á
