605.4. Triggered mana abilities follow all the rules for other triggered abilities (see rule 603, ΓÇ£Handling Triggered AbilitiesΓÇ¥), with the following exception:
┬á
605.4a A triggered mana ability doesnΓÇÖt go on the stack, so it canΓÇÖt be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after the mana ability that triggered it, without waiting for priority.
Example: An enchantment reads, ΓÇ£Whenever a player taps a land for mana, that player adds one mana of any type that land produced.ΓÇ¥ If a player taps lands for mana while casting a spell, the additional mana is added immediately and can be used to pay for the spell.
┬á
605.5. Abilities that donΓÇÖt meet the criteria specified in rules 605.1aΓÇôb and spells arenΓÇÖt mana abilities.
┬á
605.5a An ability with a target is not a mana ability, even if it could put mana into a playerΓÇÖs mana pool when it resolves. The same is true for a triggered ability that could produce mana but triggers from an event other than activating a mana ability, or a triggered ability that triggers from activating a mana ability but couldnΓÇÖt produce mana. These follow the normal rules for activated or triggered abilities, as appropriate.
┬á
605.5b A spell can never be a mana ability, even if it could put mana into a playerΓÇÖs mana pool when it resolves. ItΓÇÖs cast and resolves just like any other spell. Some older cards were printed with the card type ΓÇ£mana sourceΓÇ¥; these cards have received errata in the Oracle card reference and are now instants.
┬á
606. Loyalty Abilities
┬á
606.1. Some activated abilities are loyalty abilities, which are subject to special rules.
┬á
606.2. An activated ability with a loyalty symbol in its cost is a loyalty ability. Normally, only planeswalkers have loyalty abilities.
┬á
606.3. A player may activate a loyalty ability of a permanent they control any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn, but only if no player has previously activated a loyalty ability of that permanent that turn.
┬á
606.4. The cost to activate a loyalty ability of a permanent is to put on or remove from that permanent a certain number of loyalty counters, as shown by the loyalty symbol in the abilityΓÇÖs cost. This cost may be modified by other effects.
┬á
606.5 If the total cost to activate a loyalty ability contains multiple costs to add or remove loyalty counters, those costs are combined into a single cost to add or remove loyalty counters, as appropriate.
Example: A player controls Carth the Lion, which says, in part, ΓÇ£PlaneswalkersΓÇÖ loyalty abilities you control cost an additional [+1] to activate. That player also controls a planeswalker with three loyalty counters. To activate one of that planeswalkerΓÇÖs abilities that normally costs [+1], they put two loyalty counters on it. To activate one of its abilities that normally costs [ΓêÆ4], they remove three loyalty counters from it.
┬á
606.6. A loyalty ability with a negative loyalty cost, taking into account any additional costs, canΓÇÖt be activated unless the permanent has at least that many loyalty counters on it.
┬á
607. Linked Abilities
┬á
607.1. An object may have two abilities printed on it such that one of them causes actions to be taken or objects or players to be affected and the other one directly refers to those actions, objects, or players. If so, these two abilities are linked: the second refers only to actions that were taken or objects or players that were affected by the first, and not by any other ability.
┬á
607.1a An ability printed on an object within another ability that grants that ability to that object is considered to be ΓÇ£printed onΓÇ¥ that object for these purposes.
┬á
607.1b An ability printed on either face of a nonmodal double-faced object (see rule 712) is considered to be ΓÇ£printed onΓÇ¥ that object for these purposes, regardless of which face is up.
┬á
607.1c An ability printed on an object that fulfills both criteria described in rule 607.1 is linked to itself.
┬á
607.1d Abilities printed on two objects can be linked if one object is a token, emblem, or nontoken permanent and the second object was the source of the ability that either created the token or emblem or put that nontoken permanent onto the battlefield. In these cases, the abilities fit the criteria listed for one of the different kinds of linked abilities in rule 607.2 except they are printed on two objects rather than one.
┬á
607.2. There are different kinds of linked abilities.
┬á
607.2a If an object has an activated or triggered ability printed on it that instructs a player to exile one or more cards and an ability printed on it that refers either to ΓÇ£the exiled cardsΓÇ¥ or to cards ΓÇ£exiled with [this object],ΓÇ¥ these abilities are linked. The second ability refers only to cards in the exile zone that were put there as a result of an instruction to exile them in the first ability.
┬á
607.2b If an object has an ability printed on it that generates a replacement effect which causes one or more cards to be exiled and an ability printed on it that refers either to ΓÇ£the exiled cardsΓÇ¥ or to cards ΓÇ£exiled with [this object],ΓÇ¥ these abilities are linked. The second ability refers only to cards in the exile zone that were put there as a direct result of a replacement event caused by the first ability. See rule 614, ΓÇ£Replacement Effects.ΓÇ¥
┬á
607.2c If an object has an activated or triggered ability printed on it that puts one or more objects onto the battlefield and an ability printed on it that refers to objects ΓÇ£put onto the battlefield with [this object]ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£created with [this object],ΓÇ¥ those abilities are linked. The second can refer only to objects put onto the battlefield as a result of the first.
┬á
607.2d If an object has an ability printed on it that causes a player to ΓÇ£choose a [value]ΓÇ¥ and an ability printed on it that refers to ΓÇ£the chosen [value],ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£the last chosen [value],ΓÇ¥ or similar, those abilities are linked. The second ability refers only to a choice made as a result of the first ability.
┬á
607.2e If an object has an ability printed on it that allows some information to be noted and another ability which refers to information noted for that object, those abilities are linked. The second ability refers only to information noted as a result of the first ability.
┬á
607.2f If an object has an ability printed on it that causes a player to choose from between two or more words that otherwise have no rules meaning and an ability printed on it that refers to a choice involving one or more of those words, those abilities are linked. The second can refer only to a choice made as a result of the first ability.
┬á
607.2g If an object has an ability printed on it that causes a player to pay a cost as it enters the battlefield and an ability printed on it that refers to the cost paid ΓÇ£as [this object] entered,ΓÇ¥ these abilities are linked. The second ability refers only to a cost paid as a result of the first ability.
┬á
607.2h If an object has both a static ability and one or more triggered abilities printed on it in the same paragraph, each of those triggered abilities is linked to the static ability. Each triggered ability refers only to actions taken as a result of the static ability. See rule 603.11.
┬á
607.2i If an object has an ability printed on it that allows an additional cost to be paid and an ability printed on it that refers to whether that cost was paid, those abilities are linked. The second refers only to whether the intent to pay the additional cost listed in the first was declared as the object was cast as a spell. If an ability lists multiple such costs, it may have multiple abilities linked to it. Each of those abilities will specify which cost it refers to.
Example: Stormscape Battlemage has ΓÇ£Kicker {W} and/or {2}{B}ΓÇ¥ and two abilities that may trigger when it enters the battlefield. The first triggers if it was kicked with its {W} kicker, and the second triggers if it was kicked with its {2}{B} kicker. Each of those triggered abilities is linked to its kicker ability.
┬á
607.2j If an object has an ability printed on it that causes a player to pay a variable additional cost as itΓÇÖs cast and an ability printed on it that refers to the cost paid ΓÇ£as [this object] was cast,ΓÇ¥ these abilities are linked. The second refers only to the value chosen for the cost listed in the first as the object was cast as a spell. See rule 601.2b.
┬á
607.2k The two abilities represented by the champion keyword are linked abilities. See rule 702.72, ΓÇ£Champion.ΓÇ¥
┬á
607.2m Abilities preceded by an anchor word are linked to the ability that allows a player to choose that anchor word. See rule 614.12b.
┬á
607.2n If an object has a static ability printed on it that allows a player to exile one or more cards ΓÇ£before you shuffle your deck to start the gameΓÇ¥ and an ability printed on it that refers to cards ΓÇ£exiled with cards named [this objectΓÇÖs name],ΓÇ¥ the second ability is linked to the first ability of any objects that had the specified name before the game began.
┬á
607.2p If an object has both a static ability that causes a player to make a choice for a characteristic-defining ability before the game begins and that characteristic-defining ability printed on it in the same paragraph, those abilities are linked. The second ability refers only to the choice made as a result of the first ability and continues to refer to that choice as the object changes zones during the game.
┬á
607.2q If a permanent spell has an ability printed on it that allows one or more cards to be exiled while paying a cost to cast it and the permanent that spell becomes has an ability that refers to cards ΓÇ£exiled with [this object],ΓÇ¥ those abilities are linked. The second ability refers only to cards exiled to pay the cost of the spell that became that permanent.
┬á
607.3. If, within a pair of linked abilities, one ability refers to a single object as ΓÇ£the exiled card,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£a card exiled with [this object],ΓÇ¥ or a similar phrase, and the other ability has exiled multiple cards (usually because it was copied), the ability refers to each of the exiled cards. If that ability asks for any information about the exiled card, such as a characteristic or mana value, it gets multiple answers. If these answers are used to determine the value of a variable, the sum of the answers is used. If that ability performs any actions on ΓÇ£theΓÇ¥ card, it performs that action on each exiled card. If that ability creates a token that is a copy of ΓÇ£theΓÇ¥ card, then for each exiled card, it creates a token that is a copy of that card. If that ability performs any actions on ΓÇ£aΓÇ¥ card, the controller of the ability chooses which card is affected.
┬á
607.4. An ability may be part of more than one pair of linked abilities.
Example: Paradise Plume has the following three abilities: ΓÇ£As this artifact enters, choose a color,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£Whenever a player casts a spell of the chosen color, you may gain 1 life,ΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£{T}: Add one mana of the chosen color.ΓÇ¥ The first and second abilities are linked. The first and third abilities are linked.
┬á
607.5. If an object acquires a pair of linked abilities as part of the same effect, the abilities will be similarly linked to one another on that object even though they werenΓÇÖt printed on that object. They canΓÇÖt be linked to any other ability, regardless of what other abilities the object may currently have or may have had in the past.
Example: Arc-Slogger has the ability ΓÇ£{R}, Exile the top ten cards of your library: This creature deals 2 damage to any target.ΓÇ¥ Sisters of Stone Death has the ability ΓÇ£{B}{G}: Exile target creature blocking or blocked by Sisters of Stone DeathΓÇ¥ and the ability ΓÇ£{2}{B}: Put a creature card exiled with Sisters of Stone Death onto the battlefield under your control.ΓÇ¥ Quicksilver Elemental has the ability ΓÇ£{U}: This creature gains all activated abilities of target creature until end of turn.ΓÇ¥ If a player has Quicksilver Elemental gain Arc-SloggerΓÇÖs ability, activates it, then has Quicksilver Elemental gain Sisters of Stone DeathΓÇÖs abilities, activates the exile ability, and then activates the return-to-the-battlefield ability, only the creature card Quicksilver Elemental exiled with Sisters of Stone DeathΓÇÖs ability can be returned to the battlefield. Creature cards Quicksilver Elemental exiled with Arc-SloggerΓÇÖs ability canΓÇÖt be returned.
┬á
607.5a If an object gains an ability that refers to a choice, but either (a) doesnΓÇÖt copy that abilityΓÇÖs linked ability or (b) does copy the linked ability but no choice is made for it, then the choice is considered to be ΓÇ£undefined.ΓÇ¥ If an ability refers to an undefined choice, that part of the ability wonΓÇÖt do anything.
Example: Voice of All enters the battlefield and Unstable Shapeshifter copies it. Voice of All reads, in part, ΓÇ£As this creature enters, choose a color.ΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£This creature has protection from the chosen color.ΓÇ¥ Unstable Shapeshifter never had a chance for a color to be chosen for it, because it didnΓÇÖt enter the battlefield as Voice of All so it doesnΓÇÖt gain a protection ability.
Example: A Vesuvan Doppelganger enters the battlefield as a copy of Voice of All, and the DoppelgangerΓÇÖs controller chooses blue. Later, the Doppelganger copies Quirion Elves, which has the ability, ΓÇ£{T}: Add one mana of the chosen color.ΓÇ¥ Even though a color was chosen for the Doppelganger, it wasnΓÇÖt chosen for the ability linked to the mana ability copied from the Elves. If that mana ability of the Doppelganger is activated, it will not produce mana.
┬á
608. Resolving Spells and Abilities
┬á
608.1. Each time all players pass in succession, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves. (See rule 609, ΓÇ£Effects.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
608.2. If the object thatΓÇÖs resolving is an instant spell, a sorcery spell, or an ability, its resolution may involve several steps. The steps described in rules 608.2a and 608.2b are followed first. The steps described in rules 608.2cΓÇôm are then followed as appropriate, in no specific order. The steps described in rule 608.2n and 608.2p are followed last.
┬á
608.2a If a triggered ability has an intervening ΓÇ£ifΓÇ¥ clause, it checks whether the clauseΓÇÖs condition is true. If it isnΓÇÖt, the ability is removed from the stack and does nothing. Otherwise, it continues to resolve. See rule 603.4.
┬á
608.2b If the spell or ability specifies targets, it checks whether the targets are still legal. A target thatΓÇÖs no longer in the zone it was in when it was targeted is illegal. Other changes to the game state may cause a target to no longer be legal; for example, its characteristics may have changed or an effect may have changed the text of the spell. If the source of an ability has left the zone it was in, its last known information is used during this process. If all its targets, for every instance of the word ΓÇ£target,ΓÇ¥ are now illegal, the spell or ability doesnΓÇÖt resolve. ItΓÇÖs removed from the stack and, if itΓÇÖs a spell, put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. Otherwise, the spell or ability will resolve normally. Illegal targets, if any, wonΓÇÖt be affected by parts of a resolving spellΓÇÖs effect for which theyΓÇÖre illegal. Other parts of the effect for which those targets are not illegal may still affect them. If the spell or ability creates any continuous effects that affect game rules (see rule 613.11), those effects donΓÇÖt apply to illegal targets. If part of the effect requires information about an illegal target, it fails to determine any such information. Any part of the effect that requires that information wonΓÇÖt happen.
Example: SorinΓÇÖs Thirst is a black instant that reads, ΓÇ£SorinΓÇÖs Thirst deals 2 damage to target creature and you gain 2 life.ΓÇ¥ If the creature isnΓÇÖt a legal target during the resolution of SorinΓÇÖs Thirst (say, if the creature has gained protection from black or left the battlefield), then SorinΓÇÖs Thirst doesnΓÇÖt resolve. Its controller doesnΓÇÖt gain any life.
Example: Plague Spores reads, ΓÇ£Destroy target nonblack creature and target land. They canΓÇÖt be regenerated.ΓÇ¥ Suppose the same creature land is chosen both as the nonblack creature and as the land, and the color of the creature land is changed to black before Plague Spores resolves. Plague Spores still resolves because the black creature land is still a legal target for the ΓÇ£target landΓÇ¥ part of the spell. The ΓÇ£destroy target nonblack creatureΓÇ¥ part of the spell wonΓÇÖt affect that permanent, but the ΓÇ£destroy target landΓÇ¥ part of the spell will still destroy it. It canΓÇÖt be regenerated.
┬á
608.2c The controller of the spell or ability follows its instructions in the order written. However, replacement effects may modify these actions. In some cases, later text on the card may modify the meaning of earlier text (for example, ΓÇ£Destroy target creature. It canΓÇÖt be regeneratedΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£Counter target spell. If that spell is countered this way, put it on top of its ownerΓÇÖs library instead of into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard.ΓÇ¥) DonΓÇÖt just apply effects step by step without thinking in these casesΓÇöread the whole text and apply the rules of English to the text.
┬á
608.2d If an effect of a spell or ability offers any choices other than choices already made as part of casting the spell, activating the ability, or otherwise putting the spell or ability on the stack, the player announces these while applying the effect. The player canΓÇÖt choose an option thatΓÇÖs illegal or impossible, with the exception that having a library with no cards in it doesnΓÇÖt make drawing a card an impossible action (see rule 121.3). If an effect divides or distributes something, such as damage or counters, as a player chooses among any number of untargeted players and/or objects, the player chooses the amount and division such that each chosen player or object receives at least one of whatever is being divided. (Note that if an effect divides or distributes something, such as damage or counters, as a player chooses among some number of target objects and/or players, the amount and division were determined as the spell or ability was put onto the stack rather than at this time; see rule 601.2d.)
Example: A spellΓÇÖs instruction reads, ΓÇ£You may sacrifice a creature. If you donΓÇÖt, you lose 4 life.ΓÇ¥ A player who controls no creatures canΓÇÖt choose the sacrifice option.
┬á
608.2e Some spells and abilities have multiple steps or actions, denoted by separate sentences or clauses, that involve multiple players. In these cases, the choices for the first action are made in APNAP order, and then the first action is processed simultaneously. Then the choices for the second action are made in APNAP order, and then that action is processed simultaneously, and so on. See rule 101.4.
┬á
608.2f Some spells and abilities include actions taken on multiple players and/or objects. In most cases, each such action is processed simultaneously. If the action canΓÇÖt be processed simultaneously, itΓÇÖs instead processed considering each affected player or object individually. APNAP order is used to make the primary determination of the order of those actions. Secondarily, if the action is to be taken on both a player and an object they control or on multiple objects controlled by the same player, the player who controls the resolving spell or ability chooses the relative order of those actions.
Example: Blatant Thievery says ΓÇ£For each opponent, gain control of target permanent that player controls.ΓÇ¥ As Blatant Thievery resolves, its controller gains control of all permanents chosen as targets simultaneously.
Example: Soulfire Eruption says, in part, ΓÇ£Choose any number of target creatures, planeswalkers, and/or players. For each of them, exile the top card of your library, then Soulfire Eruption deals damage equal to that cardΓÇÖs mana value to that permanent or player.ΓÇ¥ A player casts Soulfire Eruption targeting an opponent and a creature that opponent controls. As Soulfire Eruption resolves, the player canΓÇÖt exile the top card of their library multiple times at the same time, so they first choose which target they are considering, then they exile the top card of their library, and finally Soulfire Eruption deals damage to that target. They then repeat this process for the remaining target. 
┬á
608.2g If an effect gives a player the option to pay mana, they may activate mana abilities before taking that action. If an effect specifically instructs or allows a player to cast a spell during resolution, they do so by following the steps in rules 601.2aΓÇôi, except no player receives priority after itΓÇÖs cast. That spell becomes the topmost object on the stack, and the currently resolving spell or ability continues to resolve, which may include casting other spells this way. No other spells can normally be cast and no other abilities can normally be activated during resolution.
┬á
608.2h If an effect requires information from the game (such as the number of creatures on the battlefield), the answer is determined only once, when the effect is applied. If the effect requires information from a specific object, including the source of the ability itself, the effect uses the current information of that object if itΓÇÖs in the public zone it was expected to be in; if itΓÇÖs no longer in that zone, or if the effect has moved it from a public zone to a hidden zone, the effect uses the objectΓÇÖs last known information. See rule 113.7a. If an ability states that an object does something, itΓÇÖs the object as it existsΓÇöor as it most recently existedΓÇöthat does it, not the ability.
┬á
608.2i Some effects look back in time and require information about previous game states and actions rather than considering the current game state. If such an effect requires information from the game about an object or group of objects, and that effect is not taking any actions on those objects, they donΓÇÖt need to be currently in the zone they were in at the time of that previous game state or action, nor do they need to currently meet the criteria described in the action, as long as they did so at the specified time. This is an exception to 608.2h.
Example: A player attacks with Bear Cub. Later in the turn, an effect causes Bear Cub to become a noncreature permanent. The same player then casts Search Party Captain, a spell that says in part ΓÇ£This spell costs {1} less to cast for each creature you attacked with this turn.ΓÇ¥ That spell costs {1} less because the player attacked with a creature, even though the Bear Cub they attacked with is no longer a creature.
┬á
608.2j If an effect refers to certain characteristics, it checks only for the value of the specified characteristics, regardless of any related ones an object may also have.
Example: An effect that reads ΓÇ£Destroy all black creaturesΓÇ¥ destroys a white-and-black creature, but one that reads ΓÇ£Destroy all nonblack creaturesΓÇ¥ doesnΓÇÖt.
┬á
608.2k If an abilityΓÇÖs effect refers to a specific untargeted object that has been previously referred to by that abilityΓÇÖs cost or trigger condition, it still affects that object even if the object has changed characteristics.
Example: Wall of Tears says ΓÇ£Whenever this creature blocks a creature, return that creature to its ownerΓÇÖs hand at end of combat.ΓÇ¥ If Wall of Tears blocks a creature, then that creature ceases to be a creature before the triggered ability resolves, the permanent will still be returned to its ownerΓÇÖs hand.
┬á
608.2m If an instant spell, sorcery spell, or ability that can legally resolve leaves the stack once it starts to resolve, it will continue to resolve fully.
┬á
608.2n As the final part of an instant or sorcery spellΓÇÖs resolution, the spell is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. As the final part of an abilityΓÇÖs resolution, the ability is removed from the stack and ceases to exist.
┬á
608.2p Once all possible steps described in 608.2cΓÇôn are completed, any abilities that trigger when that spell or ability resolves trigger.
┬á
608.3. If the object thatΓÇÖs resolving is a permanent spell, its resolution may involve several steps. The instructions in rules 608.3a and b are always performed first. Then one of the steps in rule 608.3cΓÇôe is performed, if appropriate.
┬á
608.3a If the object thatΓÇÖs resolving has no targets, it becomes a permanent and enters the battlefield under the control of the spellΓÇÖs controller.
┬á
608.3b If the object thatΓÇÖs resolving has a target, it checks whether the target is still legal, as described in 608.2b. If a spell with an illegal target is a bestowed Aura spell (see rule 702.103e) or a mutating creature spell (see rule 702.140b), it becomes a creature spell and will resolve as described in rule 608.3a. Otherwise, the spell doesnΓÇÖt resolve. It is removed from the stack and put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard.
┬á
608.3c If the object thatΓÇÖs resolving is an Aura spell, it becomes a permanent and is put onto the battlefield under the control of the spellΓÇÖs controller attached to the player or object it was targeting.
┬á
608.3d If the object thatΓÇÖs resolving is a mutating creature spell, the object representing that spell merges with the permanent it is targeting (see rule 730, ΓÇ£Merging with PermanentsΓÇ¥).
┬á
608.3e If a permanent spell resolves but its controller canΓÇÖt put it onto the battlefield, that player puts it into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard.
Example: Worms of the Earth has the ability ΓÇ£Lands canΓÇÖt enter the battlefield.ΓÇ¥ Clone says ΓÇ£You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield.ΓÇ¥ If a player casts Clone and chooses to copy Dryad Arbor (a land creature) while Worms of the Earth is on the battlefield, Clone canΓÇÖt enter the battlefield from the stack. ItΓÇÖs put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard.
┬á
608.3f If the object thatΓÇÖs resolving is a copy of a permanent spell, it will become a token permanent as it is put onto the battlefield in any of the steps above. A token put onto the battlefield this way is no longer a copy of a spell and is not ΓÇ£createdΓÇ¥ for the purposes of any rules or effects that refer to creating a token.
┬á
608.3g If the object thatΓÇÖs resolving has a static ability that functions on the stack and creates a delayed triggered ability, that delayed triggered ability is created as that permanent is put onto the battlefield in any of the steps above. (See rules 702.109, ΓÇ£Dash,ΓÇ¥ 702.152, ΓÇ£Blitz,ΓÇ¥ and 702.185, ΓÇ£Warp.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
609. Effects
┬á
609.1. An effect is something that happens in the game as a result of a spell or ability. When a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability resolves, it may create one or more one-shot or continuous effects. Static abilities may create one or more continuous effects. Text itself is never an effect.
┬á
609.2. Effects apply only to permanents unless the instructionΓÇÖs text states otherwise or they clearly can apply only to objects in one or more other zones.
Example: An effect that changes all lands into creatures wonΓÇÖt alter land cards in playersΓÇÖ graveyards. But an effect that says spells cost more to cast will apply only to spells on the stack, since a spell is always on the stack while a player is casting it.
┬á
609.3. If an effect attempts to do something impossible, it does only as much as possible.
Example: If a player is holding only one card, an effect that reads ΓÇ£Discard two cardsΓÇ¥ causes them to discard only that card. If an effect moves cards out of the library (as opposed to drawing), it moves as many as possible.
┬á
609.4. Some effects state that a player may do something ΓÇ£as thoughΓÇ¥ some condition were true or a creature can do something ΓÇ£as thoughΓÇ¥ some condition were true. This applies only to the stated effect. For purposes of that effect, treat the game exactly as if the stated condition were true. For all other purposes, treat the game normally.
┬á
609.4a If two effects state that a player may (or a creature can) do the same thing ΓÇ£as thoughΓÇ¥ different conditions were true, both conditions could apply. If one ΓÇ£as thoughΓÇ¥ effect satisfies the requirements for another ΓÇ£as thoughΓÇ¥ effect, then both effects will apply.
Example: A player controls Vedalken Orrery, an artifact that says ΓÇ£You may cast spells as though they had flash.ΓÇ¥ That player casts ShamanΓÇÖs Trance, an instant that says, in part, ΓÇ£You may play lands and cast spells from other playersΓÇÖ graveyards this turn as though those cards were in your graveyard.ΓÇ¥ The player may cast a sorcery with flashback from another playerΓÇÖs graveyard as though it were in that playerΓÇÖs graveyard and as though it had flash.
┬á
609.4b If an effect allows a player to spend mana ΓÇ£as though it were mana of any [type or color],ΓÇ¥ this affects only how the player may pay a cost. It doesnΓÇÖt change that cost, and it doesnΓÇÖt change what mana was actually spent to pay that cost. The same is true for effects that say ΓÇ£mana of any type can be spent.ΓÇ¥
┬á
609.5. If an effect could result in a tie, the text of the spell or ability that created the effect will specify what to do in the event of a tie. The Magic game has no default for ties.
┬á
609.6. Some continuous effects are replacement effects or prevention effects. See rules 614 and 615.
┬á
609.7. Some effects apply to damage from a sourceΓÇöfor example, ΓÇ£The next time a red source of your choice would deal damage to you this turn, prevent that damage.ΓÇ¥
┬á
609.7a If an effect requires a player to choose a source of damage, they may choose a permanent; a spell on the stack (including a permanent spell); any object referred to by an object on the stack, by a replacement or prevention effect thatΓÇÖs waiting to apply, or by a delayed triggered ability thatΓÇÖs waiting to trigger (even if that object is no longer in the zone it used to be in); or a face-up object in the command zone. A source doesnΓÇÖt need to be capable of dealing damage to be a legal choice. The source is chosen when the effect is created. If the player chooses a permanent, the effect will apply to the next damage dealt by that permanent, regardless of whether itΓÇÖs combat damage or damage dealt as the result of a spell or ability. If the player chooses a permanent spell, the effect will apply to any damage dealt by that spell and any damage dealt by the permanent that spell becomes when it resolves.
┬á
609.7b Some effects from resolved spells and abilities prevent or replace damage from sources with certain properties, such as a creature or a source of a particular color. When the source would deal damage, the ΓÇ£shieldΓÇ¥ rechecks the sourceΓÇÖs properties. If the properties no longer match, the damage isnΓÇÖt prevented or replaced. If for any reason the shield prevents no damage or replaces no damage, the shield isnΓÇÖt used up.
┬á
609.7c Some effects from static abilities prevent or replace damage from sources with certain properties. For these effects, the prevention or replacement applies to sources that are permanents with that property and to any sources that arenΓÇÖt on the battlefield that have that property.
┬á
610. One-Shot Effects
┬á
610.1. A one-shot effect does something just once and doesnΓÇÖt have a duration. Examples include dealing damage, destroying a permanent, creating a token, and moving an object from one zone to another.
┬á
610.2. Some one-shot effects create a delayed triggered ability, which instructs a player to do something later in the game (usually at a specific time) rather than as the spell or ability thatΓÇÖs creating the one-shot effect resolves. See rule 603.7.
┬á
610.3. Some one-shot effects cause an object to change zones ΓÇ£untilΓÇ¥ a specified event occurs. A second one-shot effect is created immediately after the specified event. This second one-shot effect returns the object to its previous zone.
┬á
610.3a If a resolving spell or activated ability creates the initial one-shot effect that causes the object to change zones, and the specified event has already occurred before that one-shot effect would occur but after that spell or ability was put onto the stack, the object doesnΓÇÖt move.
┬á
610.3b If a resolving triggered ability creates the initial one-shot effect that causes the object to change zones, and the specified event has already occurred before that one-shot effect would occur but after that ability triggered, the object doesnΓÇÖt move.
┬á
610.3c An object returned to the battlefield this way returns under its ownerΓÇÖs control unless otherwise specified.
┬á
610.3d If multiple one-shot effects are created this way immediately after one or more simultaneous events, those one-shot effects are also simultaneous.
Example: Two Banisher Priests have each exiled a card. All creatures are destroyed at the same time by Day of Judgment. The two exiled cards are returned to the battlefield at the same time.
┬á
610.4. Some one-shot effects cause a permanent to phase out ΓÇ£untilΓÇ¥ a specified event occurs. A second one-shot effect is created immediately after the specified event. This second one-shot effect causes the permanent to phase in.
┬á
610.4a A permanent phased out this way doesnΓÇÖt phase in as a result of the turn-based action during a playerΓÇÖs untap step (see rule 502.1). Other effects may cause it to phase in. If a permanent phased out this way phases in due to another effect, the second one-shot effect doesnΓÇÖt happen, even if that permanent has phased out again.
┬á
610.4b If a resolving spell or activated ability creates the initial one-shot effect that causes the permanent to phase out, and the specified event has already occurred before that one-shot effect would occur but after that spell or ability was put onto the stack, the permanent doesnΓÇÖt phase out.
┬á
610.4c If a resolving triggered ability creates the initial one-shot effect that causes the permanent to phase out, and the specified event has already occurred before that one-shot effect would occur but after that ability triggered, the permanent doesnΓÇÖt phase out.
┬á
610.4d If multiple one-shot effects are created this way immediately after one or more simultaneous events, those one-shot effects are also simultaneous.
┬á
610.5. Some static abilities create one-shot effects that cause spells a player casts to gain an ability as that player casts them. These effects begin to apply to appropriate spells at the time the player puts such a spell on the stack. See rule 601.2a.
┬á
611. Continuous Effects
┬á
611.1. A continuous effect modifies characteristics of objects, modifies control of objects, or affects players or the rules of the game, for a fixed or indefinite period.
┬á
611.2. A continuous effect may be generated by the resolution of a spell or ability.
┬á
611.2a A continuous effect generated by the resolution of a spell or ability lasts as long as stated by the spell or ability creating it (such as ΓÇ£until end of turnΓÇ¥). If no duration is stated, it lasts until the end of the game.
┬á
611.2b Some continuous effects generated by the resolution of a spell or ability have durations worded ΓÇ£for as long as . . . .ΓÇ¥ If the ΓÇ£for as long asΓÇ¥ duration never starts, the effect does nothing. Similarly, if that duration ends before the moment the effect would first be applied and doesnΓÇÖt begin again during that spell or abilityΓÇÖs resolution, the effect does nothing. It doesnΓÇÖt start and immediately stop again, and it doesnΓÇÖt last forever.
Example: Master Thief has the ability ΓÇ£When this creature enters, gain control of target artifact for as long as you control this creature.ΓÇ¥ If you lose control of Master Thief before the ability resolves, it does nothing, because its durationΓÇöas long as you control Master ThiefΓÇöwas over before the effect began.
┬á
611.2c If a continuous effect generated by the resolution of a spell or ability modifies the characteristics or changes the controller of any objects, the set of objects it affects is determined when that continuous effect begins. After that point, the set wonΓÇÖt change. (Note that this works differently than a continuous effect from a static ability.) A continuous effect generated by the resolution of a spell or ability that doesnΓÇÖt modify the characteristics or change the controller of any objects modifies the rules of the game, so it can affect objects that werenΓÇÖt affected when that continuous effect began. If a single continuous effect has parts that modify the characteristics or changes the controller of any objects and other parts that donΓÇÖt, the set of objects each part applies to is determined independently.
Example: An effect that reads ΓÇ£All white creatures get +1/+1 until end of turnΓÇ¥ gives the bonus to all permanents that are white creatures when the spell or ability resolvesΓÇöeven if they change color laterΓÇöand doesnΓÇÖt affect those that enter the battlefield or turn white afterward.
Example: An effect that reads ΓÇ£Prevent all damage creatures would deal this turnΓÇ¥ doesnΓÇÖt modify any objectΓÇÖs characteristics, so itΓÇÖs modifying the rules of the game. That means the effect will apply even to damage from creatures that werenΓÇÖt on the battlefield when the continuous effect began. It also affects damage from permanents that become creatures later in the turn.
┬á
611.2d If a resolving spell or ability that creates a continuous effect contains a variable such as X, the value of that variable is determined only once, on resolution. See rule 608.2h.
┬á
611.2e If a resolving spell or ability both puts a nontoken permanent onto the battlefield and creates a continuous effect stating that the permanent ΓÇ£is [characteristic],ΓÇ¥ that it ΓÇ£has [characteristic],ΓÇ¥ or that it doesnΓÇÖt have a particular characteristic, that continuous effect applies simultaneously with the permanent entering the battlefield. This characteristic is usually a color or a creature type. If the continuous effect says the permanent ΓÇ£becomes [characteristic]ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£gains [an ability],ΓÇ¥ that effect applies after the permanent is on the battlefield.
Example: Arbiter of the Ideal puts an artifact, creature, or land card onto the battlefield and says, in part, ΓÇ£That permanent is an enchantment in addition to its other types.ΓÇ¥ An ability that triggers whenever an enchantment enters the battlefield would trigger. The permanent doesnΓÇÖt enter the battlefield and then become an enchantment.
┬á
611.2f Some spells and abilities generate a continuous effect that modifies the characteristics of the next spell a player casts, the next spell that fulfills certain conditions a player casts during some duration, or similar. These effects do not begin immediately. Rather, they begin to apply at the time that player next puts an appropriate spell on the stack, and they apply to that spell. See rule 601.2a.
┬á
611.3. A continuous effect may be generated by the static ability of an object.
┬á
611.3a A continuous effect generated by a static ability isnΓÇÖt ΓÇ£locked inΓÇ¥; it applies at any given moment to whatever its text indicates.
┬á
611.3b The effect applies at all times that the permanent generating it is on the battlefield or the object generating it is in the appropriate zone.
Example: A permanent with the static ability ΓÇ£All white creatures get +1/+1ΓÇ¥ generates an effect that continuously gives +1/+1 to each white creature on the battlefield. If a creature becomes white, it gets this bonus; a creature that stops being white loses it.
┬á
611.3c Continuous effects that modify characteristics of permanents do so simultaneously with the permanent entering the battlefield. They donΓÇÖt wait until the permanent is on the battlefield and then change it. Because such effects apply as the permanent enters the battlefield, they are applied before determining whether the permanent will cause an ability to trigger when it enters the battlefield.
Example: A permanent with the static ability ΓÇ£All white creatures get +1/+1ΓÇ¥ is on the battlefield. A creature spell that would normally create a 1/1 white creature instead creates a 2/2 white creature. The creature doesnΓÇÖt enter the battlefield as 1/1 and then change to 2/2.
┬á
611.3d Continuous effects from static abilities may allow a player to play a land or cast a permanent spell, or may grant an ability to a permanent spell or card that allows it to be cast. If the effect also grants that object an ability that functions only on the battlefield, that ability lasts as long as stated by the effect granting that permission or ability. If no duration is stated, it lasts until the end of the game. This is an exception to rules 611.3aΓÇôb.
┬á
612. Text-Changing Effects
┬á
612.1. Some continuous effects change an objectΓÇÖs text. This can apply to any words or symbols printed on that object, but generally affects only that objectΓÇÖs rules text (which appears in its text box) and/or the text that appears in its type line. Such an effect is a text-changing effect.
┬á
612.2. A text-changing effect changes only those words that are used in the correct way (for example, a Magic color word being used as a color word, a land type word used as a land type, or a creature type word used as a creature type). An effect that changes a color word or a subtype canΓÇÖt change a card name, even if that name contains a word or a series of letters that is the same as a Magic color word, basic land type, or creature type.
┬á
612.2a Most spells and abilities that create creature tokens use creature types to define both the creature types and the names of the tokens. A text-changing effect that affects such a spell or an object with such an ability can change these words because theyΓÇÖre being used as creature types, even though theyΓÇÖre also being used as names.
┬á
612.3. Effects that add or remove abilities donΓÇÖt change the text of the objects they affect, so any abilities that are granted to an object canΓÇÖt be modified by text-changing effects that affect that object.
┬á
612.4. A tokenΓÇÖs subtypes and rules text are defined by the spell or ability that created the token. A text-changing effect that affects a token can change these characteristics.
┬á
612.5. One card (Exchange of Words) instructs a player to exchange the text boxes of two objects. This replaces all of the rules text of each object with the rules text of the other object. (In games involving certain cards that arenΓÇÖt covered by these rules, other elements of the text box may also be exchanged. See rule 100.7.)
┬á
612.6. One card (VolrathΓÇÖs Shapeshifter) states that an object has the ΓÇ£full textΓÇ¥ of another object. This changes not just the text that appears in the objectΓÇÖs text box and type line, but also changes the text that represents its name, mana cost, color indicator, power, and toughness.
┬á
612.7. One card (Spy Kit) states that an object has ΓÇ£all names of nonlegendary creature cards.ΓÇ¥ This changes the text that represents the objectΓÇÖs name. That object has the name of each nonlegendary creature card in the Oracle card reference. (See rule 108.1.)
┬á
612.8. Some cards create a continuous effect that sets the name of an object. This changes the text that represents the objectΓÇÖs name. That object loses any names it had and has only the specified name.
┬á
612.9. A name sticker on a permanent or on a card not on the battlefield creates a continuous effect that adds a word to the text that represents the objectΓÇÖs name. (See rule 123.6.)
┬á
612.10. A splice ability changes a spellΓÇÖs text by adding the rules text of the card with splice to the spell, following that spellΓÇÖs own rules text. It doesnΓÇÖt modify or replace any of that spellΓÇÖs own text. (See rule 702.47, ΓÇ£Splice.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
613. Interaction of Continuous Effects
┬á
613.1. The values of an objectΓÇÖs characteristics are determined by starting with the actual object. For a card, that means the values of the characteristics printed on that card. For a token or a copy of a spell or card, that means the values of the characteristics defined by the effect that created it. Then all applicable continuous effects are applied in a series of layers in the following order:
┬á
613.1a Layer 1: Rules and effects that modify copiable values are applied.
┬á
613.1b Layer 2: Control-changing effects are applied.
┬á
613.1c Layer 3: Text-changing effects are applied. See rule 612, ΓÇ£Text-Changing Effects.ΓÇ¥
┬á
613.1d Layer 4: Type-changing effects are applied. These include effects that change an objectΓÇÖs card type, subtype, and/or supertype.
┬á
613.1e Layer 5: Color-changing effects are applied.
┬á
613.1f Layer 6: Ability-adding effects, keyword counters, ability-removing effects, and effects that say an object canΓÇÖt have an ability are applied.
┬á
613.1g Layer 7: Power- and/or toughness-changing effects are applied.
┬á
613.2. Within layer 1, apply effects in a series of sublayers in the order described below. Within each sublayer, apply effects in timestamp order (see rule 613.7). Note that dependency may alter the order in which effects are applied within a sublayer. (See rule 613.8.)
┬á
613.2a Layer 1a: Copiable effects are applied. This includes copy effects (see rule 707, ΓÇ£Copying ObjectsΓÇ¥) and changes to an objectΓÇÖs characteristics determined by merging an object with a permanent (see rule 730, ΓÇ£Merging with PermanentsΓÇ¥). ΓÇ£As . . . entersΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£as . . . is turned face upΓÇ¥ abilities generate copiable effects if they set power and toughness, even if they also define other characteristics.
┬á
613.2b Layer 1b: Face-down spells and permanents have their characteristics modified as defined in rule 708.2.
┬á
613.2c After all rules and effects in layer 1 have been applied, the objectΓÇÖs characteristics are its copiable values. (See rule 707.2.)
┬á
613.3. Within layers 2ΓÇô6, apply effects from characteristic-defining abilities first (see rule 604.3), then all other effects in timestamp order (see rule 613.7). Note that dependency may alter the order in which effects are applied within a layer. (See rule 613.8.)
┬á
613.4. Within layer 7, apply effects in a series of sublayers in the order described below. Within each sublayer, apply effects in timestamp order. (See rule 613.7.) Note that dependency may alter the order in which effects are applied within a sublayer. (See rule 613.8.)
┬á
613.4a Layer 7a: Effects from characteristic-defining abilities that define power and/or toughness are applied. See rule 604.3.
┬á
613.4b Layer 7b: Effects that set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value are applied. Effects that refer to the base power and/or toughness of a creature apply in this layer.
┬á
613.4c Layer 7c: Effects and counters that modify power and/or toughness (but donΓÇÖt set power and/or toughness to a specific number or value) are applied.
┬á
613.4d Layer 7d: Effects that switch a creatureΓÇÖs power and toughness are applied. Such effects take the value of power and apply it to the creatureΓÇÖs toughness, and take the value of toughness and apply it to the creatureΓÇÖs power.
Example: A 1/3 creature is given +0/+1 by an effect. Then another effect switches the creatureΓÇÖs power and toughness. Its new power and toughness is 4/1. A new effect gives the creature +5/+0. Its ΓÇ£unswitchedΓÇ¥ power and toughness would be 6/4, so its actual power and toughness is 4/6.
Example: A 1/3 creature is given +0/+1 by an effect. Then another effect switches the creatureΓÇÖs power and toughness. Its new power and toughness is 4/1. If the +0/+1 effect ends before the switch effect ends, the creature becomes 3/1.
Example: A 1/3 creature is given +0/+1 by an effect. Then another effect switches the creatureΓÇÖs power and toughness. Then another effect switches its power and toughness again. The two switches essentially cancel each other, and the creature becomes 1/4.
┬á
613.5. The application of continuous effects as described by the layer system is continually and automatically performed by the game. All resulting changes to an objectΓÇÖs characteristics are instantaneous.
Example: Honor of the Pure is an enchantment that reads ΓÇ£White creatures you control get +1/+1.ΓÇ¥ Honor of the Pure and a 2/2 black creature are on the battlefield under your control. If an effect then turns the creature white (layer 5), it gets +1/+1 from Honor of the Pure (layer 7c), becoming 3/3. If the creatureΓÇÖs color is later changed to red (layer 5), Honor of the PureΓÇÖs effect stops applying to it, and it will return to being 2/2.
Example: Gray Ogre, a 2/2 creature, is on the battlefield. An effect puts a +1/+1 counter on it (layer 7c), making it 3/3. A spell targeting it that says ΓÇ£Target creature gets +4/+4 until end of turnΓÇ¥ resolves (layer 7c), making it 7/7. An enchantment that says ΓÇ£Creatures you control get +0/+2ΓÇ¥ enters the battlefield (layer 7c), making it 7/9. An effect that says ΓÇ£Target creature becomes 0/1 until end of turnΓÇ¥ is applied to it (layer 7b), making it 5/8 (0/1, with +4/+4 from the resolved spell, +0/+2 from the enchantment, and +1/+1 from the counter).
┬á
613.6. If an effect should be applied in different layers and/or sublayers, the parts of the effect each apply in their appropriate ones. If an effect starts to apply in one layer and/or sublayer, it will continue to be applied to the same set of objects in each other applicable layer and/or sublayer, even if the ability generating the effect is removed during this process.
Example: An effect that reads ΓÇ£This creature gets +1/+1 and becomes the color of your choice until end of turnΓÇ¥ is both a power- and toughness-changing effect and a color-changing effect. The ΓÇ£becomes the color of your choiceΓÇ¥ part is applied in layer 5, and then the ΓÇ£gets +1/+1ΓÇ¥ part is applied in layer 7c.
Example: Act of Treason has an effect that reads ΓÇ£Gain control of target creature until end of turn. Untap that creature. It gains haste until end of turn.ΓÇ¥ This is both a control-changing effect and an effect that adds an ability to an object. The ΓÇ£gain controlΓÇ¥ part is applied in layer 2, and then the ΓÇ£it gains hasteΓÇ¥ part is applied in layer 6.
Example: An effect that reads ΓÇ£All noncreature artifacts become 2/2 artifact creatures until end of turnΓÇ¥ is both a type-changing effect and a power- and toughness-setting effect. The type-changing effect is applied to all noncreature artifacts in layer 4 and the power- and toughness-setting effect is applied to those same permanents in layer 7b, even though those permanents arenΓÇÖt noncreature artifacts by then.
Example: Svogthos, the Restless Tomb, is on the battlefield. An effect that says ΓÇ£Until end of turn, target land becomes a 3/3 creature thatΓÇÖs still a landΓÇ¥ is applied to it (layers 4 and 7b). An effect that says ΓÇ£Target creature gets +1/+1 until end of turnΓÇ¥ is applied to it (layer 7c), making it a 4/4 land creature. Then while you have ten creature cards in your graveyard, you activate SvogthosΓÇÖs ability: ΓÇ£Until end of turn, this land becomes a black and green Plant Zombie creature with ΓÇÿThis creatureΓÇÖs power and toughness are each equal to the number of creature cards in your graveyard.ΓÇÖ ItΓÇÖs still a land.ΓÇ¥ (layers 4, 5, and 7b). It becomes an 11/11 land creature. If a creature card enters or leaves your graveyard, SvogthosΓÇÖs power and toughness will be modified accordingly. If the first effect is applied to it again, it will become a 4/4 land creature again.
┬á
613.7. Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is usually done using a timestamp system. An effect with an earlier timestamp is applied before an effect with a later timestamp.
┬á
613.7a A continuous effect generated by a static ability has the same timestamp as the object the static ability is on, or the timestamp of the effect that created the ability, whichever is later. If the effect that created the ability has the later timestamp and the object the ability is on receives a new timestamp, each continuous effect generated by static abilities of that object receives a new timestamp as well, but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same.
Example: Rune of Flight is an Aura that grants enchanted Equipment ΓÇ£Equipped creature has flying.ΓÇ¥ A player attaches Rune of Flight to Colossus Hammer, an Equipment with ΓÇ£Equipped creature gets +10/+10 and loses flying.ΓÇ¥ The ability granted by Rune of Flight shares Rune of FlightΓÇÖs timestamp because it is later than Colossus HammerΓÇÖs timestamp. If Colossus Hammer becomes attached to a creature, both of its abilities receive new timestamps (see rule 613.7e), but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same.
┬á
613.7b A continuous effect generated by the resolution of a spell or ability receives a timestamp at the time itΓÇÖs created.
┬á
613.7c Each counter receives a timestamp as itΓÇÖs put on an object or player. If that object or player already has a counter of that kind on it, each counter of that kind receives a new timestamp identical to that of the new counter.
┬á
613.7d An object receives a timestamp at the time it enters a zone.
┬á
613.7e An Aura, Equipment, or Fortification receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object or player.
┬á
613.7f A permanent receives a new timestamp each time it turns face up or face down.
┬á
613.7g A double-faced permanent receives a new timestamp each time it transforms or converts.
┬á
613.7h A face-up plane card, phenomenon card, or scheme card receives a timestamp at the time itΓÇÖs turned face up.
┬á
613.7i A face-up vanguard card receives a timestamp at the beginning of the game.
┬á
613.7j A conspiracy card receives a timestamp at the beginning of the game. If itΓÇÖs face down, it receives a new timestamp at the time it turns face up.
┬á
613.7k A sticker receives a new timestamp each time itΓÇÖs put on an object. If the object a sticker is on receives a new timestamp, the sticker receives a new timestamp immediately after that one. If the object a sticker is on becomes part of a merged permanent on the battlefield, the sticker receives a new timestamp at that time. If an object has more than one sticker on it as it enters a zone or becomes part of a merged permanent, the relative timestamp order of those stickers remains unchanged.
┬á
613.7m If two or more objects would receive a timestamp simultaneously, such as by entering a zone simultaneously or becoming attached simultaneously, their relative timestamps are determined in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). Objects controlled by the active player (or owned by the active player, if they have no controller) have an earlier relative timestamp in the order of that playerΓÇÖs choice, followed by each other player in turn order.
┬á
613.7n If a continuous effect generated by a static ability of an object and a continuous effect generated by a resolving spell or ability that applies to that object would receive a timestamp simultaneously, such as due to an effect that puts that object onto the battlefield and sets its characteristics (see rule 611.2e), the continuous effect from the objectΓÇÖs own static ability receives an earlier relative timestamp.
┬á
613.8. Within a layer or sublayer, determining which order effects are applied in is sometimes done using a dependency system. If a dependency exists, it will override the timestamp system.
┬á
613.8a An effect is said to ΓÇ£depend onΓÇ¥ another if (a) itΓÇÖs applied in the same layer (and, if applicable, sublayer) as the other effect; (b) applying the other would change the text or the existence of the first effect, what it applies to, or what it does to any of the things it applies to; and (c) neither effect is from a characteristic-defining ability or both effects are from characteristic-defining abilities. Otherwise, the effect is considered to be independent of the other effect.
┬á
613.8b An effect dependent on one or more other effects waits to apply until just after all of those effects have been applied. If multiple dependent effects would apply simultaneously in this way, theyΓÇÖre applied in timestamp order relative to each other. If several dependent effects form a dependency loop, then this rule is ignored and the effects in the dependency loop are applied in timestamp order.
┬á
613.8c After each effect is applied, the order of remaining effects is reevaluated and may change if an effect that has not yet been applied becomes dependent on or independent of one or more other effects that have not yet been applied.
┬á
613.9. One continuous effect can override another. Sometimes the results of one effect determine whether another effect applies or what another effect does.
Example: Two effects are affecting the same creature: one from an Aura that says ΓÇ£Enchanted creature has flyingΓÇ¥ and one from an Aura that says ΓÇ£Enchanted creature loses flying.ΓÇ¥ Neither of these depends on the other, since nothing changes what they affect or what theyΓÇÖre doing to it. Applying them in timestamp order means the one that was generated last ΓÇ£wins.ΓÇ¥ The same process would be followed, and the same result reached, if either of the effects had a duration (such as ΓÇ£Target creature loses flying until end of turnΓÇ¥) or came from a non-Aura source (such as ΓÇ£All creatures lose flyingΓÇ¥).
Example: One effect reads, ΓÇ£White creatures get +1/+1,ΓÇ¥ and another reads, ΓÇ£Enchanted creature is white.ΓÇ¥ The enchanted creature gets +1/+1 from the first effect, regardless of its previous color.
┬á
613.10. Some continuous effects affect players rather than objects. For example, an effect might give a player protection from red. All such effects are applied in timestamp order after the determination of objectsΓÇÖ characteristics. See also the rules for timestamp order and dependency (rules 613.7 and 613.8).
┬á
613.11. Some continuous effects affect game rules rather than objects. For example, effects may modify a playerΓÇÖs maximum hand size, or say that a creature must attack this turn if able. These effects are applied after all other continuous effects have been applied. Continuous effects that affect the costs of spells or abilities are applied according to the order specified in rule 601.2f. All other such effects are applied in timestamp order. See also the rules for timestamp order and dependency (rules 613.7 and 613.8).
┬á
614. Replacement Effects
┬á
614.1. Some continuous effects are replacement effects. Like prevention effects (see rule 615), replacement effects apply continuously as events happenΓÇöthey arenΓÇÖt locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like ΓÇ£shieldsΓÇ¥ around whatever theyΓÇÖre affecting.
┬á
614.1a Effects that use the word ΓÇ£insteadΓÇ¥ are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word ΓÇ£insteadΓÇ¥ to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.
┬á
614.1b Effects that use the word ΓÇ£skipΓÇ¥ are replacement effects. These replacement effects use the word ΓÇ£skipΓÇ¥ to indicate what events, steps, phases, or turns will be replaced with nothing.
┬á
614.1c Effects that read ΓÇ£[This permanent] enters with . . . ,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£As [this permanent] enters . . . ,ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£[This permanent] enters as . . . ΓÇ£ are replacement effects.
┬á
614.1d Continuous effects that read ΓÇ£[This permanent] enters . . .ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£[Objects] enter [the battlefield] . . .ΓÇ¥ are replacement effects.
┬á
614.1e Effects that read ΓÇ£As [this permanent] is turned face up . . . ,ΓÇ¥ are replacement effects.
┬á
614.2. Some replacement effects apply to damage from a source. See rule 609.7.
┬á
614.3. There are no special restrictions on casting a spell or activating an ability that generates a replacement effect. Such effects last until theyΓÇÖre used up or their duration has expired.
┬á
614.4. Replacement effects must exist before the appropriate event occursΓÇöthey canΓÇÖt ΓÇ£go back in timeΓÇ¥ and change something thatΓÇÖs already happened. Spells or abilities that generate these effects are often cast or activated in response to whatever would produce the event and thus resolve before that event would occur.
Example: A player can activate an ability to regenerate a creature in response to a spell that would destroy it. Once the spell resolves, though, itΓÇÖs too late to regenerate the creature.
┬á
614.5. A replacement effect doesnΓÇÖt invoke itself repeatedly; it gets only one opportunity to affect an event or any modified events that may replace that event.
Example: A player controls two permanents, each with an ability that reads ΓÇ£If a creature you control would deal damage to a permanent or player, it deals double that damage to that permanent or player instead.ΓÇ¥ A creature that normally deals 2 damage will deal 8 damageΓÇönot just 4, and not an infinite amount.
┬á
614.6. If an event is replaced, it never happens. A modified event occurs instead, which may in turn trigger abilities. Note that the modified event may contain instructions that canΓÇÖt be carried out, in which case the impossible instruction is simply ignored.
┬á
614.7. If a replacement effect would replace an event, but that event never happens, the replacement effect simply doesnΓÇÖt do anything.
┬á
614.7a If a source would deal 0 damage, it does not deal damage at all. Replacement effects that would increase the damage dealt by that source, or would have that source deal that damage to a different object or player, have no event to replace, so they have no effect.
┬á
614.8. Regeneration is a destruction-replacement effect. The word ΓÇ£insteadΓÇ¥ doesnΓÇÖt appear on the card but is implicit in the definition of regeneration. ΓÇ£Regenerate [permanent]ΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£The next time [permanent] would be destroyed this turn, instead remove all damage marked on it and its controller taps it. If itΓÇÖs an attacking or blocking creature, remove it from combat.ΓÇ¥ Abilities that trigger from damage being dealt still trigger even if the permanent regenerates. See rule 701.19.
┬á
614.9. Some effects replace damage dealt to one battle, creature, planeswalker, or player with the same damage dealt to another battle, creature, planeswalker, or player; such effects are called redirection effects. If one of those permanents is no longer on the battlefield when the damage would be redirected, or is no longer a battle, creature, or planeswalker when the damage would be redirected, the effect does nothing. If damage would be redirected to or from a player who has left the game, the effect does nothing.
┬á
614.10. An effect that causes a player to skip an event, step, phase, or turn is a replacement effect. ΓÇ£Skip [something]ΓÇ¥ is the same as ΓÇ£Instead of doing [something], do nothing.ΓÇ¥ Once a step, phase, or turn has started, it can no longer be skippedΓÇöany skip effects will wait until the next occurrence.
┬á
614.10a Anything scheduled for a skipped step, phase, or turn wonΓÇÖt happen. Anything scheduled for the ΓÇ£nextΓÇ¥ occurrence of something waits for the first occurrence that isnΓÇÖt skipped. If two effects each cause a player to skip their next occurrence, that player must skip the next two; one effect will be satisfied in skipping the first occurrence, while the other will remain until another occurrence can be skipped.
┬á
614.10b Some effects cause a player to skip a step, phase, or turn, then take another action. That action is considered to be the first thing that happens during the next step, phase, or turn to actually occur.
┬á
614.11. Some effects replace card draws. These effects are applied even if no cards could be drawn because there are no cards in the affected playerΓÇÖs library.
┬á
614.11a If an effect replaces a draw within a sequence of card draws, all actions required by the replacement are completed, if possible, before resuming the sequence.
┬á
614.11b If an effect would have a player both draw a card and perform an additional action on that card, and the draw is replaced, the additional action is not performed on any cards that are drawn as a result of that replacement effect.
┬á
614.12. Some replacement effects modify how a permanent enters the battlefield. (See rules 614.1cΓÇôd.) Such effects may come from the permanent itself if they affect only that permanent (as opposed to a general subset of permanents that includes it). They may also come from other sources. To determine which replacement effects apply and how they apply, check the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account replacement effects that have already modified how it enters the battlefield (see rule 616.1), continuous effects from the permanentΓÇÖs own static abilities that would apply to it once itΓÇÖs on the battlefield, and continuous effects that already exist and would apply to the permanent.
Example: Voice of All says ΓÇ£As this creature enters, choose a colorΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£This creature has protection from the chosen color.ΓÇ¥ An effect creates a token thatΓÇÖs a copy of Voice of All. As that token is created, the tokenΓÇÖs controller chooses a color for it.
Example: Yixlid Jailer says ΓÇ£Cards in graveyards lose all abilities.ΓÇ¥ Scarwood Treefolk says ΓÇ£This creature enters tapped.ΓÇ¥ A Scarwood Treefolk thatΓÇÖs put onto the battlefield from a graveyard enters the battlefield tapped.
Example: Orb of Dreams is an artifact that says ΓÇ£Permanents enter tapped.ΓÇ¥ It wonΓÇÖt affect itself, so Orb of Dreams enters the battlefield untapped.
┬á
614.12a If a replacement effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield requires a choice, that choice is made before the permanent enters the battlefield.
┬á
614.12b If multiple replacement effects that require choices from a player would modify how multiple permanents enter the battlefield simultaneously, that player may not make choices for those effects that would cause the combined costs of those effects to not be payable.
┬á
614.12c Some replacement effects cause a permanent to enter the battlefield with its controllerΓÇÖs choice of one of two abilities, each marked with an anchor word and preceded by a bullet point. ΓÇ£[Anchor word] ΓÇö [ability]ΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£As long as [anchor word] was chosen as this permanent entered the battlefield, this permanent has [ability].ΓÇ¥ The abilities preceded by anchor words are each linked to the ability that causes a player to choose between them. See rule 607, ΓÇ£Linked Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
614.13. An effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield may cause other objects to change zones.
┬á
614.13a While applying an effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield, you may have to choose a number of objects that will also change zones. You canΓÇÖt choose the object that will become that permanent or any other object entering the battlefield at the same time as that object.
Example: Sutured Ghoul says, in part, ΓÇ£As this creature enters, exile any number of creature cards from your graveyard.ΓÇ¥ If Sutured Ghoul and Runeclaw Bear enter the battlefield from your graveyard at the same time, you canΓÇÖt choose to exile either of them when applying Sutured GhoulΓÇÖs replacement effect.
┬á
614.13b The same object canΓÇÖt be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how one or more permanents enter the battlefield.
Example: Jund (a plane card) says, ΓÇ£Whenever a player casts a black, red, or green creature spell, it gains devour 5.ΓÇ¥ A player controls Runeclaw Bear and casts Thunder-Thrash Elder, a red creature spell with devour 3. As Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield, its controller can choose to sacrifice Runeclaw Bear when applying the devour 3 effect or when applying the devour 5 effect, but not both. Thunder-Thrash Elder will enter the battlefield with zero, three, or five +1/+1 counters, depending on this choice.
┬á
614.13c While applying a replacement effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield, another replacement effect may cause a player to mill cards or exile cards from the top of a library. In that case, any card that is entering the battlefield from that library wonΓÇÖt be included in that effect, even though those cards are in the library as the effect is applied.
Example: Ashiok, Wicked Manipulator has an ability that reads ΓÇ£If you would pay life while your library has at least that many cards in it, exile that many cards from the top of your library instead.ΓÇ¥ Breeding Pool is a land that reads, in part, ΓÇ£As this land enters, you may pay 2 life.ΓÇ¥ If an effect allows a player to play Breeding Pool from the top of their library while they control Ashiok, and they choose to pay life as Breeding Pool enters, AshiokΓÇÖs replacement effect will ignore Breeding Pool, because it is entering the battlefield, and the next two cards will be exiled.
┬á
614.14. An object may have one ability printed on it that generates a replacement effect which causes one or more cards to be exiled, and another ability that refers either to ΓÇ£the exiled cardsΓÇ¥ or to cards ΓÇ£exiled with [this object].ΓÇ¥ These abilities are linked: the second refers only to cards in the exile zone that were put there as a direct result of the replacement event caused by the first. If another object gains a pair of linked abilities, the abilities will be similarly linked on that object. They canΓÇÖt be linked to any other ability, regardless of what other abilities the object may currently have or may have had in the past. See rule 607, ΓÇ£Linked Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
614.15. Some replacement effects are not continuous effects. Rather, they are an effect of a resolving spell or ability that replace part or all of that spell or abilityΓÇÖs own effect(s). Such effects are called self-replacement effects. The text creating a self-replacement effect is usually part of the ability whose effect is being replaced, but the text can be a separate ability, particularly when preceded by an ability word. When applying replacement effects to an event, self-replacement effects are applied before other replacement effects.
┬á
614.16. Some replacement effects apply ΓÇ£if an effect would create one or more tokensΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£if an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent.ΓÇ¥ These replacement effects apply if the effect of a resolving spell or ability creates a token or puts a counter on a permanent, and they also apply if another replacement or prevention effect does so, even if the original event being modified wasnΓÇÖt itself an effect. 
┬á
614.17. Some effects state that something canΓÇÖt happen. These effects arenΓÇÖt replacement effects, but follow similar rules.
┬á
614.17a ΓÇ£CanΓÇÖtΓÇ¥ effects must exist before the appropriate event occursΓÇöthey canΓÇÖt ΓÇ£go back in timeΓÇ¥ and change something thatΓÇÖs already happened.
┬á
614.17b If an event canΓÇÖt happen, a player canΓÇÖt choose to pay a cost that includes that event.
┬á
614.17c If an event canΓÇÖt happen, it can only be replaced by a self-replacement effect (see rule 614.15). Other replacement and/or prevention effects canΓÇÖt modify or replace it.
┬á
614.17d Some ΓÇ£canΓÇÖtΓÇ¥ effects modify how a permanent enters the battlefield or whether it can enter the battlefield. Such effects may come from the permanent itself if they affect only that permanent (as opposed to a general subset of permanents that includes it). They may also come from other sources. To determine which ΓÇ£canΓÇÖtΓÇ¥ effects apply, check the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account replacement effects that have already modified how it enters the battlefield (see rule 616.1), continuous effects from the permanentΓÇÖs own static abilities that would apply to it once itΓÇÖs on the battlefield, and continuous effects that already exist and would apply to the permanent.
┬á
615. Prevention Effects
┬á
615.1. Some continuous effects are prevention effects. Like replacement effects (see rule 614), prevention effects apply continuously as events happenΓÇöthey arenΓÇÖt locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a damage event that would happen and completely or partially prevent the damage that would be dealt. They act like ΓÇ£shieldsΓÇ¥ around whatever theyΓÇÖre affecting.
┬á
615.1a Effects that use the word ΓÇ£preventΓÇ¥ are prevention effects. Prevention effects use ΓÇ£preventΓÇ¥ to indicate what damage will not be dealt.
┬á
615.2. Many prevention effects apply to damage from a source. See rule 609.7.
┬á
615.3. There are no special restrictions on casting a spell or activating an ability that generates a prevention effect. Such effects last until theyΓÇÖre used up or their duration has expired.
┬á
615.4. Prevention effects must exist before the appropriate damage event occursΓÇöthey canΓÇÖt ΓÇ£go back in timeΓÇ¥ and change something thatΓÇÖs already happened. Spells or abilities that generate these effects are often cast or activated in response to whatever would produce the event and thus resolve before that event would occur.
Example: A player can activate an ability that prevents damage in response to a spell that would deal damage. Once the spell resolves, though, itΓÇÖs too late to prevent the damage.
┬á
615.5. Some prevention effects also include an additional effect, which may refer to the amount of damage that was prevented. The prevention takes place at the time the original event would have happened; the rest of the effect takes place immediately afterward.
┬á
615.6. If damage that would be dealt is prevented, it never happens. A modified event may occur instead, which may in turn trigger abilities. Note that the modified event may contain instructions that canΓÇÖt be carried out, in which case the impossible instruction is simply ignored.
┬á
615.7. Some prevention effects generated by the resolution of a spell or ability refer to a specific amount of damageΓÇöfor example, ΓÇ£Prevent the next 3 damage that would be dealt to any target this turn.ΓÇ¥ These work like shields. Each 1 damage that would be dealt to the ΓÇ£shieldedΓÇ¥ permanent or player is prevented. Preventing 1 damage reduces the remaining shield by 1. If damage would be dealt to the shielded permanent or player by two or more applicable sources at the same time, the player or the controller of the permanent chooses which damage the shield prevents. Once the shield has been reduced to 0, any remaining damage is dealt normally. Such effects count only the amount of damage; the number of events or sources dealing it doesnΓÇÖt matter.
┬á
615.8. Some prevention effects generated by the resolution of a spell or ability refer to the next time a specific source would deal damage. These effects prevent the next instance of damage from that source, regardless of how much damage that is. Once an instance of damage from that source has been prevented, any subsequent instances of damage that would be dealt by that source are dealt normally.
┬á
615.9. Some effects generated by the resolution of a spell or ability prevent damage from a source of a playerΓÇÖs choice with certain properties. When the source would deal damage, the shield rechecks the sourceΓÇÖs properties. If the properties no longer match, the damage isnΓÇÖt prevented or replaced and the shield isnΓÇÖt used up. See rule 609.7b.
┬á
615.10. Some prevention effects generated by static abilities refer to a specific amount of damageΓÇöfor example, ΓÇ£If a source would deal damage to you, prevent 1 of that damage.ΓÇ¥ Such an effect prevents only the indicated amount of damage in any applicable damage event at any given time. It will apply separately to damage from other applicable events that would happen at the same time, or at a different time.
Example: Daunting Defender says ΓÇ£If a source would deal damage to a Cleric creature you control, prevent 1 of that damage.ΓÇ¥ Pyroclasm says ΓÇ£Pyroclasm deals 2 damage to each creature.ΓÇ¥ Pyroclasm will deal 1 damage to each Cleric creature controlled by Daunting DefenderΓÇÖs controller. It will deal 2 damage to each other creature.
┬á
615.11. Some prevention effects prevent the next N damage that would be dealt to each of a number of untargeted creatures. Such an effect creates a prevention shield for each applicable creature when the spell or ability that generates that effect resolves.
Example: Wojek Apothecary has an ability that says ΓÇ£{T}: Prevent the next 1 damage that would be dealt to target creature and each other creature that shares a color with it this turn.ΓÇ¥ When the ability resolves, it gives the target creature and each other creature on the battlefield that shares a color with it at that time a shield preventing the next 1 damage that would be dealt to it. Changing creaturesΓÇÖ colors after the ability resolves doesnΓÇÖt add or remove shields, and creatures that enter the battlefield later in the turn donΓÇÖt get the shield.
┬á
615.12. Some effects state that damage ΓÇ£canΓÇÖt be prevented.ΓÇ¥ If unpreventable damage would be dealt, any applicable prevention effects are still applied to it. Those effects wonΓÇÖt prevent any damage, but any additional effects they have will take place. Existing damage prevention shields wonΓÇÖt be reduced by damage that canΓÇÖt be prevented.
┬á
615.12a A prevention effect is applied to any particular unpreventable damage event just once. It wonΓÇÖt invoke itself repeatedly trying to prevent that damage.
┬á
615.13. Some triggered abilities trigger when damage that would be dealt is prevented. Such an ability triggers each time a prevention effect is applied to one or more simultaneous damage events and prevents some or all of that damage.
┬á
616. Interaction of Replacement and/or Prevention Effects
┬á
616.1. If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected objectΓÇÖs controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below. If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4).
┬á
616.1a If any of the replacement and/or prevention effects are self-replacement effects (see rule 614.15), one of them must be chosen. If not, proceed to rule 616.1b.
┬á
616.1b If any of the replacement and/or prevention effects would modify under whose control an object would enter the battlefield, one of them must be chosen. If not, proceed to rule 616.1c.
┬á
616.1c If any of the replacement and/or prevention effects would cause an object to become a copy of another object as it enters the battlefield, one of them must be chosen. If not, proceed to rule 616.1d.
┬á
616.1d If any of the replacement and/or prevention effects would cause a card to enter the battlefield with its back face up, one of them must be chosen (See rule 701.27, ΓÇ£Transform,ΓÇ¥ and rule 701.28, ΓÇ£Convert.ΓÇ¥). If not, proceed to 616.1e.
┬á
616.1e Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen.
┬á
616.1f Once the chosen effect has been applied, this process is repeated (taking into account only replacement or prevention effects that would now be applicable) until there are no more left to apply.
Example: Two permanents are on the battlefield. One is an enchantment that reads ΓÇ£If a card would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, instead exile it,ΓÇ¥ and the other is a creature that reads ΓÇ£If this creature would die, instead shuffle it into its ownerΓÇÖs library.ΓÇ¥ If the creature is destroyed, its controller decides which replacement to apply first; the other does nothing.
