Example: Essence of the Wild reads ΓÇ£Creatures you control enter as a copy of this creature.ΓÇ¥ A player who controls Essence of the Wild casts Rusted Sentinel, which normally enters the battlefield tapped. As it enters the battlefield, the copy effect from Essence of the Wild is applied first. As a result, it no longer has the ability that causes it to enter the battlefield tapped. Rusted Sentinel will enter the battlefield as an untapped copy of Essence of the Wild.
┬á
616.1g While following the steps in 616.1aΓÇôf, one replacement or prevention effect may apply to an event, and another may apply to an event contained within the first event. In this case, the second effect canΓÇÖt be chosen until after the first effect has been chosen.
Example: A player is instructed to create a token thatΓÇÖs a copy of Voice of All, which has the ability ΓÇ£As this creature enters, choose a color.ΓÇ¥ Doubling Season has an ability that reads ΓÇ£If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, it creates twice that many of those tokens instead.ΓÇ¥ Because entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating a token, the effect of Doubling Season must be applied first, and then the effects of the two Voice of All tokens may be applied in either order.
┬á
616.2. A replacement or prevention effect can become applicable to an event as the result of another replacement or prevention effect that modifies the event.
Example: One effect reads ΓÇ£If you would gain life, draw that many cards instead,ΓÇ¥ and another reads ΓÇ£If you would draw a card, return a card from your graveyard to your hand instead.ΓÇ¥ Both effects combine (regardless of the order they came into existence): Instead of gaining 1 life, the player puts a card from their graveyard into their hand.
┬á

7. Additional Rules
┬á
700. General
┬á
700.1. Anything that happens in a game is an event. Multiple events may take place during the resolution of a spell or ability. The text of triggered abilities and replacement effects defines the event theyΓÇÖre looking for. One ΓÇ£happeningΓÇ¥ may be treated as a single event by one ability and as multiple events by another.
Example: If an attacking creature is blocked by two creatures, this is one event for a triggered ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever this creature becomes blockedΓÇ¥ but two events for a triggered ability that reads ΓÇ£Whenever this creature becomes blocked by a creature.ΓÇ¥
┬á
700.2. A spell or ability is modal if it has two or more options in a bulleted list preceded by instructions for a player to choose a number of those options, such as ΓÇ£Choose one ΓÇö.ΓÇ¥ Each of those options is a mode. Modal cards printed prior to the Khans of TarkirΓäó set didnΓÇÖt use bulleted lists for the modes; these cards have received errata in the Oracle card reference so the modes do appear in a bulleted list.
┬á
700.2a The controller of a modal spell or activated ability chooses the mode(s) as part of casting that spell or activating that ability. If one of the modes would be illegal (due to an inability to choose legal targets, for example), that mode canΓÇÖt be chosen. (See rule 601.2b.)
┬á
700.2b The controller of a modal triggered ability chooses the mode(s) as part of putting that ability on the stack. If one of the modes would be illegal (due to an inability to choose legal targets, for example), that mode canΓÇÖt be chosen. If no mode is chosen, the ability is removed from the stack. (See rule 603.3c.)
┬á
700.2c If a spell or ability targets one or more targets only if a particular mode is chosen for it, its controller will need to choose those targets only if they chose that mode. Otherwise, the spell or ability is treated as though it did not have those targets. (See rule 601.2c.)
┬á
700.2d If a player is allowed to choose more than one mode for a modal spell or ability, that player normally canΓÇÖt choose the same mode more than once. However, some modal spells include the instruction ΓÇ£You may choose the same mode more than once.ΓÇ¥ If a particular mode is chosen multiple times, the spell is treated as if that mode appeared that many times in sequence. If that mode requires a target, the same player or object may be chosen as the target for each of those modes, or different targets may be chosen.
┬á
700.2e Some spells and abilities specify that a player other than their controller chooses a mode for it. In that case, the other player does so when the spell or abilityΓÇÖs controller normally would do so. If there is more than one other player who could make such a choice, the spell or abilityΓÇÖs controller decides which of those players will make the choice.
┬á
700.2f Modal spells and abilities may have different targeting requirements for each mode. Changing a spell or abilityΓÇÖs target canΓÇÖt change its mode.
┬á
700.2g A copy of a modal spell or ability copies the mode(s) chosen for it. The controller of the copy canΓÇÖt choose a different mode. (See rule 707.10.)
┬á
700.2h Some modal spells have one or more modes with a cost listed before the effect of that mode. This indicates that the mode has an additional cost that must be paid as the spell is cast if that mode is chosen. If more than one such mode is chosen, all additional costs must be paid to cast that spell. Paying these costs follows the rules for paying additional costs in rules 601.2b and 601.2fΓÇôh.
┬á
700.2i Some modal spells have one or more pawprint symbols ({P}) rather than bullet points, as well as an instruction to choose up to a specified number of {P} ΓÇ£worth of modes.ΓÇ¥ While casting such a spell, its controller can choose any number of modes such that the total number of pawprint symbols listed for the chosen modes is not greater than the specified number.
┬á
700.3. Some effects cause objects to be temporarily grouped into piles.
┬á
700.3a Each of the affected objects must be put into exactly one of those piles, unless the effect specifies otherwise.
┬á
700.3b Each object in a pile is still an individual object. The pile is not an object.
┬á
700.3c Objects grouped into piles donΓÇÖt leave the zone theyΓÇÖre currently in. If cards in a graveyard are split into piles, the order of the graveyard must be maintained.
Example: Fact or Fiction reads, ΓÇ£Reveal the top five cards of your library. An opponent separates those cards into two piles. Put one pile into your hand and the other into your graveyard.ΓÇ¥ While an opponent is separating the revealed cards into piles, theyΓÇÖre still in their ownerΓÇÖs library. They donΓÇÖt leave the library until theyΓÇÖre put into their ownerΓÇÖs hand or graveyard.
┬á
700.3d A pile can contain zero or more objects.
┬á
700.4. The term dies means ΓÇ£is put into a graveyard from the battlefield.ΓÇ¥
┬á
700.5. A playerΓÇÖs devotion to [color] is equal to the number of mana symbols of that color among the mana costs of permanents that player controls. A playerΓÇÖs devotion to [color 1] and [color 2] is equal to the number of mana symbols among the mana costs of permanents that player controls that are [color 1], [color 2], or both colors.
┬á
700.5a A playerΓÇÖs devotion to each color and combination of colors, taking into account any effects that modify devotion, is calculated after considering any copy, control, or text-changing effects but before any other effects that modify the characteristics of permanents. This is an exception to 613.10. See also rule 613, ΓÇ£Interaction of Continuous Effects.ΓÇ¥
Example: Altar of the Pantheon is an artifact with no colored mana in its cost and an ability that says ΓÇ£Your devotion to each color and each combination of colors is increased by one.ΓÇ¥ Purphoros, God of the Forge is a permanent mana cost {3}{R} and an ability that says ΓÇ£As long as your devotion to red is less than five, Purphoros isnΓÇÖt a creature.ΓÇ¥ If a player controls both of these permanents and another permanent that costs {R}{R}{R}, that playerΓÇÖs devotion to red is calculated to be five before PurphorosΓÇÖs type-changing effect is applied, and Purphoros is a creature.
┬á
700.6. The term historic refers to an object that has the legendary supertype, the artifact card type, or the Saga subtype.
┬á
700.7. If an ability uses a phrase such as ΓÇ£this [something]ΓÇ¥ to identify an object, where [something] is a characteristic or other quality, it is referring to that particular object, even if it isnΓÇÖt the appropriate quality at the time.
Example: An ability reads ΓÇ£Target creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn. Destroy that creature at the beginning of the next end step.ΓÇ¥ The ability will destroy the object it gave +2/+2 to even if that object isnΓÇÖt a creature at the beginning of the next end step.
┬á
700.8. Some cards refer to a playerΓÇÖs party. A playerΓÇÖs party consists of up to one Cleric creature that player controls, up to one Rogue creature they control, up to one Warrior creature they control, and up to one Wizard creature they control.
┬á
700.8a If a spell, ability, or effect needs to determine the number of creatures in a playerΓÇÖs party, the calculation of that number is performed automatically by the game and results in a number between zero and four. Players donΓÇÖt declare which specific creatures they control are in their party for such an effect.
┬á

700.9. Some cards refer to modified permanents. A permanent is modified if it has one or more counters on it (see rule 122), if it is equipped (see rule 301.5), or if it is enchanted by an Aura that is controlled by that permanentΓÇÖs controller (see rule 303.4).

ΓÇ£The number of times [a player] descended this turnΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£the number of permanent cards put into [that playerΓÇÖs] graveyard from anywhere this turn.ΓÇ¥ In both cases, no permanent cards put into the playerΓÇÖs graveyard that turn are required to still be in that graveyard.

700.15. The term enter[s] is short for ΓÇ£enter[s] the battlefield.ΓÇ¥

701. Keyword Actions
┬á
701.1. Most actions described in a cardΓÇÖs rules text use the standard English definitions of the verbs within, but some specialized verbs are used whose meanings may not be clear. These ΓÇ£keywordsΓÇ¥ are game terms; sometimes reminder text summarizes their meanings.
┬á
701.2. Activate
┬á
701.2a To activate an activated ability is to put it onto the stack and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Only an objectΓÇÖs controller (or its owner, if it doesnΓÇÖt have a controller) can activate its activated ability unless the object specifically says otherwise. A player may activate an ability if they have priority. See rule 602, ΓÇ£Activating Activated Abilities.ΓÇ¥

701.3. Attach

701.3a To attach an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification to an object or player means to take it from where it currently is and put it onto that object or player. If something is attached to a permanent on the battlefield, itΓÇÖs customary to place it so that itΓÇÖs physically touching the permanent. An Aura, Equipment, or Fortification canΓÇÖt be attached to an object or player it couldnΓÇÖt enchant, equip, or fortify, respectively.

701.3b If an effect tries to attach an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification to an object or player it canΓÇÖt be attached to, the Aura, Equipment, or Fortification doesnΓÇÖt move. If an effect tries to attach an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification to the object or player itΓÇÖs already attached to, the effect does nothing. If an effect tries to attach an object that isnΓÇÖt an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification to another object or player, the effect does nothing and the first object doesnΓÇÖt move.

701.3c Attaching an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification on the battlefield to a different object or player causes the Aura, Equipment, or Fortification to receive a new timestamp.

701.3d To ΓÇ£unattachΓÇ¥ an Equipment from a creature means to move it away from that creature so the Equipment is on the battlefield but is not equipping anything. It should no longer be physically touching any creature. If an Aura, Equipment, or Fortification that was attached to an object or player ceases to be attached to it, that counts as ΓÇ£becoming unattached [from that object or player]ΓÇ¥; this includes if that Aura, Equipment, or Fortification leaves the battlefield, the object leaves the zone it was in, or that player leaves the game.

701.4. Behold

701.4a ΓÇ£Behold a [quality]ΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£Reveal a [quality] card from your hand or choose a [quality] permanent you control on the battlefield.ΓÇ¥

701.4b The phrase ΓÇ£if a [quality] was beheldΓÇ¥ refers to whether or not the object had that quality at the time the player took that action, regardless of whether or not the revealed card or chosen permanent still has that quality as the spell or ability including that phrase resolves.

701.5. Cast
┬á
701.5a To cast a spell is to take it from the zone itΓÇÖs in (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. A player may cast a spell if they have priority. See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥

701.5b To cast a card is to cast it as a spell.

701.6b The player who cast a countered spell or activated a countered ability doesnΓÇÖt get a ΓÇ£refundΓÇ¥ of any costs that were paid.

701.7. Create

701.7b If a replacement effect applies to a token being created, that effect applies before considering any continuous effects that will modify the characteristics of that token. If a replacement effect applies to a token entering the battlefield, that effect applies after considering any continuous effects that will modify the characteristics of that token.

701.7c Previously, an effect that created tokens instructed a player to ΓÇ£put [those tokens] onto the battlefield.ΓÇ¥ Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference so they now ΓÇ£createΓÇ¥ those tokens.

If a permanent is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard for any other reason, it hasnΓÇÖt been ΓÇ£destroyed.ΓÇ¥

701.8c A regeneration effect replaces a destruction event. See rule 701.19, ΓÇ£Regenerate.ΓÇ¥

701.9. Discard

701.9b By default, effects that cause a player to discard a card allow the affected player to choose which card to discard. Some effects, however, require a random discard or allow another player to choose which card is discarded.

701.9c If a card is discarded, but an effect causes it to be put into a hidden zone instead of into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard without being revealed, all values of that cardΓÇÖs characteristics are considered to be undefined. 701.10. Double
┬á
701.10a Doubling a creatureΓÇÖs power and/or toughness creates a continuous effect. This effect modifies that creatureΓÇÖs power and/or toughness but doesnΓÇÖt set those characteristics to a specific value. See rule 613.4c.

701.10b To double a creatureΓÇÖs power, that creature gets +X/+0, where X is that creatureΓÇÖs power as the spell or ability that doubles its power resolves. 701.11. Triple
┬á
701.11a Tripling a creatureΓÇÖs power and/or toughness creates a continuous effect. This effect modifies that creatureΓÇÖs power and/or toughness but doesnΓÇÖt set those characteristics to a specific value. See rule 613.4c.

701.11b To triple a creatureΓÇÖs power, that creature gets +X/+0, where X is twice that creatureΓÇÖs power as the spell or ability that triples its power resolves. Similarly, an effect that triples a creatureΓÇÖs toughness gives it +0/+X, where X is twice that creatureΓÇÖs toughness. Similarly, if its toughness is less than 0 when tripled, it gets -0/-X. If one characteristicΓÇÖs value is negative but the other isnΓÇÖt when both are tripled, it gets -X/+Y or +X/-Y, as appropriate.

701.12. Exchange
┬á
701.12a A spell or ability may instruct players to exchange something (for example, life totals or control of two permanents) as part of its resolution. When such a spell or ability resolves, if the entire exchange canΓÇÖt be completed, no part of the exchange occurs.
Example: If a spell attempts to exchange control of two target creatures but one of those creatures is destroyed before the spell resolves, the spell does nothing to the other creature.

701.12b When control of two permanents is exchanged, if those permanents are controlled by different players, each of those players simultaneously gains control of the permanent that was controlled by the other player. If, on the other hand, those permanents are controlled by the same player, the exchange effect does nothing.

701.12c When life totals are exchanged, each player gains or loses the amount of life necessary to equal the other playerΓÇÖs previous life total. A player who canΓÇÖt gain life canΓÇÖt be given a higher life total this way, and a player who canΓÇÖt lose life canΓÇÖt be given a lower life total this way (see rules 119.7ΓÇô8).

These spells and abilities work the same as other ΓÇ£exchangeΓÇ¥ spells and abilities, except they can exchange the cards only if all the cards are owned by the same player, and they can exchange the cards even if one zone is empty.

┬á
701.12f If a spell or ability instructs a player to simply exchange two zones, and one of the zones is empty, the cards in the zones are still exchanged.

701.12g A spell or ability may instruct a player to exchange two numerical values. In such an exchange, each value becomes equal to the previous value of the other. If either of those values is a life total, the affected player gains or loses the amount of life necessary to equal the other value. Replacement effects may modify this gain or loss, and triggered abilities may trigger on it. A player who canΓÇÖt gain life canΓÇÖt be given a higher life total this way, and a player who canΓÇÖt lose life canΓÇÖt be given a lower life total this way (see rules 119.7ΓÇô8). 701.12h One card (Exchange of Words) instructs a player to exchange the text boxes of two creatures. This creates a text-changing effect (see rule 612, ΓÇ£Text-Changing EffectsΓÇ¥). In such an exchange, the rules text of each permanent becomes the previous rules text of the other.

701.15b Goaded is a designation a permanent can have. A goaded creature attacks each combat if able and attacks a player other than the controller of the permanent, spell, or ability that caused it to be goaded if able. Goaded is neither an ability nor part of the permanentΓÇÖs copiable values.

701.16. Investigate

701.16a ΓÇ£InvestigateΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£Create a Clue token.ΓÇ¥ See rule 111.10f.

701.17. Mill

If instructed to do so, they mill as many as possible. Similarly, the player canΓÇÖt pay a cost that includes milling a number of cards greater than the number of cards in their library.

701.18. Play
┬á
701.18a To play a land means to put it onto the battlefield from the zone itΓÇÖs in (usually the hand). ┬á
701.18c Some effects instruct a player to ΓÇ£playΓÇ¥ with a certain aspect of the game changed, such as ΓÇ£Play with the top card of your library revealed.ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£PlayΓÇ¥ in this sense means to play the Magic game.

701.18d Previously, the action of casting a spell, or casting a card as a spell, was referred to on cards as ΓÇ£playingΓÇ¥ that spell or that card. Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference so they now refer to ΓÇ£castingΓÇ¥ that spell or that card.

701.18e Previously, the action of using an activated ability was referred to on cards as ΓÇ£playingΓÇ¥ that ability. Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference so they now refer to ΓÇ£activatingΓÇ¥ that ability.

701.19. Regenerate
┬á
701.19a If the effect of a resolving spell or ability regenerates a permanent, it creates a replacement effect that protects the permanent the next time it would be destroyed this turn. In this case, ΓÇ£Regenerate [permanent]ΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£The next time [permanent] would be destroyed this turn, instead remove all damage marked on it and its controller taps it. 701.23. Search

701.23a To search for a card in a zone, look at all cards in that zone (even if itΓÇÖs a hidden zone) and find a card that matches the given description.

701.23b If a player is searching a hidden zone for cards with a stated quality, such as a card with a certain card type or color, that player isnΓÇÖt required to find some or all of those cards even if theyΓÇÖre present in that zone.

Then that player shuffles their library.ΓÇ¥ A player casts Splinter targeting Howling Mine (an artifact). Howling MineΓÇÖs controller has another Howling Mine in her graveyard and two more in her library. SplinterΓÇÖs controller must find the Howling Mine in the graveyard, but may choose to find zero, one, or two of the Howling Mines in the library.

701.23c If a player is instructed to search a hidden zone for cards that match an undefined quality, that player may still search that zone but canΓÇÖt find any cards.

701.23d If a player is searching a hidden zone simply for a quantity of cards, such as ΓÇ£a cardΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£three cards,ΓÇ¥ that player must find that many cards (or as many as possible, if the zone doesnΓÇÖt contain enough cards).

701.23e If the effect that contains the search instruction doesnΓÇÖt also contain instructions to reveal the found card(s), then theyΓÇÖre not revealed.

701.23f If searching a zone is replaced with searching a portion of that zone, any other instructions that refer to searching the zone still apply. Any abilities that trigger on a library being searched will trigger.
Example: Aven Mindcensor says, in part, ΓÇ£If an opponent would search a library, that player searches the top four cards of that library instead.ΓÇ¥ Veteran Explorer says ΓÇ£When this creature dies, each player may search their library for up to two basic land cards, put them onto the battlefield, then shuffle.ΓÇ¥ An opponent who searched the top four cards of their library because of Veteran ExplorerΓÇÖs ability would shuffle the entire library.

┬á

701.24. Shuffle
┬á
701.24a To shuffle a library or a face-down pile of cards, randomize the cards within it so that no player knows their order.
┬á
701.24b Some effects cause a player to search a library for a card or cards, shuffle that library, then put some or all of the found cards into a different zone or in a certain position in that library. In such cases, the found cards arenΓÇÖt included in the shuffle, even though they remain in the library at that time. Rather, all the cards in that library except those are shuffled. 702. Keyword Abilities
┬á
702.1. Most abilities describe exactly what they do in the cardΓÇÖs rules text. Some, though, are very common or would require too much space to define on the card. In these cases, the object lists only the name of the ability as a ΓÇ£keywordΓÇ¥; sometimes reminder text summarizes the game rule.

702.1a If an effect refers to a ΓÇ£[keyword ability] cost,ΓÇ¥ it refers only to the variable costs for that keyword.
Example: Varolz, the Scar-Striped has an ability that says ΓÇ£Each creature card in your graveyard has scavenge. The scavenge cost is equal to its mana cost.ΓÇ¥ A creature cardΓÇÖs scavenge cost is an amount of mana equal to its mana cost, and the activation cost of the scavenge ability is that amount of mana plus ΓÇ£Exile this card from your graveyard.ΓÇ¥

702.1b An effect that grants an object a keyword ability may define a variable in that ability based on characteristics of that object or other information about the game state. For these abilities, the value of that variable is constantly reevaluated.
Example: Volcano Hellion has the ability ΓÇ£This creature has echo {X}, where X is your life total.ΓÇ¥ If your life total is 10 when Volcano HellionΓÇÖs echo ability triggers but 5 when it resolves, the echo cost to pay is {5}.
Example: Fire//Ice is a split card whose halves have the mana costs {1}{R} and {1}{U}. Past in Flames reads ΓÇ£Each instant and sorcery card in your graveyard gains flashback until end of turn. The flashback cost is equal to its mana cost.ΓÇ¥ Fire//Ice has ΓÇ£Flashback {2}{U}{R}ΓÇ¥ while it is in your graveyard, but if you choose to cast Fire, the resulting spell has ΓÇ£Flashback {1}{R}.ΓÇ¥

702.1c An effect may state that ΓÇ£the same is true forΓÇ¥ a list of keyword abilities or similar. If one of those keyword abilities has variants or variables and the effect grants that keyword or counters of that keyword to one or more objects and/or players, it grants each appropriate variant and variable of that keyword.
Example: Concerted Effort is an enchantment that reads ΓÇ£At the beginning of each upkeep, creatures you control gain flying until end of turn if a creature you control has flying. The same is true for fear, first strike, double strike, landwalk, protection, trample, and vigilance.ΓÇ¥ As that triggered ability resolves, each landwalk and protection ability from among creatures you control is granted to each creature you control.

702.1d An effect may refer to an object ΓÇ£with [keyword ability]ΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£that has [keyword ability].ΓÇ¥ This means the same thing as an object ΓÇ£with a [keyword ability] abilityΓÇ¥ or an object ΓÇ£that has a [keyword ability] ability.ΓÇ¥

702.4b If at least one attacking or blocking creature has first strike (see rule 702.7) or double strike as the combat damage step begins, the only creatures that assign combat damage in that step are those with first strike or double strike. After that step, instead of proceeding to the end of combat step, the phase gets a second combat damage step. The only creatures that assign combat damage in that step are the remaining attackers and blockers that had neither first strike nor double strike as the first combat damage step began, as well as the remaining attackers and blockers that currently have double strike. After that step, the phase proceeds to the end of combat step.

Example: Tapestry Warden has as ability that reads ΓÇ£Each creature you control with toughness greater than its power stations permanents using its toughness rather than its power.ΓÇ¥

ΓÇ£Warp [cost]ΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£You may cast this card from your hand by paying [cost] rather than its mana costΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£If this spellΓÇÖs warp cost was paid, exile the permanent this spell becomes at the beginning of the next end step. Its owner may cast this card after the current turn has ended for as long as it remains exiled.ΓÇ¥ Casting a spell for its warp cost follows the rules for paying alternative costs in rules 601.2b and 601.2fΓÇôh.

703. Turn-Based Actions
┬á
703.1. Turn-based actions are game actions that happen automatically when certain steps or phases begin, or when each step and phase ends. Turn-based actions donΓÇÖt use the stack.
┬á
703.1a Abilities that watch for a specified step or phase to begin are triggered abilities, not turn-based actions. (See rule 603, ΓÇ£Handling Triggered Abilities.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
703.2. Turn-based actions are not controlled by any player.
┬á
703.3. Whenever a step or phase begins, if itΓÇÖs a step or phase that has any turn-based action associated with it, those turn-based actions are automatically dealt with first. This happens before state-based actions are checked, before triggered abilities are put on the stack, and before players receive priority.
┬á
703.4. The turn-based actions are as follows:
┬á
703.4a Immediately after the untap step begins, all phased-in permanents with phasing that the active player controls phase out, and all phased-out permanents that the active player controlled when they phased out phase in. This all happens simultaneously. See rule 502.1.
┬á
703.4b Immediately after the phasing action has been completed during the untap step, if the game has either the day or night designation, it checks to see whether that designation should change. If itΓÇÖs neither day nor night, this check doesnΓÇÖt happen. See rule 502.2.
┬á
703.4c Immediately after the game checks to see if its day or night designation should change during the untap step or, if the game doesnΓÇÖt have a day or night designation, immediately after the phasing action has been completed during the untap step, the active player determines which permanents they control will untap. Then they untap them all simultaneously. See rule 502.3.
┬á
703.4d Immediately after the draw step begins, the active player draws a card. See rule 504.1.
┬á
703.4e In an Archenemy game (see rule 904), immediately after the archenemyΓÇÖs precombat main phase begins, that player sets the top card of their scheme deck in motion. See rule 701.32.
┬á
703.4f Immediately after a playerΓÇÖs precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga enchantment they control with one or more chapter abilities. In an Archenemy game, this happens after the archenemyΓÇÖs scheme action. See rule 714, ΓÇ£Saga Cards.ΓÇ¥
┬á
703.4g Immediately after the action of placing lore counters has been completed, if the active player controls any Attractions, that player rolls to visit their Attractions. See rule 701.52, ΓÇ£Roll to Visit Your Attractions.ΓÇ¥
┬á
703.4h Immediately after the beginning of combat step begins, if the game being played is a multiplayer game in which the active playerΓÇÖs opponents donΓÇÖt all automatically become defending players, the active player chooses one of their opponents. That player becomes the defending player. See rule 507.1.
┬á
703.4i Immediately after the declare attackers step begins, the active player declares attackers. See rule 508.1.
┬á
703.4j Immediately after the declare blockers step begins, the defending player declares blockers. See rule 509.1.
┬á
703.4k Immediately after the combat damage step begins, each player in APNAP order announces how each attacking or blocking creature they control assigns its combat damage. See rule 510.1.
┬á
703.4m Immediately after combat damage has been assigned during the combat damage step, all combat damage is dealt simultaneously. See rule 510.2.
┬á
703.4n Immediately after the cleanup step begins, if the active playerΓÇÖs hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size (normally seven), they discard enough cards to reduce their hand size to that number. See rule 514.1.
┬á
703.4p Immediately after the active player has discarded cards (if necessary) during the cleanup step, all damage is removed from permanents and all ΓÇ£until end of turnΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£this turnΓÇ¥ effects end. These actions happen simultaneously. See rule 514.2.
┬á
703.4q As each step or phase ends, any unspent mana left in a playerΓÇÖs mana pool empties. See rule 500.5.
┬á
704. State-Based Actions
┬á
704.1. State-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions (listed below) are met. State-based actions donΓÇÖt use the stack.
┬á
704.1a Abilities that watch for a specified game state are triggered abilities, not state-based actions. (See rule 603, ΓÇ£Handling Triggered Abilities.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
704.2. State-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player.
┬á
704.3. Whenever a player would get priority (see rule 117, ΓÇ£Timing and PriorityΓÇ¥), the game checks for any of the listed conditions for state-based actions, then performs all applicable state-based actions simultaneously as a single event. If any state-based actions are performed as a result of a check, the check is repeated; otherwise all triggered abilities that are waiting to be put on the stack are put on the stack, then the check is repeated. Once no more state-based actions have been performed as the result of a check and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, the appropriate player gets priority. This process also occurs during the cleanup step (see rule 514), except that if no state-based actions are performed as the result of the stepΓÇÖs first check and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, then no player gets priority and the step ends.
┬á
704.4. Unlike triggered abilities, state-based actions pay no attention to what happens during the resolution of a spell or ability.
Example: A player controls Maro, a creature with the ability ΓÇ£MaroΓÇÖs power and toughness are each equal to the number of cards in your handΓÇ¥ and casts a spell whose effect is ΓÇ£Discard your hand, then draw seven cards.ΓÇ¥ Maro will temporarily have toughness 0 in the middle of the spellΓÇÖs resolution but will be back up to toughness 7 when the spell finishes resolving. Thus Maro will survive when state-based actions are checked. In contrast, an ability that triggers when the player has no cards in hand goes on the stack after the spell resolves, because its trigger event happened during resolution.
┬á
704.5. The state-based actions are as follows:
┬á
704.5a If a player has 0 or less life, that player loses the game.
┬á
704.5b If a player attempted to draw a card from a library with no cards in it since the last time state-based actions were checked, that player loses the game.
┬á
704.5c If a player has ten or more poison counters, that player loses the game. Ignore this rule in Two-Headed Giant games; see rule 704.6b instead.
┬á
704.5d If a token is in a zone other than the battlefield, it ceases to exist.
┬á
704.5e If a copy of a spell is in a zone other than the stack, it ceases to exist. If a copy of a card is in any zone other than the stack or the battlefield, it ceases to exist.
┬á
704.5f If a creature has toughness 0 or less, itΓÇÖs put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. Regeneration canΓÇÖt replace this event.
┬á
704.5g If a creature has toughness greater than 0, it has damage marked on it, and the total damage marked on it is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed. Regeneration can replace this event.
┬á
704.5h If a creature has toughness greater than 0, and itΓÇÖs been dealt damage by a source with deathtouch since the last time state-based actions were checked, that creature is destroyed. Regeneration can replace this event.
┬á
704.5i If a planeswalker has loyalty 0, itΓÇÖs put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard.
┬á
704.5j If two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one of them, and the rest are put into their ownersΓÇÖ graveyards. This is called the ΓÇ£legend rule.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.5k If two or more permanents have the supertype world, all except the one that has had the world supertype for the shortest amount of time are put into their ownersΓÇÖ graveyards. In the event of a tie for the shortest amount of time, all are put into their ownersΓÇÖ graveyards. This is called the ΓÇ£world rule.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.5m If an Aura is attached to an illegal object or player, or is not attached to an object or player, that Aura is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard.
┬á
704.5n If an Equipment or Fortification is attached to an illegal permanent or to a player, it becomes unattached from that permanent or player. It remains on the battlefield.
┬á
704.5p If a battle or creature is attached to an object or player, it becomes unattached and remains on the battlefield. Similarly, if any nonbattle, noncreature permanent thatΓÇÖs neither an Aura, an Equipment, nor a Fortification is attached to an object or player, it becomes unattached and remains on the battlefield.
┬á
704.5q If a permanent has both a +1/+1 counter and a -1/-1 counter on it, N +1/+1 and N -1/-1 counters are removed from it, where N is the smaller of the number of +1/+1 and -1/-1 counters on it.
┬á
704.5r If a permanent with an ability that says it canΓÇÖt have more than N counters of a certain kind on it has more than N counters of that kind on it, all but N of those counters are removed from it.
┬á
704.5s If the number of lore counters on a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities is greater than or equal to its final chapter number and it isnΓÇÖt the source of a chapter ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, that SagaΓÇÖs controller sacrifices it. See rule 714, ΓÇ£Saga Cards.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.5t If a playerΓÇÖs venture marker is on the bottommost room of a dungeon card, and that dungeon card isnΓÇÖt the source of a room ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, the dungeon cardΓÇÖs owner removes it from the game. See rule 309, ΓÇ£Dungeons.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.5u If a permanent with space sculptor and any creatures without a sector designation are on the battlefield, each player who controls one or more of those creatures and doesnΓÇÖt control a permanent with space sculptor chooses a sector designation for each of those creatures they control. Then, each other player who controls one or more of those creatures chooses a sector designation for each of those creatures they control. See rule 702.158, ΓÇ£Space Sculptor.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.5v If a Siege battle has defense 0 and it isnΓÇÖt the source of an ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, itΓÇÖs put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard.
┬á
704.5w If a non-Siege battle has defense 0, itΓÇÖs put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard.
┬á
704.5x If a battle has no player in the game designated as its protector and no attacking creatures are currently attacking that battle, that battleΓÇÖs controller chooses an appropriate player to be its protector based on its battle type. If the battle has no battle type, its controller must be chosen. If no player can be chosen this way, the battle is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. See rule 310, ΓÇ£Battles.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.5y If a battleΓÇÖs protector is a player who canΓÇÖt be its protector, that battleΓÇÖs controller chooses an appropriate player to become its protector. If no player can be chosen this way, the battle is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard. See rule 310, ΓÇ£Battles.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.5z If a permanent has more than one Role controlled by the same player attached to it, each of those Roles except the one with the most recent timestamp is put into its ownerΓÇÖs graveyard.
┬á
704.5aa If a player controls a permanent with start your engines! and that player has no speed, that playerΓÇÖs speed becomes 1. See rule 702.179, ΓÇ£Start Your Engines!ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.6. Some variant games include additional state-based actions that arenΓÇÖt normally applicable:
┬á
704.6a In a Two-Headed Giant game, if a team has 0 or less life, that team loses the game. See rule 810, ΓÇ£Two-Headed Giant Variant.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.6b In a Two-Headed Giant game, if a team has fifteen or more poison counters, that team loses the game. See rule 810, ΓÇ£Two-Headed Giant Variant.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.6c In a Commander game, a player whoΓÇÖs been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses the game. See rule 903, ΓÇ£Commander.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.6d In a Commander game, if a commander is in a graveyard or in exile and that object was put into that zone since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put it into the command zone. See rule 903, ΓÇ£Commander.ΓÇ¥ 
┬á
704.6e In an Archenemy game, if a non-ongoing scheme card is face up in the command zone, and no triggered abilities of any scheme are on the stack or waiting to be put on the stack, that scheme card is turned face down and put on the bottom of its ownerΓÇÖs scheme deck. See rule 904, ΓÇ£Archenemy.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.6f In a Planechase game, if a phenomenon card is face up in the command zone, and it isnΓÇÖt the source of a triggered ability that has triggered but not yet left the stack, the planar controller planeswalks. See rule 901, ΓÇ£Planechase.ΓÇ¥
┬á
704.7. If multiple state-based actions would have the same result at the same time, a single replacement effect will replace all of them.
Example: You control LichΓÇÖs Mirror, which says ΓÇ£If you would lose the game, instead shuffle your hand, your graveyard, and all permanents you own into your library, then draw seven cards and your life total becomes 20.ΓÇ¥ ThereΓÇÖs one card in your library and your life total is 1. A spell causes you to draw two cards and lose 2 life. The next time state-based actions are checked, youΓÇÖd lose the game due to rule 704.5a and rule 704.5b. Instead, LichΓÇÖs Mirror replaces that game loss and you keep playing.
┬á
704.8. If a state-based action results in a permanent leaving the battlefield at the same time other state-based actions were performed, that permanentΓÇÖs last known information is derived from the game state before any of those state-based actions were performed.
Example: You control Young Wolf, a 1/1 creature with undying, and it has a +1/+1 counter on it. A spell puts three -1/-1 counters on Young Wolf. Before state-based actions are performed, Young Wolf has one +1/+1 counter and three -1/-1 counters on it. After state-based actions are performed, Young Wolf is in the graveyard. When it was last on the battlefield, it had a +1/+1 counter on it, so undying will not trigger.
┬á
705. Flipping a Coin
┬á
705.1. Some cards refer to flipping a coin. A coin used in a flip must be a two-sided object with easily distinguished sides and equal likelihood that either side lands face up. If the coin thatΓÇÖs being flipped doesnΓÇÖt have an obvious ΓÇ£headsΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£tails,ΓÇ¥ designate one side to be ΓÇ£heads,ΓÇ¥ and the other side to be ΓÇ£tails.ΓÇ¥ Other methods of randomization may be substituted for flipping a coin as long as there are two possible outcomes of equal likelihood and all players agree to the substitution. For example, the player may roll an even-sided die and call ΓÇ£oddsΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£evens,ΓÇ¥ or roll an even-sided die and designate that ΓÇ£oddsΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£headsΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£evensΓÇ¥ means ΓÇ£tails.ΓÇ¥
┬á
705.2. Some effects that instruct a player to flip a coin care only about whether the coin comes up heads or tails. No player wins or loses a coin flip for this kind of effect. For all other effects that instruct a player to flip a coin, the player that flips the coin calls ΓÇ£headsΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£tails.ΓÇ¥ If the call matches the result, the player wins the flip. Otherwise, the player loses the flip. Only the player who flips the coin wins or loses the flip; no other players are involved.
┬á
705.3. An effect may state that a coin flip has a certain result and/or that a certain player wins a coin flip. In that case, ignore the actual results of that flip and use the indicated results instead. This can cause a player to win a flip that couldnΓÇÖt otherwise be won.
┬á
706. Rolling a Die
┬á
706.1. An effect that instructs a player to roll a die will specify what kind of die to roll and how many of those dice to roll.
┬á
706.1a Such an effect may refer to an ΓÇ£N-sided die,ΓÇ¥ ΓÇ£N-sided dice,ΓÇ¥ or one or more ΓÇ£dN,ΓÇ¥ where N is a positive integer. In those cases, the die must have N equally likely outcomes, numbered from 1 to N. For example, a d20 is a twenty-sided die with possible outcomes from 1 to 20.
┬á
706.1b Players may agree to use an alternate method for rolling a die, including a digital substitute, as long as the method used has the same number of equally likely outcomes as the die specified in the instruction.
┬á
706.2. After the roll, the number indicated on the top face of the die before any modifiers is the natural result. The instruction may include modifiers to the roll which add to or subtract from the natural result. Modifiers may also come from other sources. After considering all applicable modifiers, the final number is the result of the die roll.
┬á
706.2a Modifiers may be optional and/or have associated costs. If a modifier has an associated mana cost, the player who rolled has the chance to activate mana abilities before applying it.
┬á
706.2b If two or more effects are attempting to modify the natural result, the player who rolled chooses one to apply, following these steps: First, consider any effects that modify the result of a die roll by rerolling that die. Second, consider any effects that modify the result of a die roll by increasing or decreasing that result by a specified amount.
┬á
706.3. Some abilities that instruct a player to roll one or more dice include a results table.
┬á
706.3a The results table appears as a list or as a chart with multiple striations. Each list item or striation includes possible results and an effect associated with those results. The possible results indicated could be a single number, a range of numbers with two endpoints in the form ΓÇ£N1ΓÇôN2,ΓÇ¥ or a range with a single endpoint in the form ΓÇ£N+.ΓÇ¥ Each one means ΓÇ£If the result was in this range, [effect].ΓÇ¥ After a die roll, use the result to determine which effect listed on the results table happens, if any.
┬á
706.3b An instruction to roll one or more dice, any instructions to modify that roll printed in the same paragraph, any additional instructions based on the result of the roll, and the associated results table are all part of one ability.
┬á
706.3c Some effects in results charts include the text ΓÇ£Roll again.ΓÇ¥ This additional roll uses the same kind of and number of dice originally called for, including any applicable modifiers.
┬á
706.4. Some abilities that instruct a player to roll one or more dice do not include a results table. The text of those abilities will indicate how to use the results of the die rolls, if at all.
┬á
706.5. One card (Celebr-8000) has an ability that instructs a player to roll two dice and has an additional effect if that player ΓÇ£rolled doubles.ΓÇ¥ A player has rolled doubles if the result of each of those rolls is equal to the other.
┬á
706.6. If a player is instructed to ignore a roll, that roll is considered to have never happened. No abilities trigger because of the ignored roll, and no effects apply to that roll. If that player was instructed to ignore the lowest roll and multiple results are tied for the lowest, the player chooses one of those rolls to be ignored.
┬á
706.7. In a Planechase game, rolling the planar die will cause any ability that triggers whenever a player rolls one or more dice to trigger. However, any effect that refers to a numerical result of a die roll, including ones that exchange the results of that roll with another value or compare the results of that roll to other rolls or to a given number, ignores the rolling of the planar die. See rule 901, ΓÇ£Planechase.ΓÇ¥
┬á
706.8. One card (Centaur of Attention) has an ability that instructs a player to roll dice and ΓÇ£storeΓÇ¥ those results on it and another ability that allows a player to reroll any number of those results.
┬á
706.8a To store the result of a die roll on a permanent means to note both the kind of die rolled and the result of that roll. That noted information is considered a ΓÇ£stored resultΓÇ¥ of that permanent, and the result is the ΓÇ£valueΓÇ¥ of that stored result.
┬á
706.8b To reroll one or more stored results of a permanent, roll one of the kind of die noted for each of them. If one kind of die is noted for more than one of those results, roll that many of that kind of die. The results you rerolled stop being stored results, and you store the results of each of the new die rolls on that permanent.
┬á
706.8c If a permanent has an ability that stores results on it and another ability that refers to the stored results, those abilities are linked. (See rule 607.2e.)
┬á
707. Copying Objects
┬á
707.1. Some objects become or turn another object into a ΓÇ£copyΓÇ¥ of a spell, permanent, or card. Some effects create a token thatΓÇÖs a copy of another object. (Certain older cards were printed with the phrase ΓÇ£search for a copy.ΓÇ¥ This section doesnΓÇÖt cover those cards, which have received new text in the Oracle card reference.)
┬á
707.2. When copying an object, the copy acquires the copiable values of the original objectΓÇÖs characteristics and, for an object on the stack, choices made when casting or activating it (mode, targets, the value of X, whether it was kicked, how it will affect multiple targets, and so on). The copiable values are the values derived from the text printed on the object (that text being name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty), as modified by other copy effects, by its face-down status, and by ΓÇ£as . . . entersΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£as . . . is turned face upΓÇ¥ abilities that set power and toughness (and may also set additional characteristics). Other effects (including type-changing and text-changing effects), status, counters, and stickers are not copied.
Example: Chimeric Staff is an artifact that reads, ΓÇ£{X}: This artifact becomes an X/X Construct artifact creature until end of turn.ΓÇ¥ Clone is a creature that reads, ΓÇ£You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield.ΓÇ¥ After a Staff has become a 5/5 Construct artifact creature, a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of it. The Clone is an artifact, not a 5/5 Construct artifact creature. (The copy has the StaffΓÇÖs ability, however, and will become a creature if that ability is activated.)
Example: Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of a face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph {2}{B}{B}). The Clone is a colorless 2/2 creature with no name, no types, no abilities, and no mana cost. It will still be face up. Its controller canΓÇÖt pay {2}{B}{B} to turn it face up.
┬á
707.2a A copy acquires the color of the object itΓÇÖs copying because that value is derived from its mana cost or color indicator. A copy acquires the abilities of the object itΓÇÖs copying because those values are derived from its rules text. A copy doesnΓÇÖt wind up with two values of each ability (that is, it doesnΓÇÖt copy the objectΓÇÖs abilities and its rules text, then have that rules text define a new set of abilities).
┬á
707.2b Once an object has been copied, changing the copiable values of the original object wonΓÇÖt cause the copy to change.
┬á
707.2c If a static ability generates a continuous effect thatΓÇÖs a copy effect, the copiable values that effect grants are determined only at the time that effect first starts to apply.
┬á
707.3. The copyΓÇÖs copiable values become the copied information, as modified by the copyΓÇÖs status (see rule 110.5). Objects that copy the object will use the new copiable values.
Example: Vesuvan Doppelganger reads, ΓÇ£You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield, except it doesnΓÇÖt copy that creatureΓÇÖs color and it has ΓÇÿAt the beginning of your upkeep, you may have this creature become a copy of target creature, except it doesnΓÇÖt copy that creatureΓÇÖs color and it has this ability.ΓÇÖΓÇ¥ A Vesuvan Doppelganger enters the battlefield as a copy of Runeclaw Bear (a 2/2 green Bear creature with no abilities). Then a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of the Doppelganger. The Clone is a 2/2 blue Bear named Runeclaw Bear that has the DoppelgangerΓÇÖs upkeep-triggered ability.
Example: Tomoya the Revealer (a flipped flip card) becomes a copy of Nezumi Shortfang (an unflipped flip card). TomoyaΓÇÖs characteristics become the characteristics of Stabwhisker the Odious, which is the flipped version of Nezumi Shortfang.
Example: A face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph) becomes a copy of a face-up Branchsnap Lorian (a 4/1 green creature with trample and morph {G}). The DemonΓÇÖs characteristics become the characteristics of Branchsnap Lorian. However, since the creature is face down, it remains a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, types, or abilities, and no mana cost. It can be turned face up for {G}. If itΓÇÖs turned face up, it will have the characteristics of Branchsnap Lorian.
Example: A face-down Grinning Demon (a creature with morph) becomes a copy of Wandering Ones (a 1/1 blue Spirit creature that doesnΓÇÖt have morph). It will be a face-down Wandering Ones. It remains a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, types, or abilities, and no mana cost. Its controller canΓÇÖt turn it face up as a special action. If an effect turns it face up, it will have the characteristics of Wandering Ones.
┬á
707.4. Some effects cause a permanent thatΓÇÖs copying a permanent to copy a different object while remaining on the battlefield. The change doesnΓÇÖt cause enters-the-battlefield or leaves-the-battlefield abilities to trigger. This also doesnΓÇÖt change any noncopy effects presently affecting the permanent.
Example: Unstable Shapeshifter reads, ΓÇ£Whenever another creature enters, this creature becomes a copy of that creature, except it has this ability.ΓÇ¥ ItΓÇÖs affected by Giant Growth, which reads ΓÇ£Target creature gets +3/+3 until end of turn.ΓÇ¥ If a creature enters the battlefield later this turn, Unstable Shapeshifter will become a copy of that creature, but it will still get +3/+3 from the Giant Growth.
┬á
707.5. An object that enters the battlefield ΓÇ£as a copyΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£thatΓÇÖs a copyΓÇ¥ of another object becomes a copy as it enters the battlefield. It doesnΓÇÖt enter the battlefield, and then become a copy of that permanent. If the text thatΓÇÖs being copied includes any abilities that replace the enters-the-battlefield event (such as ΓÇ£enters withΓÇ¥ or ΓÇ£as [this] entersΓÇ¥ abilities), those abilities will take effect. Also, any enters-the-battlefield triggered abilities of the copy will have a chance to trigger.
Example: Skyshroud Behemoth reads, ΓÇ£Fading 2 (This creature enters with two fade counters on it. At the beginning of your upkeep, remove a fade counter from it. If you canΓÇÖt, sacrifice it.)ΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£This creature enters tapped.ΓÇ¥ A Clone that enters the battlefield as a copy of a Skyshroud Behemoth will also enter the battlefield tapped with two fade counters on it.
Example: Wall of Omens reads, ΓÇ£When this creature enters, draw a card.ΓÇ¥ A Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of Wall of Omens. The Clone has the WallΓÇÖs enters-the-battlefield triggered ability, so the CloneΓÇÖs controller draws a card.
┬á
707.6. When copying a permanent, any choices that have been made for that permanent arenΓÇÖt copied. Instead, if an object enters the battlefield as a copy of another permanent, the objectΓÇÖs controller will get to make any ΓÇ£as [this] enters the battlefieldΓÇ¥ choices for it.
Example: A Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of Adaptive Automaton. Adaptive Automaton reads, in part, ΓÇ£As this creature enters, choose a creature type.ΓÇ¥ The Clone wonΓÇÖt copy the creature type choice of the Automaton; rather, the controller of the Clone will get to make a new choice.
┬á
707.7. If a pair of linked abilities are copied, those abilities will be similarly linked to one another on the object that copied them. One ability refers only to actions that were taken or objects that were affected by the other. They canΓÇÖt be linked to any other ability, regardless of what other abilities the copy may currently have or may have had in the past. See rule 607, ΓÇ£Linked Abilities.ΓÇ¥
┬á
707.8. When copying a melded permanent or other double-faced permanent, use the copiable values of the face thatΓÇÖs currently up to determine the characteristics of the copy. See rule 712, ΓÇ£Double-Faced Cards.ΓÇ¥
┬á
707.8a If an effect creates a token that is a copy of a double-faced permanent or a double-faced card not on the battlefield, the resulting token is a double-faced token that has both a front face and a back face. The characteristics of each face are determined by the copiable values of the same face of the permanent or card it is a copy of, as modified by any other copy effects that apply to that object. If the token is a copy of a double-faced permanent with its back face up, the token enters the battlefield with its back face up. This rule does not apply to tokens that are created with their own set of characteristics and enter the battlefield as a copy of a double-faced object due to a replacement effect.
Example: Afflicted Deserter is the front face of a double-faced card, and the name of its back face is Werewolf Ransacker. If an effect creates a token that is a copy of that permanent, the token also has the same two faces and can transform. It enters the battlefield with the same face up as the permanent that it is a copy of.
Example: Clone is not a double-faced card, so a token that is created as a copy of a Clone is not a double-faced token, even if it enters the battlefield as a copy of a permanent due to CloneΓÇÖs replacement effect.
┬á
707.9. Copy effects may include modifications or exceptions to the copying process.
┬á
707.9a Some copy effects cause the copy to gain an ability as part of the copying process. This ability becomes part of the copiable values for the copy, along with any other abilities that were copied.
Example: Quirion Elves enters the battlefield and an Unstable Shapeshifter copies it. The copiable values of the Shapeshifter now match those of the Elves, except that the Shapeshifter also has the ability ΓÇ£Whenever another creature enters, this creature becomes a copy of that creature, except it has this ability.ΓÇ¥ Then a Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of the Unstable Shapeshifter. The Clone copies the new copiable values of the Shapeshifter, including the ability that the Shapeshifter gave itself when it copied the Elves.
┬á
707.9b Some copy effects modify a characteristic as part of the copying process. The final set of values for that characteristic becomes part of the copiable values of the copy.
Example: Copy Artifact is an enchantment that reads, ΓÇ£You may have this enchantment enter as a copy of any artifact on the battlefield, except itΓÇÖs an enchantment in addition to its other types.ΓÇ¥ It enters the battlefield as a copy of Juggernaut. The copiable values of the Copy Artifact now match those of Juggernaut with one modification: its types are now artifact, creature, and enchantment.
┬á
707.9c Some copy effects specifically state that they donΓÇÖt copy certain characteristics and the affected objects instead retain their original values. Copy effects may also simply state that certain characteristics are not copied.
┬á
707.9d When applying a copy effect that doesnΓÇÖt copy a certain characteristic, retains one or more original values for a certain characteristic, or provides a specific set of values for a certain characteristic, any characteristic-defining ability (see rule 604.3) of the object being copied that defines that characteristic is not copied. If that characteristic is color, any color indicator (see rule 204) of that object is also not copied. This rule does not apply to copy effects with exceptions that state the object is a certain card type, supertype, and/or subtype ΓÇ£in addition to its other types.ΓÇ¥ In those cases, any characteristic-defining ability that defines card type, supertype, and/or subtype is copied.
Example: Quicksilver Gargantuan is a creature that reads, ΓÇ£You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield, except itΓÇÖs 7/7.ΓÇ¥ Quicksilver Gargantuan enters the battlefield as a copy of Tarmogoyf, which has a characteristic-defining ability that defines its power and toughness. Quicksilver Gargantuan does not have that ability. It will be 7/7.
Example: Glasspool Mimic is a creature that reads ΓÇ£You may have this creature enter as a copy of a creature you control, except itΓÇÖs a Shapeshifter Rogue in addition to its other types.ΓÇ¥ Glasspool Mimic enters as a copy of a creature with changeling. Glasspool Mimic will have changeling and will have all creature types.
┬á
707.9e Some replacement effects that generate copy effects include an exception thatΓÇÖs an additional effect rather than a modification of the affected objectΓÇÖs characteristics. If another copy effect is applied to that object after applying the copy effect with that exception, the exceptionΓÇÖs effect doesnΓÇÖt happen.
Example: Altered Ego reads, ΓÇ£You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield, except it enters with X additional +1/+1 counters on it.ΓÇ¥ You choose for it to enter the battlefield as a copy of Clone, which reads ΓÇ£You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield,ΓÇ¥ for which no creature was chosen as it entered the battlefield. If you then choose a creature to copy as you apply the replacement effect Altered Ego gains by copying Clone, Altered EgoΓÇÖs replacement effect wonΓÇÖt cause it to enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters on it.
┬á
707.9f Some exceptions to the copying process apply only if the copy is or has certain characteristics. To determine whether such an exception applies, consider what the resulting permanentΓÇÖs characteristics would be if the copy effect were applied without that exception, taking into account any other exceptions that effect includes.
Example: Moritte of the Frost says, in part, ΓÇ£You may have Moritte enter as a copy of a permanent you control, except itΓÇÖs legendary and snow in addition to its other types and, if itΓÇÖs a creature, it enters with two additional +1/+1 counters on it and it has changeling.ΓÇ¥ Moritte of the Frost copies a land that has become a creature until end of turn. It would enter as a noncreature permanent, so it wonΓÇÖt enter with two additional +1+1 counters on it and it wonΓÇÖt have changeling, even if it becomes a creature later in the turn.
┬á
707.9g Some replacement effects that generate copy effects are linked to triggered abilities written in the same paragraph. (See rule 603.11.) If another copy effect is applied to that object after applying the copy effect with the linked triggered ability, the ability doesnΓÇÖt trigger.
┬á
707.10. To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isnΓÇÖt cast and a copy of an activated ability isnΓÇÖt activated. A copy of a spell or ability copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including modes, targets, the value of X, and additional or alternative costs. (See rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells.ΓÇ¥) Choices that are normally made on resolution are not copied. If an effect of the copy refers to objects used to pay its costs, it uses the objects used to pay the costs of the original spell or ability. A copy of a spell is owned by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell or ability is controlled by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell is itself a spell, even though it has no spell card associated with it. A copy of an ability is itself an ability.
Example: A player casts Fork, targeting an Emerald Charm. Fork reads, ΓÇ£Copy target instant or sorcery spell, except that the copy is red. You may choose new targets for the copy.ΓÇ¥ Emerald Charm is a modal green instant. When the Fork resolves, it puts a copy of the Emerald Charm on the stack except the copy is red, not green. The copy has the same mode that was chosen for the original Emerald Charm. It does not necessarily have the same target, but only because Fork allows choosing of new targets.
Example: Fling is an instant that reads, ΓÇ£As an additional cost to cast this spell, sacrifice a creatureΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£Fling deals damage equal to the sacrificed creatureΓÇÖs power to any target.ΓÇ¥ When determining how much damage a copy of Fling deals, it checks the power of the creature sacrificed to pay for the original Fling.
Example: Dawnglow Infusion is a sorcery that reads, ΓÇ£You gain X life if {G} was spent to cast this spell and X life if {W} was spent to cast it.ΓÇ¥ Because mana isnΓÇÖt an object, a copy of Dawnglow Infusion wonΓÇÖt cause you to gain any life, no matter what mana was spent to cast the original spell.
┬á
707.10a If a copy of a spell is in a zone other than the stack, it ceases to exist. If a copy of a card is in any zone other than the stack or the battlefield, it ceases to exist. These are state-based actions. See rule 704.
┬á
707.10b A copy of an ability has the same source as the original ability. If the ability refers to its source by name, the copy refers to that same object and not to any other object with the same name. The copy is considered to be the same ability by effects that count how many times that ability has resolved during the turn.
┬á
707.10c Some effects copy a spell or ability and state that its controller may choose new targets for the copy. The player may leave any number of the targets unchanged, even if those targets would be illegal. If the player chooses to change some or all of the targets, the new targets must be legal. Once the player has decided what the copyΓÇÖs targets will be, the copy is put onto the stack with those targets.
┬á
707.10d Some effects copy a spell or ability for each player or object it ΓÇ£could target.ΓÇ¥ The copies are put onto the stack with those targets in the order of their controllerΓÇÖs choice. If the spell or ability has more than one target, each of its targets must be the same player or object. If that player or object isnΓÇÖt a legal target for each instance of the word ΓÇ£target,ΓÇ¥ a copy isnΓÇÖt created for that player or object.
┬á
707.10e Some effects copy a spell or ability and specify a new target for the copy. If the spell or ability has more than one target, each of the copyΓÇÖs targets must be that player or object. If that player or object isnΓÇÖt a legal target for each instance of the word ΓÇ£target,ΓÇ¥ the copy isnΓÇÖt created. In the case where a replacement effect causes the copy to target more than one object, the copyΓÇÖs controller chooses one of them to be the new target. The chosen target must be a legal target for that spell or ability.
Example: Frontline Heroism is an enchantment with the ability ΓÇ£Whenever you cast a spell that targets only a single creature you control, create a 1/1 red Soldier creature token with haste, then copy that spell. The copy targets that token.ΓÇ¥ Anointed Procession is an enchantment with the ability ΓÇ£If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, it creates twice that many of those tokens instead.ΓÇ¥ If you control both and cast Moment of Triumph targeting a creature you control, Frontline HeroismΓÇÖs ability triggers. As that ability resolves, you create two 1/1 red Soldier creature tokens with haste, then copy Moment of Triumph and the copy targets one of those tokens of your choice. The copy doesnΓÇÖt target both the tokens.
┬á
707.10f Some effects copy a permanent spell. As that copy resolves, it ceases being a copy of a spell and becomes a token permanent. (See rule 608.3f.)
┬á
707.10g If an effect creates a copy of a double-faced permanent spell, the copy is also a double-faced permanent spell that has both a front face and a back face. The characteristics of its front and back face are determined by the copiable values of the same face of the spell it is a copy of, as modified by any other copy effects. If the spell it is a copy of has its back face up, the copy is created with its back face up. The token thatΓÇÖs put onto the battlefield as that spell resolves is a double-faced token.
┬á
707.11. If an effect refers to a permanent by name, the effect still tracks that permanent even if it changes names or becomes a copy of something else.
Example: An Unstable Shapeshifter copies an Olivia Voldaren. Olivia Voldaren reads, ΓÇ£{1}{R}: Olivia Voldaren deals 1 damage to another target creature. That creature becomes a Vampire in addition to its other types. Put a +1/+1 counter on Olivia Voldaren.ΓÇ¥ If this ability of the Shapeshifter is activated, the Shapeshifter will deal 1 damage and you will put a +1/+1 counter on it, even if itΓÇÖs no longer a copy of Olivia Voldaren at that time.
┬á
707.12. An effect that instructs a player to cast a copy of an object (and not just copy a spell) follows the rules for casting spells, except that the copy is created in the same zone the object is in and then cast while another spell or ability is resolving. Casting a copy of an object follows steps 601.2aΓÇôh of rule 601, ΓÇ£Casting Spells,ΓÇ¥ and then the copy becomes cast. Once cast, the copy is a spell on the stack, and just like any other spell it can resolve or be countered.
┬á
707.12a An effect that creates multiple copies and says a player ΓÇ£may castΓÇ¥ those objects allows that player to choose individually, for each of those objects, whether or not to cast it.
┬á
707.13. One card (Garth One-Eye) instructs a player to create a copy of a card defined by name rather than by indicating an object to be copied. To do so, the player uses the Oracle card reference to determine the characteristics of the copy and creates the copy outside of the game.
┬á
707.14. One card (Magar of the Magic Strings) instructs a player to note the name of a particular card in a graveyard and create a copy of the card with the noted name. To do so, use the characteristics of that card as it last existed in the graveyard to determine the copiable values of the copy. (See rule 608.2h.)
┬á
708. Face-Down Spells and Permanents
┬á
708.1. Some cards allow spells and permanents to be face down.
┬á
708.2. Face-down spells and face-down permanents have no characteristics other than those listed by the ability or rules that allowed the spell or permanent to be face down. Any listed characteristics are the copiable values of that objectΓÇÖs characteristics. (See rule 613, ΓÇ£Interaction of Continuous Effects,ΓÇ¥ and rule 707, ΓÇ£Copying Objects.ΓÇ¥)
┬á
708.2a If a face-up permanent is turned face down by a spell or ability that doesnΓÇÖt list any characteristics for that object, it becomes a 2/2 face-down creature with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost. A permanent that enters the battlefield face down also has these characteristics unless otherwise specified by the effect that put it onto the battlefield face down or allowed it to be cast face down. These values are the copiable values of that objectΓÇÖs characteristics.
┬á
708.2b A face-down permanent canΓÇÖt be turned face down. If a spell or ability attempts to turn a face-down permanent face down, nothing happens and that effect doesnΓÇÖt change any of its characteristics or their copiable values.
┬á
708.3. Objects that are put onto the battlefield face down are turned face down before they enter the battlefield, so the permanentΓÇÖs enters-the-battlefield abilities wonΓÇÖt trigger (if triggered) or have any effect (if static).
┬á
708.4. Objects that are cast face down are turned face down before they are put onto the stack, so effects that care about the characteristics of a spell will see only the face-down spellΓÇÖs characteristics. Any effects or prohibitions that would apply to casting an object with these characteristics (and not the face-up objectΓÇÖs characteristics) are applied to casting this object. The permanent the spell becomes will be a face-down permanent.
┬á
708.5. At any time, you may look at a face-down spell you control on the stack or a face-down permanent you control (even if itΓÇÖs phased out). You canΓÇÖt look at face-down cards in any other zone or face-down spells or permanents controlled by another player.
┬á
708.6. If you control multiple face-down spells or face-down permanents, you must ensure at all times that your face-down spells and permanents can be easily differentiated from each other. This includes, but is not limited to, knowing what ability or rules caused the permanents to be face down, the order spells were cast, the order that face-down permanents entered the battlefield, which creature(s) attacked last turn, and any other differences between face-down spells or permanents. Common methods for distinguishing between face-down objects include using counters or dice to mark the different objects, or clearly placing those objects in order on the table.
┬á
708.7. The ability or rules that allow a permanent to be face down may also allow the permanentΓÇÖs controller to turn it face up. Spells normally canΓÇÖt be turned face up.
┬á
708.8. As a face-down permanent is turned face up, its copiable values revert to its normal copiable values. Any effects that have been applied to the face-down permanent still apply to the face-up permanent. Any abilities relating to the permanent entering the battlefield donΓÇÖt trigger and donΓÇÖt have any effect, because the permanent has already entered the battlefield.
┬á
708.9. If a face-down permanent or a face-down component of a merged permanent moves from the battlefield to any other zone, its owner must reveal it to all players as they move it. If a face-down spell moves from the stack to any zone other than the battlefield, its owner must reveal it to all players as they move it. If a player leaves the game, all face-down permanents, face-down components of merged permanents, and face-down spells owned by that player must be revealed to all players. At the end of each game, all face-down permanents, face-down components of merged permanents, and face-down spells must be revealed to all players.
┬á
708.10. If a face-down permanent becomes a copy of another permanent, its copiable values become the copiable values of that permanent, as modified by its face-down status. Its characteristics therefore remain the same: the characteristics listed by the ability or rules that allowed it to be turned face down. However, if it is turned face up, its copiable values become the values it copied from the other permanent. See rule 707.3.
┬á
708.11. If a face-down permanent would have an ΓÇ£As [this permanent] is turned face up . . .ΓÇ¥ ability after itΓÇÖs turned face up, that ability is applied while that permanent is being turned face up, not afterward.
┬á
708.12. If a spell or ability that instructs a player to reveal a face-down permanent needs information about the revealed object, it uses the characteristics of that object ignoring any continuous effects that may be applying to it.
┬á
709. Split Cards
┬á
709.1. Split cards have two card faces on a single card. The back of a split card is the normal Magic card back.
┬á
709.2. Although split cards have two castable halves, each split card is only one card. For example, a player who has drawn or discarded a split card has drawn or discarded one card, not two.
┬á
709.3. A player chooses which half of a split card they are casting before putting it onto the stack.
┬á
709.3a Only the chosen half is evaluated to see if it can be cast. Only that half is considered to be put onto the stack.
┬á
709.3b While on the stack, only the characteristics of the half being cast exist. The other halfΓÇÖs characteristics are treated as though they didnΓÇÖt exist.
┬á
709.3c An effect may create a copy of a split card and allow a player to cast the copy. That copy retains the characteristics of the two halves separated into the same two halves as the original card. (See rule 707.12.)
┬á
709.4. In every zone except the stack, the characteristics of a split card are those of its two halves combined.
┬á
709.4a Each split card has two names. If an effect instructs a player to choose a card name and the player wants to choose a split cardΓÇÖs name, the player must choose one of those names and not both. An object has the chosen name if one of its names is the chosen name.
┬á
709.4b The mana cost of a split card is the combined mana costs of its two halves. A split cardΓÇÖs colors and mana value are determined from its combined mana cost. An effect that refers specifically to the symbols in a split cardΓÇÖs mana cost sees the separate symbols rather than the whole mana cost.
Example: Assault//BatteryΓÇÖs mana cost is {3}{R}{G}. ItΓÇÖs a red and green card with a mana value of 5. If you cast Assault, the resulting spell is a red spell with a mana value of 1.
Example: Fire//IceΓÇÖs mana cost is {2}{U}{R}. It has the same mana cost as Steam Augury, but an effect such as that of Jegantha, the Wellspring sees that it contains the mana symbol {1} twice.
┬á
709.4c A split card has each card type specified on either of its halves and each ability in the text box of each half.
┬á
709.4d The characteristics of a fused split spell on the stack are also those of its two halves combined (see rule 702.102, ΓÇ£FuseΓÇ¥).
┬á
709.5. Some split cards are permanent cards with a single shared type line. A shared type line on such an object represents two static abilities that function on the battlefield. These are ΓÇ£As long as this permanent doesnΓÇÖt have the ΓÇÿleft half unlockedΓÇÖ designation, it doesnΓÇÖt have the name, mana cost, or rules text of this objectΓÇÖs left halfΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£As long as this permanent doesnΓÇÖt have the ΓÇÿright half unlockedΓÇÖ designation, it doesnΓÇÖt have the name, mana cost, or rules text of this objectΓÇÖs right half.ΓÇ¥ These abilities, as well as which half of that permanent a characteristic is in, are part of that objectΓÇÖs copiable values.
┬á
709.5a Each half of a split card with a shared type line shares the types and subtypes listed on that cardΓÇÖs shared type line.
┬á
709.5b The existence of each half of an object with a shared type line is part of that objectΓÇÖs copiable values, even if that object is a spell on the stack. This is an exception to rule 709.3b.
┬á
709.5c ΓÇ£Left half unlockedΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£right half unlockedΓÇ¥ are designations that a permanent on the battlefield can have. Together, they are called the unlocked designations. A particular half of a permanent is said to be ΓÇ£unlockedΓÇ¥ if it has the appropriate unlocked designation. Otherwise, that half is said to be ΓÇ£locked.ΓÇ¥
┬á
709.5d A permanent with a shared type line is given the ΓÇ£left half unlockedΓÇ¥ designation as it enters the battlefield if its left half was cast as a spell. It is given the ΓÇ£right half unlockedΓÇ¥ designation as it enters the battlefield if its right half was a cast as a spell. If itΓÇÖs entering the battlefield and neither half was cast as a spell, it enters with neither unlocked designation.
┬á
709.5e A player who controls a permanent that has one or more locked halves may pay the mana cost of a locked half of that permanent to give that permanent the appropriate unlocked designation. This cost is referred to as an ΓÇ£unlock cost.ΓÇ¥ This is a special action (see rule 116). A player can take this action any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn.
┬á
709.5f Some spells and abilities instruct a player to ΓÇ£unlockΓÇ¥ half of a permanent. To unlock half of a permanent, a player chooses a locked half of that permanent, and that permanent is given the appropriate unlocked designation.
┬á
709.5g Some spells and abilities instruct a player to ΓÇ£lockΓÇ¥ half of a permanent. To lock half of a permanent, a player chooses an unlocked half of that permanent, and that permanent loses the appropriate unlocked designation.
┬á
709.5h Some abilities trigger when a player unlocks a particular half of a permanent. These abilities trigger when that permanent is given the appropriate unlocked designation, regardless of whether it was given that designation while entering the battlefield or after entering the battlefield.
┬á
709.5i Some abilities trigger when a player ΓÇ£fully unlocksΓÇ¥ a permanent with a shared type line. Such an ability triggers when that permanent has one of the two unlocked designations and gets the other, or when it has neither designation and gains both.
